items.title: “Impressive level of openness”: Xiaomi goes way beyond the usual open-weight playbook with MiMo-V2.6
items.summary: New models are coming out thick and fast, almost on a weekly cadence, ranging from the powerful proprietary systems coming out of the major US AI labs to the more open alternatives being released by some of China’s biggest tech companies. On Tuesday alone, Anthropic debuted Claude Opus 5.5 , while OpenAI launched GPT-6 Sol and Luna , each accompanied by their the usual claims about how they outperform their rivals. Amidst all the hullabaloo of the frontier-model frenzy, however, Xiaomi also debuted MiMo-V2.6 , another powerful open model from one of China’s growing ranks of AI developers. All the initial headline numbers look pretty promising, too. The flagship MiMo-V2.6-Pro is a trillion-parameter model, with 42 billion parameters active at a time, a one-million-token context window, and support for text, images, audio and video. Broadly speaking, that puts it in the same frontier territory as the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic: GPT-6 Sol has a 1.05-million-token context window, while Claude Opus 5.5 has a one-million-token window, though neither company discloses comparable parameter counts. Xiaomi, for its part, makes broad claims of frontier-level performance across coding, agentic tasks, cybersecurity, multimodal work and research. Independent analysis lends some weight to those claims –Artificial Analysis gives MiMo-V2.6-Pro an Intelligence Index score of 46, ranking it first among the 114 large open-weight models it tracks. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index So far, so good. But arguably the bigger story in Xiaomi’s offering is the manner in which it trained the model, how much of that process it showed in public, and what it’s releasing afterward. A public record Xiaomi livestreamed its RL training through a public dashboard, exposing metrics from the production reinforcement-learning runs in real time over a five-day period starting on September 15. By the time the runs had finished, the dashboard showed costs of $854,044 for the smaller MiMo-V2.6-Flash model and $2,620,670 for Pro — about $3.5 million combined. Xiaomi livestreamed its RL runs over a 5-day period. It’s worth noting that this figure covers only the RL stage; Xiaomi hasn’t said what pretraining the models cost. Even so, public RL bills are rare. The closest precedents came last year, when MiniMax said the RL phase of its 456-billion-parameter MiniMax-M1 cost $534,700 in GPU rental, and DeepSeek put the RL training of its 671-billion-parameter R1 at $294,000 . Both were leading open reasoning models when they launched, though the comparison only goes so far: MiMo-V2.6-Pro is larger, and its RL run targeted longer, agentic tasks. Shortly after the stream began, Fuli Luo , who leads Xiaomi’s MiMo team after previously working at DeepSeek, took to X to explain the thinking behind the project. The team, she said, had spent almost six months exploring how far RL could be pushed, increasing the amount of training, the variety of environments and agent setups, and the resources used to grade the model’s attempts. “We’ll open-source the details piece by piece over the coming weeks,” she added. Nearly half a year of silence. We spent it studying one problem: how far RL can scale. MiMo-V2.6 is in the middle of its RL run right now. Three things we scaled: compute (~2B tokens per step, 1568 prompts × 16 rollouts, fully async), environments and harnesses (multi-task… — Fuli Luo (@_LuoFuli) September 16, 2026 Responding on X, Hugging Face co-founder and chief science officer Thomas Wolf called the move an “Impressive level of openness on such a large run.” However, what Xiaomi’s putting out alongside the finished models is arguably just as interesting. The company has released the model weights under the permissive MIT license, alongside its technical report and a 9-billion-parameter Qwen-based model , intended as a starting point for further agentic RL research. “Impressive level of openness on such a large run.” Xiaomi says it has also “fully open-sourced” a broader set of RL resources: more than 7,000 task environments spanning software engineering, vulnerability reproduction, knowledge work and web development; an end-to-end training framework covering everything from environment interaction to reward evaluation and policy optimization; and lightweight agent harnesses for experimenting with different tools, prompts and context setups. At the time of writing, however, Xiaomi’s link to the open-source collection on Hugging Face contain only the three model releases, with the 7,000-plus environments and other supporting resources not surfaced there. Luo had said earlier that Xiaomi would be open-sourcing the various elements “over the coming weeks.” As the results began arriving this week , attention in the research community quickly moved beyond the benchmark score to what Xiaomi had committed to releasing overall. Elie Bakouch , a former Hugging Face researcher who is now a research engineer at Prime Intellect, singled out the promised RL resources. “The most insane part, they will release ~7k RL training data and the framework leading to this top 6 model on AA,” Bakouch writes on X . “They also shipped the model + tech report less than 1 week after starting the final RL run.” Wolf went further, arguing that access to the environments in which models learn may now be especially valuable for open research, as more model development shifts toward RL with verifiable rewards ( RLVR ). Many “open” models amount largely to downloadable weights — essentially, the vast collection of numerical values a model learned during training, which can then be used to run or fine-tune it — while much of what went into producing them remains closed. Some companies have gone further in muddying those terms. Meta, for example, has often referred to its Llama models as open-source despite significant restrictions that have led open-source advocates to push back heavily on that description. And so MiMo-V2.6 goes further than most open-source releases. Independent analysis lends some weight to those claims –Artificial Analysis gives MiMo-V2.6-Pro an Intelligence Index score of 46, ranking it first among the 114 large open-weight models it tracks.

Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index



So far, so good. But arguably the bigger story in Xiaomi’s offering is the manner in which it trained the model, how much of that process it showed in public, and what it’s releasing afterward.

A public record

Xiaomi livestreamed its RL training through a public dashboard, exposing metrics from the production reinforcement-learning runs in real time over a five-day period starting on September 15. By the time the runs had finished, the dashboard showed costs of $854,044 for the smaller MiMo-V2.6-Flash model and $2,620,670 for Pro — about $3.5 million combined.

Xiaomi livestreamed its RL runs over a 5-day period.

It’s worth noting that this figure covers only the RL stage; Xiaomi hasn’t said what pretraining the models cost. Even so, public RL bills are rare. The closest precedents came last year, when MiniMax said the RL phase of its 456-billion-parameter MiniMax-M1 cost $534,700 in GPU rental, and DeepSeek put the RL training of its 671-billion-parameter R1 at $294,000. Both were leading open reasoning models when they launched, though the comparison only goes so far: MiMo-V2.6-Pro is larger, and its RL run targeted longer, agentic tasks.

Shortly after the stream began, Fuli Luo, who leads Xiaomi’s MiMo team after previously working at DeepSeek, took to X to explain the thinking behind the project. The team, she said, had spent almost six months exploring how far RL could be pushed, increasing the amount of training, the variety of environments and agent setups, and the resources used to grade the model’s attempts.

“We’ll open-source the details piece by piece over the coming weeks,” she added.

Nearly half a year of silence. We spent it studying one problem: how far RL can scale.

MiMo-V2.6 is in the middle of its RL run right now. Three things we scaled: compute (~2B tokens per step, 1568 prompts × 16 rollouts, fully async), environments and harnesses (multi-task…

— Fuli Luo (@_LuoFuli) September 16, 2026

Responding on X, Hugging Face co-founder and chief science officer Thomas Wolf called the move an “Impressive level of openness on such a large run.”

However, what Xiaomi’s putting out alongside the finished models is arguably just as interesting. The company has released the model weights under the permissive MIT license, alongside its technical report and a 9-billion-parameter Qwen-based model, intended as a starting point for further agentic RL research.

“Impressive level of openness on such a large run.”

Xiaomi says it has also “fully open-sourced” a broader set of RL resources: more than 7,000 task environments spanning software engineering, vulnerability reproduction, knowledge work and web development; an end-to-end training framework covering everything from environment interaction to reward evaluation and policy optimization; and lightweight agent harnesses for experimenting with different tools, prompts and context setups. At the time of writing, however, Xiaomi’s link to the open-source collection on Hugging Face contain only the three model releases, with the 7,000-plus environments and other supporting resources not surfaced there. Luo had said earlier that Xiaomi would be open-sourcing the various elements “over the coming weeks.”

As the results began arriving this week, attention in the research community quickly moved beyond the benchmark score to what Xiaomi had committed to releasing overall. Elie Bakouch, a former Hugging Face researcher who is now a research engineer at Prime Intellect, singled out the promised RL resources.

“The most insane part, they will release ~7k RL training data and the framework leading to this top 6 model on AA,” Bakouch writes on X. “They also shipped the model + tech report less than 1 week after starting the final RL run.”

Wolf went further, arguing that access to the environments in which models learn may now be especially valuable for open research, as more model development shifts toward RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Because RLVR depends on tasks whose outcomes can be automatically checked — whether code passes a test, for example — the environments themselves become a crucial ingredient in training.

“Releasing many high quality open-source RL environments is the most impactful thing anyone can do to push the open-source frontier right now.”

“Releasing many high quality open-source RL environments is the most impactful thing anyone can do to push the open-source frontier right now,” Wolf writes. “The equivalent of sharing high quality pretraining data, but in the new RLVR paradigm.”

Open-weight vs open-source

So while the benchmarks around Xiaomi’s latest model are notable in their own right, it’s the company’s approach that is generating much of the fanfare so far.

Indeed, MiMo-V2.6 serves as a useful example of a distinction that often gets muddied in the AI sphere: “open-weight” and “open-source” are routinely used as though they mean the same thing, but they don’t. Many “open” models amount largely to downloadable weights — essentially, the vast collection of numerical values a model learned during training, which can then be used to run or fine-tune it — while much of what went into producing them remains closed.

Some companies have gone further in muddying those terms. Meta, for example, has often referred to its Llama models as open-source despite significant restrictions that have led open-source advocates to push back heavily on that description.

And so MiMo-V2.6 goes further than most open-source releases. Its MIT license carries none of the conditions that the likes of Moonshot’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max attach for large commercial users. And if the environments are released as promised, outside researchers will have much more of the post-training process to inspect and build on.

items.title: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
items.summary: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting Google has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a feature Google calls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting. “AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, last August . In May, the company said more AI is coming .

items.title: Where should NZ stand on global AI risk? 3 principles to guide a stronger strategy
items.summary: Getty Images If some current warnings are to be believed, artificial intelligence may be the human invention that outwits its creators. Understandably, there are now global calls to regulate the technology. At the current gathering of the United Nations General Assembly, 20 nations (including Australia and Canada) are calling for increased oversight of advanced AI systems. New Zealand – along with the United States and China, which dominate the global AI industry – did not join the initiative. According to the MIT AI Risk Initiative , incidents of concern are on the rise rapidly. Overall, the global AI industry is raising profound questions about ethics, economy, equity and security. While there is disagreement between those warning of a potential doomsday scenario and others who take a more benign view of AI’s likely trajectory, investment in the industry is forecast to exceed US$1 trillion this year . Little wonder the preliminary report of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI found “the gap between rapidly improving capabilities and effective risk management methods may lead to catastrophic outcomes”. At the same time, the claimed economic benefits of AI often take precedence. Fearing losing the advantage to China, US President Donald Trump has called safety fears a “ hoax ” and rejected calls for global regulation. New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has argued the opportunities still outweigh the risks. If there are concerns, he says, they are best dealt with in concert with “like-minded friends”. This optimism is reflected in the government’s “‘ light touch approach ” to regulation which avoids new laws. (It might also explain New Zealand ranking 32nd out of 45 high-income countries in the Global Index on Responsible AI .) Conversely, the Labour opposition has promised to establish an Office of AI within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet to coordinate policy across government. It would work with Australia to align regional standards on safety and security. Neither approach really addresses the kind of existential risk now being discussed globally. To do that, New Zealand could set three goals, each anchored in established international precedent. Advocate for a precautionary approach Like most OECD countries, a precautionary principle guides New Zealand policy making: when reputable sources suggest there is risk associated with a lack of action, taking preventive measures against potential harm is justified. Scientific uncertainty or the lack of immediately obvious negative impacts should warrant an amber light, not a green one. The burden of proof should be on those developing a new technology to demonstrate it is safe through mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation. If there is reasonable doubt, pausing development until a technology is shown to be safe should be the default position. Scientific diplomacy The UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI lacks the comprehensive governmental buy-in necessary to move international policy forward at pace and scale. A different model, akin to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ), would allow for more coordinated scientific advice, and be larger and more inclusive. As with climate change, only authoritative, transparent data and shared understanding of the risks around unchecked AI development offer a real chance of building political agreement. Prioritise the greatest risks New frameworks can be built in all areas of concern, from ethics to equity. But the highest priority should be those associated with the greatest risk: war and conflict, biological hazards and global financial systems. Pathways to achieve this already exist – for example, the UN resolution adopted last year addressing the “possible risks of the integration of artificial intelligence into command, control and communications systems of nuclear weapons”. New Zealand foreign policy could also advocate for the positive use of AI to improve verification of the existing Biological Weapons Convention, as part of the necessary new protocol required to ensure its efficacy. Similarly, there is an opportunity in November to seek a binding protocol on meaningful human control, accountability and compliance with the laws of war and conventional weapons when the UN meets to review the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in November. International laws and protocols for dealing with cyber-attacks involving AI – which could potentially trigger wars – also need urgent attention. Finally, at a time when war games and military exercises risk spiralling out of control , New Zealand can encourage confidence-building measures to de-escalate conflicts between geopolitical adversaries. Here, too, there is emerging precedent: US and Chinese officials only recently proposed a new mechanism for sharing information about serious AI threats. Such developments should be welcomed as a positive first step. items.title: Google Gemini Enterprise Connects With Linear for AI-Assisted Issue Workflows
items.summary: Google Gemini Enterprise now has an official connector for Linear, bringing issue and project data into Gemini for AI-assisted work . The integration lets authorized users search, summarize and analyze Linear information, as well as create new issues or pull data from existing issues and projects without leaving the Gemini interface. For teams that use Linear to plan and track product work, this creates a natural-language route to information that might otherwise require manual filtering, searching and status review. The capability is documented in Google Cloud's official Linear connector configuration guide and on Linear's Gemini Enterprise integration page. It is a Gemini Enterprise integration, not a general announcement that every Gemini user can access Linear data automatically. Access depends on an organization configuring the connector and authorizing it through Linear. A request such as asking Gemini to show high-priority issues assigned to a user illustrates the intended interaction. Rather than navigating through issue views first, a user can ask Gemini to retrieve relevant Linear data. The value is not that Gemini replaces Linear's project-management functions. It is that Linear information can become part of a broader Gemini Enterprise workflow spanning connected work applications. How the Gemini Enterprise Linear connector works The connector uses OAuth. Google Cloud's setup process requires an administrator or authorized implementer to create a Linear OAuth application , obtain client credentials and configure a Linear data store in Gemini Enterprise. That configuration establishes the connection Gemini Enterprise needs to work with Linear data. This is an important practical distinction. The integration is not simply a consumer app toggle. Organizations need to complete a technical setup process and decide who can use the connected data. Teams should also test the connector against their existing Linear projects and issue conventions before treating Gemini responses as an operational shortcut. Once configured, the documented capabilities include: Searching Linear data from Gemini Enterprise . Summarizing and analyzing information across connected work applications. Pulling data from existing Linear issues and projects. Creating new Linear issues without leaving Gemini. Linear's integration page positions the connection within Gemini Enterprise's wider ability to work across business applications. That matters because project questions are often not isolated. A manager may need to connect issue status with planning context, documentation or other work information available through their organization's Gemini Enterprise environment. What this changes for Linear users For a team already working in Linear, the most immediate change is conversational access to issue and project information. Users can frame questions around priorities, assignments or project context instead of beginning with a manual search. The example of retrieving high-priority assigned issues is useful because it is a common status-checking task that can be expressed clearly in natural language. The integration can also reduce context switching when Gemini Enterprise is already being used as a work assistant. Creating an issue from within Gemini may be useful when a discussion, summary or analysis reveals a follow-up task. Pulling in an existing project or issue can similarly keep a question and its relevant work-tracking context together. That said, the supplied documentation does not define the full range of supported prompts, the quality of summaries, permission behavior in every deployment or the exact actions available beyond the documented examples. Businesses should validate the connector with representative projects and workflows, especially where issue labels, priorities and ownership conventions are central to reporting. Rollout and pricing questions The official material confirms that the Linear connector exists for Gemini Enterprise and provides a configuration path. It does not provide pricing for the connector in the supplied research. It also does not establish that the integration is included with every Gemini offering, including consumer Gemini products. For buyers and administrators, the relevant next step is to check their Gemini Enterprise plan and implementation requirements, then assess whether the connector fits the team's current use of Linear. The connector setup itself requires Linear OAuth credentials and Gemini Enterprise data-store configuration, so implementation effort is part of the practical decision. The research also supports a broader conclusion: Linear is part of Gemini Enterprise's expanding connector ecosystem. However, it does not provide verified details needed to compare this Linear integration with Airtable, Monday.com or Webflow integrations . A feature-by-feature comparison would therefore risk overstating what is known. For businesses, the opportunity is to turn routine project-status questions and issue creation into connected AI-assisted tasks rather than another destination users must open and manage separately. The payoff depends on thoughtful setup, clean Linear data and workflows where Gemini can reliably help people find or create the right work item. If you want to connect AI tools to the systems your team already relies on, Scalevise's AI workflow automation service can help design practical, reliable workflows that reduce manual handoffs and fit daily operations. Discuss an AI automation project with Scalevise. Frequently Asked Questions What is the Gemini Enterprise Linear integration? It is an official connector that lets Gemini Enterprise work with Linear data. Users can search, summarize and analyze Linear information, pull data from issues and projects, and create new Linear issues from Gemini. Can Gemini Enterprise show my high-priority Linear issues? The documented integration supports searching Linear data from Gemini Enterprise. Asking for high-priority issues assigned to a user is an example of the type of natural-language request the integration is designed to support. What is required to set up the Linear connector? The Google Cloud configuration guide requires creating a Linear OAuth application, obtaining client credentials and configuring a Linear data store in Gemini Enterprise. Is the Linear integration available in all Gemini products? The supplied official documentation describes the connector for Gemini Enterprise. It does not confirm availability in every Gemini product or plan. How much does the Gemini Enterprise Linear connector cost? The supplied research does not state separate pricing for the Linear connector. Organizations should check their Gemini Enterprise plan details and implementation requirements. Conclusion The Gemini Enterprise and Linear connection is a confirmed integration that brings issue and project data into Gemini's AI-assisted workspace. Its practical value is conversational access to Linear information and the ability to create issues within the same interface. Google Gemini Enterprise now has an official connector for Linear, bringing issue and project data into Gemini for AI-assisted work. The integration lets authorized users search, summarize and analyze Linear information, as well as create new issues or pull data from existing issues and projects without leaving the Gemini interface. For teams that use Linear to plan and track product work, this creates a natural-language route to information that might otherwise require manual filtering, searching and status review.

The capability is documented in Google Cloud's official Linear connector configuration guide and on Linear's Gemini Enterprise integration page. It is a Gemini Enterprise integration, not a general announcement that every Gemini user can access Linear data automatically. Access depends on an organization configuring the connector and authorizing it through Linear.

A request such as asking Gemini to show high-priority issues assigned to a user illustrates the intended interaction. Rather than navigating through issue views first, a user can ask Gemini to retrieve relevant Linear data. The value is not that Gemini replaces Linear's project-management functions. It is that Linear information can become part of a broader Gemini Enterprise workflow spanning connected work applications.

How the Gemini Enterprise Linear connector works

The connector uses OAuth. Google Cloud's setup process requires an administrator or authorized implementer to create a Linear OAuth application, obtain client credentials and configure a Linear data store in Gemini Enterprise. That configuration establishes the connection Gemini Enterprise needs to work with Linear data.

This is an important practical distinction. The integration is not simply a consumer app toggle. Organizations need to complete a technical setup process and decide who can use the connected data. Teams should also test the connector against their existing Linear projects and issue conventions before treating Gemini responses as an operational shortcut.

Once configured, the documented capabilities include:

  • Searching Linear data from Gemini Enterprise.
  • Summarizing and analyzing information across connected work applications.
  • Pulling data from existing Linear issues and projects.
  • Creating new Linear issues without leaving Gemini.

Linear's integration page positions the connection within Gemini Enterprise's wider ability to work across business applications. That matters because project questions are often not isolated. A manager may need to connect issue status with planning context, documentation or other work information available through their organization's Gemini Enterprise environment.

What this changes for Linear users

For a team already working in Linear, the most immediate change is conversational access to issue and project information. Users can frame questions around priorities, assignments or project context instead of beginning with a manual search. The example of retrieving high-priority assigned issues is useful because it is a common status-checking task that can be expressed clearly in natural language.

The integration can also reduce context switching when Gemini Enterprise is already being used as a work assistant. Creating an issue from within Gemini may be useful when a discussion, summary or analysis reveals a follow-up task. Pulling in an existing project or issue can similarly keep a question and its relevant work-tracking context together.

That said, the supplied documentation does not define the full range of supported prompts, the quality of summaries, permission behavior in every deployment or the exact actions available beyond the documented examples. Businesses should validate the connector with representative projects and workflows, especially where issue labels, priorities and ownership conventions are central to reporting.

Rollout and pricing questions

The official material confirms that the Linear connector exists for Gemini Enterprise and provides a configuration path. It does not provide pricing for the connector in the supplied research. It also does not establish that the integration is included with every Gemini offering, including consumer Gemini products.

For buyers and administrators, the relevant next step is to check their Gemini Enterprise plan and implementation requirements, then assess whether the connector fits the team's current use of Linear. The connector setup itself requires Linear OAuth credentials and Gemini Enterprise data-store configuration, so implementation effort is part of the practical decision.

The research also supports a broader conclusion: Linear is part of Gemini Enterprise's expanding connector ecosystem. However, it does not provide verified details needed to compare this Linear integration with Airtable, Monday.com or Webflow integrations. A feature-by-feature comparison would therefore risk overstating what is known.

For businesses, the opportunity is to turn routine project-status questions and issue creation into connected AI-assisted tasks rather than another destination users must open and manage separately. The payoff depends on thoughtful setup, clean Linear data and workflows where Gemini can reliably help people find or create the right work item. If you want to connect AI tools to the systems your team already relies on, Scalevise's AI workflow automation service can help design practical, reliable workflows that reduce manual handoffs and fit daily operations. Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Gemini Enterprise Linear integration?

It is an official connector that lets Gemini Enterprise work with Linear data. Users can search, summarize and analyze Linear information, pull data from issues and projects, and create new Linear issues from Gemini.

Can Gemini Enterprise show my high-priority Linear issues?

The documented integration supports searching Linear data from Gemini Enterprise. Asking for high-priority issues assigned to a user is an example of the type of natural-language request the integration is designed to support.

What is required to set up the Linear connector?

The Google Cloud configuration guide requires creating a Linear OAuth application, obtaining client credentials and configuring a Linear data store in Gemini Enterprise.

Is the Linear integration available in all Gemini products?

The supplied official documentation describes the connector for Gemini Enterprise. It does not confirm availability in every Gemini product or plan.

How much does the Gemini Enterprise Linear connector cost?

The supplied research does not state separate pricing for the Linear connector. Organizations should check their Gemini Enterprise plan details and implementation requirements.

Conclusion

The Gemini Enterprise and Linear connection is a confirmed integration that brings issue and project data into Gemini's AI-assisted workspace. Its practical value is conversational access to Linear information and the ability to create issues within the same interface. Organizations considering it should focus on connector setup, authorized access and testing against their real project workflows before relying on it for routine work management.

items.title: YouTube promises custom feeds and a lot more AI later this year
items.summary: The annual Made on YouTube event has just wrapped up, offering an early look at the features you can expect to come to Google's dominant online streaming platform in the coming months. Yes, there's plenty of AI for both viewers and creators, but there's also a handful of non-AI updates mixed in there, too. The design of YouTube's homepage feed comes under fire often, but the platform is preparing to give you more options. With Custom Feeds, you'll be able to add new tabs to the YouTube interface with content of your choice. To create a feed, just type a description and let YouTube populate the page. You can refine your description and rate video suggestions to tune the Custom Feed. Google says you'll be able to save "multiple" feeds without specifying the exact number. This feature will roll out soon in the US for web, mobile, and TV users. Interacting on YouTube will also change later this year. The platform will finally add the option to post GIFs in comments, which has apparently been a common request for some time. The comment box will let you search for popular animated thumbnails and post them on both regular videos and YouTube Shorts. The YouTube direct messaging feature is also adding support for group chat, but it's only going to be available in the US, UK, Singapore, Brazil, and some European countries to start. Read full article Comments

items.title: What is an AI Agent Harness?
items.summary: An AI agent harness is the software environment that surrounds an LLM to give it the tools and context needed to complete multi-step tasks. It turns your basic LLM calls to an operational system executing real world task. The model reasons through a prompt and decides the actions. The harness connects the agent it to the tools, systems, memory and execution environments needed to carry out those actions. In a AI harness Agents typically run in a loop: an LLM decides what to do, a tool executes, a model evaluates the results and then continues in that loop until the task is complete. Model(Reason)+ Harness(Action)= Agent (Output) Or Model (Brain) Agent (as the Body) and Harness as the hands/tools the body uses to finish a given task. You get the picture. The reason - act - observe loop This is at the core of many AI agents. Understanding this loop is critical to understanding how a harness works. Reason- The model reads everything in its context, including the task, relevant memory and previous results, then decides what action to take next. Act - The harness carries out that action by running a tool, executing code in a sandbox, calling an API or writing to storage. Observe- The harness captures the result and feeds it back to the model as new context. Repeat - The model uses that result to decide what to do next. The loop continues until the task is complete. " , " input_schema " : { " type " : " object " , " properties " : { " utc_offset_hours " : { " type " : " number " , " description " : " Hours offset from UTC, e.g. -8 for US Pacific. Defaults to 0 (UTC). " , } }, " required " : [], }, }, { " name " : " word_count " , " description " : " Count words and characters in a piece of text. " , " input_schema " : { " type " : " object " , " properties " : { " text " : { " type " : " string " , " description " : " The text to analyze. " } }, " required " : [ " text " ], }, }, { " name " : " read_local_file " , " description " : ( " Read the contents of a text file from the local working directory. " ), " input_schema " : { " type " : " object " , " properties " : { " filename " : { " type " : " string " , " description " : " Name of the file to read. " } }, " required " : [ " filename " ], }, }, ] Step 2 - Define the Tools methods def tool_calculator ( expression : str ) -> dict [ str , Any ]: try : tree = ast . parse ( expression , mode = " eval " ) result = _safe_eval ( tree . body ) return { " result " : result } except Exception as e : return { " error " : f " Could not evaluate expression: { e } " } def tool_get_current_time ( utc_offset_hours : float = 0 ) -> dict [ str , Any ]: now = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) if utc_offset_hours : from datetime import timedelta now = now + timedelta ( hours = utc_offset_hours ) return { " iso_timestamp " : now . isoformat (), " utc_offset_hours " : utc_offset_hours } def tool_word_count ( text : str ) -> dict [ str , Any ]: words = text . split () return { " word_count " : len ( words ), " character_count " : len ( text )} Step 3 - System Prompt self . system_prompt = system_prompt or ( " You are a helpful assistant with access to tools. " " Use tools whenever they would give a more accurate or reliable answer " " than reasoning alone (e.g. always use the calculator for arithmetic). An AI agent harness is the software environment that surrounds an LLM to give it the tools and context needed to complete multi-step tasks.
It turns your basic LLM calls to an operational system executing real world task.

The model reasons through a prompt and decides the actions.
The harness connects the agent it to the tools, systems, memory and execution environments needed to carry out those actions.

In a AI harness Agents typically run in a loop: an LLM decides what to do, a tool executes, a model evaluates the results and then continues in that loop until the task is complete.

Model(Reason)+ Harness(Action)= Agent (Output)
Or
Model (Brain)
Agent (as the Body)
and Harness as the hands/tools the body uses to finish a given task.
You get the picture.

The reason - act - observe loop
This is at the core of many AI agents. Understanding this loop is critical to understanding how a harness works.

Reason- The model reads everything in its context, including the task, relevant memory and previous results, then decides what action to take next.
Act - The harness carries out that action by running a tool, executing code in a sandbox, calling an API or writing to storage.
Observe- The harness captures the result and feeds it back to the model as new context.
Repeat - The model uses that result to decide what to do next. The loop continues until the task is complete.
The ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models- is published in this paper and is an excellent read.

Ok enough of "simile", let's jump to a concrete example

Let's say we have a file in our local system "sales and vendor commission.txt" and we want to perform complex and kind of weird calculation on this.
This is your final prompt -

"I have a text file called 'sales and commission.txt' in the current directory -
if it exists, extract the column with header 'Sales Person Name' , calculate it's word count.
Also, if the word count is > 20 calculate the vendor commission which is 15% of column header Sales or if the word count is < 20 calculate the vendor commission which is 10% of column header Sales
and create a new column call it vendor commission, and also get the current UTC Time and add it to report against each row"

*for the sake of an example let's say you create a Python code to do it (there are multiple way you could do it like upload the sheet into a Agent etc).

*Step 1 - Define the Tools your AGENT will have access to *

TOOLS: list[dict[str, Any]] = [
    {
        "name": "calculator",
        "description": (
            "Evaluate a basic arithmetic expression (+, -, *, /, **, %, parentheses). "
            "Use this for any math instead of computing it yourself."
        ),
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "expression": {
                    "type": "string",
                    "description": "The arithmetic expression to evaluate, e.g. '(12.5/100) * 842'",
                }
            },
            "required": ["expression"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "get_current_time",
        "description": "Get the current date and time, optionally offset by a UTC offset in hours.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "utc_offset_hours": {
                    "type": "number",
                    "description": "Hours offset from UTC, e.g. -8 for US Pacific. Defaults to 0 (UTC).",
                }
            },
            "required": [],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "word_count",
        "description": "Count words and characters in a piece of text.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "text": {"type": "string", "description": "The text to analyze."}
            },
            "required": ["text"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "read_local_file",
        "description": (
            "Read the contents of a text file from the local working directory. "
            "Paths are restricted to the sandbox directory for safety."
        ),
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "filename": {"type": "string", "description": "Name of the file to read."}
            },
            "required": ["filename"],
        },
    },
]

Step 2 - Define the Tools methods

def tool_calculator(expression: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
     try:
         tree = ast.parse(expression, mode="eval")
         result = _safe_eval(tree.body)
         return {"result": result}
     except Exception as e:

     now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
     if utc_offset_hours:
         from datetime import timedelta
         now = now + timedelta(hours=utc_offset_hours)
     return {"iso_timestamp": now.isoformat(), "utc_offset_hours": utc_offset_hours}


 def tool_word_count(text: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
     words = text.split()
    return {"word_count": len(words), "character_count": len(text)}

Step 3 - System Prompt

 self.system_prompt = system_prompt or (
            "You are a helpful assistant with access to tools. "
            "Use tools whenever they would give a more accurate or reliable answer "
            "than reasoning alone (e.g. always use the calculator for arithmetic). "
            "Once you have everything you need, give a clear, direct final answer."
        )

Step 4 - This is the heart of the whole logic, Use the stop_reason to check if the Agent is done is the reason is tool_use then keep going in a loop

if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":

items.title: A third option is emerging in the fight over AI and your data
items.summary: Not your keys, not your coins. Not your model, not your data? Over the summer, the tech industry was consumed by a debate about AI use in the enterprise and the need to protect IP. If an enterprise used proprietary models, was data leakage a necessary evil? Companies seemed to have two options: They could use state-of-the-art, proprietary models and risk losing control of their data, or they could use open-weight models and never kiss the frontier. Thankfully, a third option is emerging. Consider the concern: Company A wants to use LLM B from AI Lab C, and they want to avoid training AI Lab C how to eat Company A’s lunch by building its capabilities into LLM B. A good way to resolve the tension would be to let Company A run LLM B on its own infrastructure, so there’s no risk of its information fleeing on the wind. AI agents are “creating a whole different set of requirements at the data layer.” –Vast Data co-founder Jeff Denworth But that raises another problem: AI Lab C doesn’t want to allow Company A to run LLM B on its own GPUs because it doesn’t want to hand over its model weights. It’s the same IP issue the company ran into, in reverse. You have to solve the trust problem in both directions! Enter VAST Data co-founder Jeff Denworth and a new product called DataEnclave , which aims to let AI labs and enterprise-scale companies deploy proprietary models in secure compute environments without risking data transfer in either direction. (DataEnclave uses Nvidia’s Confidential Computing technology to make the system tick; Vast Data’s core product is AI OS, infrastructure that fits beneath a company’s AI applications.) The New Stack had Denworth on the podcast to chat about the confidential computing market. I was curious about timing. Why did Vast build DataEnclave now? Nvidia began rolling out Confidential Computing in a serious way in 2024, after all. Denworth argues that the market needed the core technology, yes, but also demand. And until late 2025, AI demand was modest compared to today’s token totals. Once agentic coding tools took off, corporate demand for AI products soared. This led to the pricing crisis we saw in early 2026, and the secure AI usage debate we endured over the summer. Performance drove demand, demand drove usage, and usage dug up fresh problems to solve. Now the question for the market is whether or not DataEnclave has solved enough concerns on both sides of the proprietary AI-proprietary data equation. The market will sort that out as it moves through early access and into general availability. Our conversation goes deep into the arc of AI, where companies are in their AI journey today, and how much data remains to be unlocked inside the enterprise. If you want to feel the acceleration, it’s a fun one!

items.title: Rethinking Intent Routing: From TF-IDF to Fine-Tuned Transformers
items.summary: A practical experiment in routing enterprise chatbot queries across APIs, LLM + RAG, and an explicit out-of-domain class — and in learning not to trust a pretty accuracy number too quickly. Source: Image generated with AI. One chatbot. Three execution paths. The router decides where the question should go before anything tries to answer it. Code, experiments, and evaluation artifacts: github.com/CamiloMedina28/Intelligent-query-router One Chatbot, Different Ways to Answer When building an enterprise chatbot, it is tempting to treat every user message the same way: send it to a language model and let the model figure it out. Convenient? Yes. Always the right architecture? Not really. Consider two requests that could reach the same interface: “What are the currently active massive incidents?” “Explain the root cause of incident INC123456.” They look similar because both are written in natural language and both belong to the same operational domain. But they require very different execution paths. The first is a structured-data problem: an API can retrieve the answer directly. The second requires context — ticket notes, history, or related documents — and is better handled by an LLM backed by retrieval. That made the first problem for the chatbot surprisingly simple to state: not “What is the answer?”, but “Which component should be responsible for answering this?” Source: Image by the author. The router has three destinations: API, LLM, and UNDETERMINED. API covers deterministic or structured operations. LLM covers requests that need retrieval and interpretation. About 3.6 million parameters became trainable, together with the classification head. Accuracy improved to 95.58% and Macro F1 to 0.9556. Better than the frozen encoder, still slightly worse than TF-IDF. Partial adaptation was moving in the right direction, but the baseline was still sitting there, being inconvenient. Full-fine tuning architecture This was the first neural configuration to clearly beat the baseline: 98.04% accuracy and 0.9804 Macro F1. I am deliberately not turning this into a claim that full fine-tuning is universally better for intent routing. The narrower statement is the useful one: for this dataset, this base model, and this routing task, full fine-tuning performed best among the four approaches tested. Real input quickly disagreed. Instead of keeping the classifier binary and inventing a rule such as if confidence < threshold: reject, the current design teaches the model a third class directly. The architectural motivation is enough: the system needed a way to learn “neither.” What I Learned Building the Router A baseline should be capable of ruining your favorite idea TF-IDF was not there to lose politely. It beat both the frozen encoder and partial fine-tuning. That made the final result more meaningful because full fine-tuning had to outperform something genuinely competitive. A Transformer is not a performance guarantee The frozen encoder was semantically richer and empirically worse. Partial adaptation helped. Full adaptation helped more. The experiment shows an association between more domain adaptation and better performance here; it does not prove a universal law or isolate the exact causal mechanism. Accuracy is the start of evaluation, not the end The 98.04% score was useful, but the audit and failure analysis were more informative. They exposed train-test redundancy, contradictory labels, noisy language, and highly confident mistakes — none of which is visible in a single headline metric. Routing is a systems problem wearing an NLP hat A wrong prediction is not merely a wrong label. It selects the wrong execution path: the wrong retrieval strategy, the wrong tool, or the wrong subsystem. That is why routing quality has to be evaluated in architectural terms, not only classifier terms. Final Thoughts Could I build this router differently today? Of course. An LLM can classify intents directly. Embedding-based routers can reduce custom training. Agent and tool-orchestration frameworks can move routing into a higher-level abstraction. Managed services can make most of this disappear behind an API. If the only goal were the shortest path to a production prototype, I might choose one of those options. But the important result of this project was not finding the shortest path. Building the router step by step forced me to understand what the abstractions hide: how labels encode architecture decisions, why a baseline matters, what frozen representations can and cannot do, what fine-tuning actually changes, how a test split can flatter a model, and why a probability of 0.99 can still be wrong. items.summary_html:
A practical experiment in routing enterprise chatbot queries across APIs, LLM + RAG, and an explicit out-of-domain class — and in learning not to trust a pretty accuracy number too quickly.Source: Image generated with AI. One chatbot. Three execution paths. The router decides where the question should go before anything tries to answer it.

Code, experiments, and evaluation artifacts: github.com/CamiloMedina28/Intelligent-query-router

One Chatbot, Different Ways to Answer

When building an enterprise chatbot, it is tempting to treat every user message the same way: send it to a language model and let the model figure it out. Convenient? Yes. Always the right architecture? Not really.

Consider two requests that could reach the same interface:

“What are the currently active massive incidents?”

“Explain the root cause of incident INC123456.”

They look similar because both are written in natural language and both belong to the same operational domain. But they require very different execution paths. The first is a structured-data problem: an API can retrieve the answer directly. The second requires context — ticket notes, history, or related documents — and is better handled by an LLM backed by retrieval.

That made the first problem for the chatbot surprisingly simple to state: not “What is the answer?”, but “Which component should be responsible for answering this?”

Source: Image by the author.

The router has three destinations: API, LLM, and UNDETERMINED. API covers deterministic or structured operations. LLM covers requests that need retrieval and interpretation. UNDETERMINED represents queries that do not reliably belong to either supported domain.

That third class matters. The earliest version was binary: every query had to become either API or LLM, even when neither made sense. Eventually UNDETERMINED became a learned class rather than a confidence-threshold fallback. In the current model, the classifier produces three logits, applies softmax, and takes the argmax. No extra threshold is involved.

A Real Dataset, with Real Constraints

The dataset comes from real enterprise queries. That made it useful — and impossible to publish. The raw questions can contain internal terminology, customer references, ticket identifiers, and operational context covered by strict confidentiality agreements. Every example in this article is therefore synthetic or anonymized while preserving the original routing intent.

The final dataset contains 9,189 queries, balanced across the three classes: 3,063 for LLM, 3,063 for API, and 3,063 for UNDETERMINED. The split used for the experiments was 6,432 training examples, 1,378 validation examples, and 1,379 test examples.

Source: Image by the author.

Because the classes are balanced, accuracy is easy to interpret and Macro F1 remains useful because it gives each route equal weight. More importantly, all four models were evaluated on the same test split, which makes the relative comparison meaningful.

From TF-IDF to Full Fine-Tuning

I did not start with the largest model I could fine-tune. I started with a baseline strong enough to be annoying.

TF-IDF + Logistic regression

The first experiment used TF-IDF with unigrams and bigrams, followed by multiclass Logistic Regression. It is simple, fast, interpretable, and particularly good at exploiting recurring domain phrases such as “active incidents” or “root cause.”

Source: Image by the author. TF-IDF + Logistic Regression architecture

The baseline reached 96.01% accuracy and a Macro F1 of 0.9601. That number changed the rest of the experiment: any Transformer now had to beat something that was cheap and already very good.

Frozen MiniLM

Next, TF-IDF was replaced by paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2. Each query became a dense 384-dimensional representation, while a small MLP learned the three routing classes. The encoder itself stayed frozen.

The result: 94.78% accuracy. The Transformer arrived and promptly lost to TF-IDF. Not exactly the dramatic entrance one expects from 2020s NLP.

The lesson was useful: pretrained semantic representations are richer, but richer does not automatically mean better for a specific decision boundary.

Source: Image by the author. frozen encoder and trainable linear head architecturePartial Fine-Tuning

The next step unfroze the final two Transformer blocks while keeping the rest of the encoder fixed. About 3.6 million parameters became trainable, together with the classification head.

Accuracy improved to 95.58% and Macro F1 to 0.9556. Better than the frozen encoder, still slightly worse than TF-IDF. Partial adaptation was moving in the right direction, but the baseline was still sitting there, being inconvenient.

Full Fine-Tuning

Finally, the entire MiniLM encoder was allowed to adapt to the routing objective. The architecture did not change; the important difference was where learning could happen. Full fine-tuning made roughly 117.7 million parameters trainable.

Source: Image by the author. Full-fine tuning architecture

This was the first neural configuration to clearly beat the baseline: 98.04% accuracy and 0.9804 Macro F1.

I am deliberately not turning this into a claim that full fine-tuning is universally better for intent routing. The narrower statement is the useful one: for this dataset, this base model, and this routing task, full fine-tuning performed best among the four approaches tested.

The Comparison That Actually Matters

Putting the four approaches side by side makes the story clearer than four separate walls of metrics:

Source: Image by the author.

The progression is not monotonic once the classical baseline is included. Moving from TF-IDF to a pretrained Transformer initially made the result worse. Partial fine-tuning recovered some performance. Only full fine-tuning produced a clear improvement over the baseline.

Complexity had to earn its place.

This is why the baseline mattered. If I had compared only the neural models, partial fine-tuning would have looked like an obvious success. TF-IDF changed the question from “Did this improve over the last Transformer?” to “Did this justify the extra complexity at all?”

Looking Beyond 98% Accuracy

98.04% looked like a victory lap. Then I audited the test set.

There were zero literal duplicate queries across the splits. After normalization, however, 87 test rows matched training examples, and 327 test queries had a training neighbor with cosine similarity of at least 0.95. The audit also found three normalized query pairs with contradictory labels, affecting two test rows.

High semantic similarity is not automatic proof of leakage, but it is a signal that the test set contains families of queries closely related to examples already seen during training. That changes what the headline number can honestly claim.

98.04% is evidence that full fine-tuning performed best on this evaluation setup. It is not evidence of 98.04% accuracy on completely new query families.

As a diagnostic, I removed the 87 normalized matches and recalculated the full fine-tuned model on the remaining 1,292 rows. Accuracy became 97.99%. That is reassuring, but it is not a new independent test: the filtering happened after the original evaluation and semantic overlap still exists.

The point is not to make the result look worse. It is to understand what the number measures. A metric without the data story behind it is mostly decoration.

What the Router Still Gets WrongSource: Image by the author. Confusion matrix for the full fine-tuned model. Rows are actual routes; columns are predictions.

Those 15 cases were worth more than another decimal place of accuracy. Eleven contained spelling errors, three used abbreviations, two were elliptical or incomplete, and one was a broad request. The categories overlap, but the pattern is clear: real users do not write benchmark-friendly sentences.

More interestingly, nine of those 15 wrong predictions assigned at least 0.99 probability to UNDETERMINED. The model was not slightly wrong. It was confidently, enthusiastically wrong.

That is a useful reminder that softmax probability is not the same thing as calibrated certainty. In this router there is no threshold after softmax; the highest-scoring class wins. A prediction near 1.0 simply means one class dominates the model’s learned score distribution.

The review also exposed label ambiguity. One short query equivalent to “active?” had contradictory labels relative to similar variants elsewhere in the data. Some errors therefore reflect the model, some the input, and some the data definition itself. A confusion matrix cannot tell those stories. Reading the errors can.

Why UNDETERMINED Is a Learned Class

The first version of the router only knew API and LLM. That implicitly assumed every query belonged to one of those two execution paths. Real input quickly disagreed.

Instead of keeping the classifier binary and inventing a rule such as if confidence < threshold: reject, the current design teaches the model a third class directly. UNDETERMINED is not the absence of confidence; it represents examples outside the supported routing domains.

Those are different ideas. A model can be uncertain between two valid routes, or extremely confident about an invalid one. The error analysis gave us examples of the latter.

Historically, introducing the third class improved the router, but the old binary experiment was not preserved under a directly comparable dataset and evaluation protocol. So I will not manufacture an improvement percentage for the sake of a cleaner story. The architectural motivation is enough: the system needed a way to learn “neither.”

What I Learned Building the RouterA baseline should be capable of ruining your favorite idea

TF-IDF was not there to lose politely. It beat both the frozen encoder and partial fine-tuning. That made the final result more meaningful because full fine-tuning had to outperform something genuinely competitive.

A Transformer is not a performance guarantee

The frozen encoder was semantically richer and empirically worse. Partial adaptation helped. Full adaptation helped more. The experiment shows an association between more domain adaptation and better performance here; it does not prove a universal law or isolate the exact causal mechanism.

Accuracy is the start of evaluation, not the end

The 98.04% score was useful, but the audit and failure analysis were more informative. They exposed train-test redundancy, contradictory labels, noisy language, and highly confident mistakes — none of which is visible in a single headline metric.

Routing is a systems problem wearing an NLP hat

A wrong prediction is not merely a wrong label. It selects the wrong execution path: the wrong retrieval strategy, the wrong tool, or the wrong subsystem. That is why routing quality has to be evaluated in architectural terms, not only classifier terms.

Final Thoughts

Could I build this router differently today? Of course. An LLM can classify intents directly. Embedding-based routers can reduce custom training. Agent and tool-orchestration frameworks can move routing into a higher-level abstraction. Managed services can make most of this disappear behind an API.

If the only goal were the shortest path to a production prototype, I might choose one of those options.

But the important result of this project was not finding the shortest path.

Building the router step by step forced me to understand what the abstractions hide: how labels encode architecture decisions, why a baseline matters, what frozen representations can and cannot do, what fine-tuning actually changes, how a test split can flatter a model, and why a probability of 0.99 can still be wrong.

Tools will get better. Some of the code in this project will eventually become unnecessary. That is fine. Knowing what happens underneath those tools makes it easier to choose them, evaluate them, and recognize when they fail.

The final model was useful. Understanding why it worked — and where it did not — was the real result.

items.title: Gemini Enterprise Adds PandaDoc Workflows for Creating and Sending Contracts
items.summary: Google's Gemini Enterprise now supports a PandaDoc connector that brings contract document search, creation and lifecycle actions into the Gemini workspace. The integration can support a practical workflow: start with a PandaDoc template, populate its fields, review the resulting document and send it for signature. For teams that repeatedly prepare client agreements, proposals or other standardized documents, the value is in reducing the manual handoff between an AI workspace and a contract platform. The official Gemini Enterprise PandaDoc connector documentation describes PandaDoc as a data store that Gemini can connect to. Once configured, the connector supports searching PandaDoc documents and working across templates and documents through lifecycle actions including creation, review, sending and archiving. This is a confirmed integration, not simply a suggested use case. However, the exact contract example often associated with it, such as creating a services agreement for a named customer with a $50,000 value, depends on the organization's PandaDoc template and its configured fields. The documentation supports the underlying pattern of template-based contract creation and field population, rather than identifying a universal, prebuilt services-agreement button or a fixed contract-value workflow. How the Gemini Enterprise and PandaDoc workflow works A template-led route from request to signature The connector is designed around PandaDoc's existing documents and templates. A user can ask Gemini to work with PandaDoc content, then use a template as the foundation for a new document. Where the relevant fields are configured, the workflow can populate information before the document is reviewed and sent for signature. PandaDoc's developer documentation also provides MCP-powered examples that follow this same pattern: create a contract for a named company from a template, populate fields and pricing, then send the document. That makes the integration particularly relevant where a team already has repeatable agreements and clear document variables, such as customer name, commercial terms or pricing. The documented capabilities include: Searching PandaDoc documents from Gemini Enterprise. Creating documents from PandaDoc templates. Populating fields in a generated document. Reviewing, sending and archiving documents as lifecycle actions. Working with PandaDoc data-store locations identified as Global, US and EU. The important operational distinction is that Gemini does not remove the need for a sound PandaDoc template. A prompt can initiate a workflow, but a reliable result still depends on the template structure and the fields available for the information a team wants to insert. Workflow step Gemini Enterprise PandaDoc connector PandaDoc MCP example pattern Find existing content Search PandaDoc documents through the connected data store Not the focus of the documented example Create a contract Create documents using PandaDoc templates Create a contract for a named company from a template Customize content Populate document fields Populate fields and pricing Complete the process Review, send and archive documents Send the completed document What the documented location model establishes Google's documentation identifies Global, US and EU as supported PandaDoc data-store locations for the connector. That is useful context for organizations that need to understand where a connector is configured, but it should not be overstated as a full description of regional product availability, data residency or compliance posture. The supplied documentation does not specify connector pricing, rollout dates, subscription requirements beyond its Gemini Enterprise context, or detailed security and compliance controls. Businesses considering a deployment should confirm those points with Google and PandaDoc, particularly if their contract process handles sensitive commercial or customer information. Why this matters for contract operations The connector's most tangible benefit is continuity. Instead of treating contract preparation as a separate task after an AI-assisted conversation, users can move from a request to a PandaDoc template-driven document in the same workspace. That can reduce repetitive copy-and-paste work when the required contract language and variables are already standardized. It also creates a more useful boundary for AI-assisted contract work. Gemini can help initiate and manage the documented PandaDoc workflow, while PandaDoc remains the system holding the templates and documents. Teams still need to define their templates carefully, decide which fields should be populated automatically and retain appropriate review steps before sending commercial documents. Contract automation delivers value only when templates, field mappings, approvals and business systems work together. Scalevise can help translate a documented Gemini and PandaDoc workflow into a practical integration that reduces repetitive document preparation without losing control of commercial terms. Our MCP setup service connects AI agents to the tools and data your team actually uses, with implementation choices suited to your process. Discuss an MCP setup project with Scalevise today. Frequently Asked Questions What does the PandaDoc connector let Gemini Enterprise do? It lets Gemini Enterprise connect to a PandaDoc data store to search documents and carry out documented lifecycle actions, including creating, reviewing, sending and archiving documents. It can also support creating a contract from a template and populating fields before sending it for signature. Can Gemini Enterprise create a $50,000 services agreement in PandaDoc? The documented workflow supports template-based contract creation and field population, including PandaDoc examples involving pricing. A specific $50,000 services agreement requires an appropriate PandaDoc template and field mappings. That exact agreement format is not identified as a universal prebuilt option in the supplied documentation. Which PandaDoc data-store locations are documented for the connector? Google's connector documentation identifies Global, US and EU data-store locations. The supplied material does not provide further detail on regional availability, data residency or compliance terms. Is pricing for the Gemini Enterprise PandaDoc connector published in the supplied documentation? No. The verified material does not state connector pricing, rollout timing or detailed subscription requirements. Organizations should confirm commercial terms directly with Google and PandaDoc. Conclusion The PandaDoc connector gives Gemini Enterprise a documented path to search, create, populate and send template-based contract documents from within the Gemini workspace. Its practical usefulness will depend on the quality of the PandaDoc templates and field mappings behind the workflow, while pricing, detailed regional terms and security requirements remain points to validate directly with the providers.

items.title: Deploying Typebot - Open-Source Conversational Form Builder
items.summary:
Typebot is an open-source, visually-driven conversational form and chatbot builder. It serves as a self-hosted alternative to hosted form and chatbot builders, giving you full data ownership and control over integrations and embedding. This guide deploys Typebot on a Linux server using Docker Compose with PostgreSQL, Redis, and Traefik for reverse proxy and TLS termination. By the end, you'll have a working Typebot instance with a published bot embedded on a sample page. Prerequisites Before you begin, you need to: Have access to a Linux-based server as a non-root user with sudo privileges. Install Docker and Docker Compose. Configure two domain A records pointing to your server, such as builder.example.com and viewer.example.com . Have an email address for Let's Encrypt certificate registration. Set Up the Directory Structure and Environment Variables To prevent data loss during container restarts or updates, the deployment relies on host-mounted volumes for PostgreSQL, Redis, and TLS certificates.
