items.title: How to Force Kubernetes to Run Your Pod on the Right Node
items.summary: You have a GPU node sitting there, ready. Kubernetes just scheduled your GPU workload somewhere else entirely. Here’s how to actually control that. nodeSelector vs nodeAffinity vs Taints and Tolerations Explained (Kubernetes) Need a Pod to land on a GPU node or specialized hardware instead of anywhere the scheduler feels like? Here’s exactly how nodeSelector, nodeAffinity, taints, and tolerations work together to control Pod placement, with practical YAML examples. You’ve got a Node in your cluster with an expensive GPU attached, specifically provisioned for exactly one kind of workload. You deploy that workload. And Kubernetes, doing exactly what it was designed to do, schedules it onto a completely ordinary, GPU-less Node instead — while your GPU sits there, idle, hosting some unrelated web server that couldn’t care less about specialized hardware. Nothing is broken here. This is the default scheduler behaving exactly as designed: spread Pods across available Nodes based on resource requests, with no inherent concept of “this workload specifically needs that particular kind of machine.” If you want the scheduler to actually respect hardware requirements, licensing constraints, or deliberate workload separation, you need to tell it — explicitly — using one of several placement mechanisms Kubernetes provides for exactly this purpose. There are four related but genuinely distinct tools here — nodeSelector, nodeAffinity, taints, and tolerations — and the confusion around them mostly comes from people reaching for the wrong one, or not realizing that two of them work as a matched pair rather than standing alone. The default scheduler isn’t careless. It’s just neutral. Placement preferences don’t exist until you write them down. Why the Default Scheduler Doesn’t Already Know This It’s worth understanding why this gap exists at all, rather than assuming it’s an oversight. The Kubernetes scheduler’s default behavior is built around general-purpose fairness — balancing resource requests (the CPU and memory numbers from the earlier article in this series) across available Nodes, trying to avoid overloading any single machine. It has no built-in awareness that “Node-7 has a GPU” matters more than “Node-7 has spare CPU,” unless something specifically tells it so. This is deliberate, not a missing feature. Not every cluster has specialized hardware. Not every workload cares which Node it lands on. Baking hardware-awareness into the default scheduling logic would add complexity that most clusters simply don’t need — so instead, Kubernetes exposes a set of optional mechanisms you apply only when placement actually matters for a specific workload. Key takeaway: The scheduler treats all Nodes as roughly interchangeable by default, on purpose — placement rules exist as opt-in tools for exactly the situations where that assumption is wrong. Step One: Labeling the Node Before any placement mechanism can work, the Node itself needs to be identifiable — Kubernetes needs a way to know “this specific Node has a GPU” in the first place. That’s done with a Node label: kubectl label nodes node-7 hardware=gpu This attaches a simple key-value tag directly to the Node object, the same labeling mechanism you’ve already seen used on Pods throughout this series for Services to find their targets. Verify it landed correctly: kubectl get nodes --show-labels Everything that follows in this article depends on this label existing — nodeSelector and nodeAffinity both work by matching against Node labels, so if this step is skipped or the label doesn't match exactly, nothing downstream will function, and you'll be left wondering why your placement rule "isn't working" when really, there's nothing for it to match against yet. items.summary_html:
You have a GPU node sitting there, ready. Kubernetes just scheduled your GPU workload somewhere else entirely. Here’s how to actually control that.nodeSelector vs nodeAffinity vs Taints and Tolerations Explained (Kubernetes)

Need a Pod to land on a GPU node or specialized hardware instead of anywhere the scheduler feels like? Here’s exactly how nodeSelector, nodeAffinity, taints, and tolerations work together to control Pod placement, with practical YAML examples.

You’ve got a Node in your cluster with an expensive GPU attached, specifically provisioned for exactly one kind of workload. You deploy that workload. And Kubernetes, doing exactly what it was designed to do, schedules it onto a completely ordinary, GPU-less Node instead — while your GPU sits there, idle, hosting some unrelated web server that couldn’t care less about specialized hardware.

Nothing is broken here. This is the default scheduler behaving exactly as designed: spread Pods across available Nodes based on resource requests, with no inherent concept of “this workload specifically needs that particular kind of machine.” If you want the scheduler to actually respect hardware requirements, licensing constraints, or deliberate workload separation, you need to tell it — explicitly — using one of several placement mechanisms Kubernetes provides for exactly this purpose.

There are four related but genuinely distinct tools here — nodeSelector, nodeAffinity, taints, and tolerations — and the confusion around them mostly comes from people reaching for the wrong one, or not realizing that two of them work as a matched pair rather than standing alone.

The default scheduler isn’t careless. It’s just neutral. Placement preferences don’t exist until you write them down.
Why the Default Scheduler Doesn’t Already Know This

It’s worth understanding why this gap exists at all, rather than assuming it’s an oversight. The Kubernetes scheduler’s default behavior is built around general-purpose fairness — balancing resource requests (the CPU and memory numbers from the earlier article in this series) across available Nodes, trying to avoid overloading any single machine. It has no built-in awareness that “Node-7 has a GPU” matters more than “Node-7 has spare CPU,” unless something specifically tells it so.

This is deliberate, not a missing feature. Not every cluster has specialized hardware. Not every workload cares which Node it lands on. Baking hardware-awareness into the default scheduling logic would add complexity that most clusters simply don’t need — so instead, Kubernetes exposes a set of optional mechanisms you apply only when placement actually matters for a specific workload.

Key takeaway: The scheduler treats all Nodes as roughly interchangeable by default, on purpose — placement rules exist as opt-in tools for exactly the situations where that assumption is wrong.

Step One: Labeling the Node

Before any placement mechanism can work, the Node itself needs to be identifiable — Kubernetes needs a way to know “this specific Node has a GPU” in the first place. That’s done with a Node label:

kubectl label nodes node-7 hardware=gpu

This attaches a simple key-value tag directly to the Node object, the same labeling mechanism you’ve already seen used on Pods throughout this series for Services to find their targets. Verify it landed correctly:

kubectl get nodes --show-labels

Everything that follows in this article depends on this label existing — nodeSelector and nodeAffinity both work by matching against Node labels, so if this step is skipped or the label doesn't match exactly, nothing downstream will function, and you'll be left wondering why your placement rule "isn't working" when really, there's nothing for it to match against yet.

Key takeaway: Node placement rules are entirely dependent on Node labels existing first — this is the step people skip and then spend an hour debugging the wrong thing.

nodeSelector: The Simple, Blunt Option

nodeSelector is the most basic placement mechanism — a straightforward, exact-match requirement added directly to a Pod's spec.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: gpu-app
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: gpu-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: gpu-app
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        hardware: gpu
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: my-gpu-app:latest

That nodeSelector block does exactly one thing: it tells the scheduler "only place this Pod on a Node with the label hardware: gpu." If no such Node exists, or none has room, the Pod simply stays Pending rather than landing somewhere unsuitable — which, while inconvenient to see, is exactly the correct, safe behavior. A Pending Pod is recoverable once capacity exists. A GPU workload silently running on a Node with no GPU is a much worse outcome.

The honest limitation here is right there in the name — it’s a selector, not a preference system. You get exact-match, all-or-nothing logic: either a Node has this exact label, or your Pod won’t go there. No “prefer this, but accept that if nothing better’s available.” No matching against multiple possible values. For anything more nuanced than a flat requirement, you need the next tool.

Key takeaway: nodeSelector is genuinely useful for simple, hard requirements — but it's binary by nature, with no concept of preference or flexibility built in.

nodeAffinity: The Flexible, Expressive Option

nodeAffinity does the same fundamental job — matching Pods to Nodes based on labels — but with meaningfully more expressiveness, including the ability to distinguish between a hard requirement and a soft preference.

spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - key: hardware
                operator: In
                values:
                  - gpu
      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - weight: 50
          preference:
            matchExpressions:
              - key: zone
                operator: In
                values:
                  - us-east-1a

That verbose field name — requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution — is intimidating on first read, but it's actually just describing its behavior precisely, once you break it apart: required during scheduling (this must be true for the Pod to be placed at all), ignored during execution (if the Node's label somehow changes after the Pod is already running, Kubernetes won't retroactively evict it over that — it only checks at scheduling time).

The genuinely valuable addition here is the preferred variant. Unlike nodeSelector's all-or-nothing behavior, a preference tells the scheduler "try to satisfy this if you can, but it's fine to proceed without it if no matching Node is available." The weight value lets you express relative importance across multiple soft preferences, which the scheduler factors into its placement scoring rather than treating as a hard gate.

The operator: In field also unlocks matching logic nodeSelector can't express at all — In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, and Lt, meaning you can match against multiple acceptable values, or express "any Node that has this label at all, regardless of value," rather than being locked to one exact key-value pair.

nodeSelector asks "does this Node match, yes or no." nodeAffinity asks "how well does this Node match, and how much do I actually care."

Key takeaway: Reach for nodeAffinity the moment you need either flexible matching logic (multiple acceptable values, existence checks) or the ability to express a preference rather than a hard requirement.

Taints and Tolerations: The Other Half of the Story

Here’s where a genuinely common point of confusion comes in, so it’s worth being direct about it upfront: nodeSelector and nodeAffinity are about Pods choosing Nodes. Taints and tolerations solve the opposite problem — Nodes rejecting Pods that haven't specifically been told they're allowed in.

This distinction matters more than it might first seem. Imagine you’ve correctly set nodeAffinity to prefer the GPU Node for your GPU workload — but nothing stops an entirely unrelated Pod, one that never mentioned GPUs at all, from also landing on that same Node, simply because it had spare CPU and memory capacity that the scheduler was happy to use. Your GPU workload might be running there correctly, but so might three other things that have no business sharing that expensive hardware.

A taint, applied to the Node itself, repels Pods by default — unless a Pod specifically carries a matching toleration granting it permission to ignore that repulsion.

kubectl taint nodes node-7 hardware=gpu:NoSchedule

This taint tells the scheduler: “do not place any Pod on this Node, unless that Pod explicitly tolerates this exact taint.” Now, even a Pod with plenty of free capacity to spare won’t land here by default — the Node has effectively closed its doors to everyone except Pods carrying the right key.

spec:
  tolerations:
    - key: "hardware"
      operator: "Equal"
      value: "gpu"
      effect: "NoSchedule"
  nodeSelector:
    hardware: gpu

Notice this Pod spec includes both a toleration and a nodeSelector. That's not redundant — it's the correct, complete pattern, and understanding why is the real payoff of this whole comparison.

Key takeaway: Taints and tolerations control who’s allowed in. nodeSelector/nodeAffinity control where a Pod wants to go. They solve genuinely opposite problems, which is exactly why serious GPU-scheduling setups use both together.

Why You Need Both, Together

This is the piece that resolves most of the lingering confusion, so it’s worth stating plainly: nodeAffinity alone doesn't stop other Pods from landing on your GPU Node — it only controls where your Pod prefers to go. Taints alone don't guarantee your GPU workload actually lands on the GPU Node — a toleration only grants permission to be scheduled there; it doesn't express any preference or requirement to actually go there instead of somewhere else entirely.

Put those two observations together, and the correct real-world pattern becomes obvious:

  • Taint the GPU Node, so ordinary workloads are repelled from it by default.
  • Add a toleration to your GPU workload’s Pod spec, so it’s specifically permitted to land there despite the taint.
  • Add a nodeSelector or nodeAffinity to that same Pod spec, so it's actually directed there — not just permitted, but positively steered toward that Node rather than wherever else it might otherwise land.

Skip the taint, and other unrelated Pods can still consume your GPU Node’s capacity. Skip the affinity/selector, and your GPU workload might tolerate the taint correctly but still get scheduled on some entirely different, taint-free Node instead, since a toleration is passive permission, not an active pull.

Key takeaway: Taints keep unwanted Pods out. Affinity/selector pulls your intended Pod in. Real specialized-hardware setups need both mechanisms working together, not either one alone.

Side-by-Side ComparisonTrying It Yourself

Using a local cluster from earlier in this series, label one of your Nodes and try the full pattern end to end:

kubectl label nodes  hardware=gpu
kubectl taint nodes  hardware=gpu:NoSchedule

kubectl apply -f gpu-deployment.yaml   # includes both toleration and nodeSelector

kubectl get pods -o wide   # confirm which Node it actually landed on
kubectl describe node    # confirm the taint is applied

Then, as a genuinely instructive test, try deploying an ordinary Pod with no toleration at all, and watch it get scheduled anywhere except your tainted Node — direct, visible confirmation that the gate is actually working, not just present in your YAML.

A Quick Word on Removing a Taint

Taints aren’t permanent — if a Node’s role changes, or you’re decommissioning a dedicated-hardware policy, removing one is a single command, using a trailing dash to indicate removal:

kubectl taint nodes node-7 hardware=gpu:NoSchedule-

It’s a small syntax detail, but forgetting that trailing - is a common typo that instead tries to apply a taint using that exact string as a key, which fails confusingly rather than doing what you meant.

The Real Mental Model to Keep

The distinction worth carrying forward isn’t the specific YAML syntax — that’s easy enough to look up each time you need it. It’s the underlying split: some placement problems are about a Pod expressing where it wants to go, and some are about a Node expressing who it’s willing to accept. nodeSelector and nodeAffinity live entirely in the first category. Taints and tolerations live entirely in the second. Confusing which category your actual problem belongs to is the fastest way to write technically valid YAML that still doesn't produce the placement behavior you expected.

Once that split is clear, the question “how do I force my Pod onto the right Node” stops being one problem and becomes two much more specific ones — “how do I steer this Pod toward where I want it,” and, separately, “how do I keep everything else away from where I don’t.”

Have you run a mixed cluster with specialized hardware — GPUs, high-memory Nodes, specific storage-attached Nodes? What placement mistakes did you make before landing on the taint-plus-affinity pattern?

items.title: AI Community Linked to Disturbing Culture of Sexual Assault
items.summary: The tech world’s potential future founders are living out hedonistic existences in giant Silicon Valley mansions, where they live with a dozen and even more like-minded individuals, and where life is more a less a constant party. These so-called hacker houses, though, have a dark side. A recent New York Times investigation has uncovered several harassment cases and rape allegations stemming from hacker houses. The most prominent of these is the AGI House — short for “artificial general intelligence” — in Hillsborough, where police have logged 37 incidents since 2022. At least 17 were related to the often large and extravagant parties and events that were regularly being thrown on the property. In December, a woman called the Hillsborough police station at 2 in the morning from a Lyft, reporting that she had been trapped at the AGI House by a male resident who tried to force her to have sex. The man told her she was old and “would be alone forever,” according to the police reported viewed by the NYT . He was “persistent in attempting to convince” the woman “to have sex with him, and she repeatedly declined.” She escaped by climbing over a gate, unharmed. The AGI House was founded by Jeremy Nixon, a former Google researcher who’s established other tech homes, with the vision of having “20 AI hackers, living in the same epic house for three months,” he told the NYT . The domicile was originally called NeoGenesis, but rebranded after OpenAI released ChatGPT and kickstarted the AI boom. And before NeoGenesis, he co-founded a hacker house called Genesis in 2019. Genesis had a dark history of its own. Not wanting for debauchery, it was also a hub for parties, with one 19-year-old tech entrepreneur claiming he used to sneak into parties when he was just 13. “It was pretty crazy,” he told the NYT . Yehong Zhu, 30, filed a police reporting accusing a former Genesis house member of rape and assault in December 2021. Zhu has lived in four tech houses, and her view of them as utopic spaces for entrepreneurs was shattered by her experience. The case is still under investigation, and the accused Genesis resident hasn’t left the house and can’t be located, she said. “I’m far from the only one this has happened to,” Zhu, who founded her own startup called Zette AI, told the NYT . To lay out the stakes, these hacker houses aren’t random gatherings. Some are directly run by tech executives like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has advised one called the Residency. AGI House regularly had tech industry royalty show up for dinners, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin. In a direct way, they’re responsible for fostering the culture and beliefs that the current and upcoming generations of AI industry workers, if not leaders, are being instilled with, along with building the network of connections that’ll shape their careers. The next Sam Altman or Elon Musk is probably spending their formative young adult years in one of these debaucherous dens. The people running them are well aware of their outsized influence. The AGI House’s current manager, venture capitalist Rocky Yu, is in an ongoing legal battle with a former manager over who owns the rights to the AGI House brand, the NYT noted. There’re other signs that all is not well behind closed doors. Police were also asked to perform welfare checks on at least four different occasions at the AGI House. On one occasion, they even sent an ambulance to the house. More on AI: Is There a Secret Reason for the Industry-Wide AI Slowdown?

items.title: AI Can Search the Web. It Still Doesn’t Know What to Look For.
items.summary: Memory, files, search, and enormous pretraining. What ties them together is the ability to notice what the current reasoning is missing. Recently I was using GPT to work out where one of my academic papers stood in peer review. A status message had arrived from the editorial office, and I wanted to understand what it meant. I went through it with GPT. The first answer was careful. It read the wording of the email, avoided claiming to know the sender’s intentions, and kept several possibilities open. That isn’t the wrong posture. But something was missing. I told it to stop reading the email in isolation and look at the whole timeline of the submission. Then I told it to compare against how peer review normally runs. Then I pointed it to the documents I had saved and to the history of the revisions. Each time, its explanation changed. What matters here is not which reading turned out to be right. What I noticed sat further upstream. GPT had a lot of what it needed. It had the earlier conversation. It had the files. It could search the web if it chose to. And yet in its first answer, it didn’t really ask itself: what do I need to look at next before I can judge this? I wasn’t handing it conclusions. I was telling it where to look before it concluded. I think that gap matters more than it seems to in today’s AI. (I’m not reproducing any private correspondence or review content here. The subject is the information-selection problem that surfaced while I worked through it with GPT.) The Next Problem for Memory Is What Drives Retrieval Memory has quickly become one of the big themes in AI: long context windows, persistent memory, project-level files, external databases, RAG. All of it is useful. But storing more does not, by itself, make judgments better. Liu and colleagues’ “Lost in the Middle” showed that even when the needed information sits inside a long context, models can fail to use it well depending on where it appears [1]. That result concerns the models and tasks studied at the time, not every model in use today. It is still a good reason to separate “can be put in the input” from “can be used when it’s needed.” In my case, too, the information existed. What was weak was the move of working backward from the current question to call up the relevant timeline, the saved documents, the normal process, and the right points of comparison. Owning a large library is different from knowing which book to open right now. Beyond capacity, the next problem for AI memory may be what drives retrieval. Humans Don’t Replay Their Whole Memory Before They Think We don’t unfold our entire life’s memory into awareness every time we make a judgment either. The current situation acts as a cue, and related memories and knowledge get called up from there. Teyler and DiScenna’s hippocampal memory indexing theory treats the hippocampus as an index for re-accessing the distributed cortical representations that were active during an experience [2]. In that view, memory is less a box that holds each event whole and more a mechanism for reconstructing the needed patterns of activity later. In a free-recall study, Polyn and colleagues found that cortical activity corresponding to a category (people, places, objects) appeared several seconds before participants recalled and said aloud an item from that category [3]. In human memory search, the context and cues active at the moment are related to what gets pulled up next. Badre and colleagues, working with semantic memory tasks, separately examined the control involved in retrieving information from weak cues and the control involved in selecting what’s needed among competing candidates, and reported that the two corresponded to different activity in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex [4]. There’s no need to copy brain regions over to AI. What’s interesting is how the functions are divided. The current object becomes the cue. Related past material gets called up. Among the candidates, the ones that matter this time get selected. If that still isn’t enough, you go looking for the next piece. AI memory may need more than topic-based archives like “work,” “family,” and “papers.” If memories carried return paths, such as which assumption I got wrong last time, what I checked that changed the judgment, and under what conditions an old conclusion stops holding, then memory could work less like a warehouse for replaying the past and more like an index for correcting present reasoning. The Information That Changes the Decision Search systems usually look for information related to the question. In reasoning, related isn’t always enough. If explanation A and explanation B are competing, what you really want is information that can change which one survives. Something that resembles both won’t do that. Markant and Gureckis compared active learning, where learners choose their own examples, with a condition in which the same examples are handed to learners passively [5]. In their analysis, what mattered was not only the act of choosing but that learners could pick the next example according to the hypotheses they currently held. With causal inference the stakes rise. Steyvers and colleagues showed that learning a causal structure improved when participants could choose their own interventions and observe the results, compared with observation alone [6]. Deciding which intervention would tell competing causal hypotheses apart becomes part of the problem itself. A web search is not an experimental intervention, and piling up search results doesn’t prove causation. The design question carries over all the same: What information could change the current explanation, rather than merely reinforce it? I think this is one of the lines between an AI that can search and an AI that can investigate. AI Has an Unusual Combination of Strengths Look at the AI side, and something interesting is happening. Modern LLMs carry knowledge and patterns acquired through large-scale pretraining. Petroni and colleagues examined how much relational factual knowledge can be drawn out of pretrained language models and showed that knowledge captured in the parameters can be queried [7]. That doesn’t make a language model a complete or accurate database. Combining that internal knowledge with external retrieval is the basic direction of RAG. Lewis and colleagues combined a pretrained model’s parametric memory with a retrievable, non-parametric memory [8]. Now add long-term memory, user-specific projects, files, web search, and a range of tools. At that point, AI can become more than a system that answers from what it already knows. It can think of a field to compare against from general knowledge. It can go back to an earlier correction through its own memory. It can pull the original wording from a file. If current information is needed, it can go to the web. If the current state only lives in an external service, it can check with a permitted tool. I’m not simply saying this beats human memory. People have bodies, experience, purposes, meaning-making, and an ongoing relationship with the world around them. AI has a different kind of strength: It can use broad learned knowledge as a cue, then go out into the world on the spot to fetch what it’s missing. With that combination, the bottleneck may shift from how much was stored to what to go and get next. Yes, This Research Already Exists If I wrote here that AI research hasn’t noticed this idea, this article would fail its own test. Research that alternates between reasoning and retrieval is already well along. ReAct interleaved a language model’s reasoning with actions in an external environment. The model gains information through actions and uses the results in later problem solving [9]. IRCoT is even closer to what I’m describing. In multi-step knowledge questions, what to retrieve depends on the reasoning so far, and that reasoning depends on what was retrieved earlier. Trivedi and colleagues built on this interdependence by interleaving retrieval with chain-of-thought reasoning [10]. Self-RAG introduced a mechanism for the model to assess when to retrieve, whether retrieved passages are relevant, and whether its output is supported by them [11]. Search-R1 uses reinforcement learning to train reasoning that includes multiple rounds of interaction with a search engine [12]. In 2025, Geng and colleagues studied tasks that reverse-engineer black-box programs and formulas [13]. They compared an active condition, in which the model chose its own inputs and observed the outputs, with a condition in which it passively received examples. Performance improved in the active condition, and passing the same data passively to a separate run did not produce the same performance. These are controlled tasks that return reliable input-output pairs, and the conditions differ in more than who does the choosing. Still, the result makes a case for evaluating the process of selecting information while updating hypotheses, alongside the information collected. So I’m not claiming to have invented a new search algorithm. What bothers me is a more practical gap. Search, memory, files, and tools can all be available. If the user still has to keep saying “now look at this,” an important part of information selection is still being done by the human. There is still a distance between what’s possible in research and what fires spontaneously, at the moment it’s needed, in an actual conversation. So How Should the Reasoning Flow Work? Working backward from this failure, the following flow seems natural to me: Current Object → Initial Causal Model → Missing Evidence → Source Routing → Evidence Typing → Causal Update → Commit or Continue First, pin down what you’re actually trying to judge. Next, build several candidate explanations from the current information and learned knowledge instead of betting on one. Then ask: What would change the ranking of these candidates? Only then decide where to go. If past exchanges or corrections are needed, go back to memory or the project. If you need the fine detail of the original material, read the files. If current rules, research, or product information may have changed, search the web. If the current state only exists in an external service, use a tool. Whatever can’t be obtained stays marked as unknown, or goes back to the human as a question. After retrieving, keep track of where each piece came from. General knowledge that surfaces from pretraining is a strong prior for deciding what to look into. On its own, it proves nothing about this particular case. Memory can bring back the past, but it can’t guarantee that an old state still holds. Secondary sources on the web help with comparison, but they don’t carry the weight of primary documents. Then update the causal model with the retrieved evidence. This is the important part. Search is there to test the first answer as much as to support it. New evidence is allowed to flip the ranking of explanations. And if the question was framed wrongly to begin with, the causal model itself can be rebuilt. Finally, if missing evidence that could still change the judgment remains, keep going. When further retrieval is unlikely to change much, answer, and say what uncertainty remains. These seven functions don’t need to be exposed to the user as a step-by-step trace. What matters is that the system performs them when the task requires them. This also suggests that caution should act at the point of commitment, not by weakening the reasoning from the start. Build strong candidates from the available material, and then be strict about what gets committed as fact. If you can’t know what someone was thinking, mark only their intentions as unknown. If you haven’t confirmed the current state, mark only that as unconfirmed. Uncertainty on the outside doesn’t justify thinning out the causality you can observe on the inside. Thinking boldly and asserting boldly are two different things. More Searching Isn’t the Answer Either There’s an opposite failure. Being able to search doesn’t mean heading to the web every time a question comes up. In a decision task where participants could pay for information, Kobayashi and Hsu showed that the value of information includes its instrumental value, which comes from improving choices, and also the value of knowing an outcome in advance [14]. They also examined neural signals related to that value in the striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex. People sometimes gather information because they want to know, not because it helps. AI can fall into the same trap if the number of searches becomes the measure of performance. Collect ten articles that agree with your explanation, and if they all trace back to a single source, you have one piece of evidence, not ten. If your search terms are phrased to confirm your hypothesis from the start, the world you find will be skewed as well. So before searching, I think this is the question to ask: What would change my current judgment? And after searching, one more: Is what I just retrieved evidence for that question, or just something on the same topic? When those questions stop getting answers, the volume of searching may be rising while the reasoning gets no deeper. What We Should Actually Measure Evaluating this idea doesn’t have to be complicated. Scatter the important information across several places: some in memory, some in files, some in current web information. Mix in outdated information and irrelevant material. The user doesn’t say which source to look at. Then see whether the AI reaches the sources it needs on its own. The number of searches is one thing to measure, and only one. Did it find the needed material before a human pointed to it? Did it put current evidence ahead of outdated memory? Did it choose information that separates competing explanations? Did new evidence actually update its judgment? Did it avoid unnecessary searching? And how many times did a human have to step in with “now look at this” before it reached the same quality? This one episode is not an experiment proving the method works. But it did make clear, at least to me, what I was frustrated about. What I wanted is easy to say and hard to build: an AI that notices what its own reasoning is missing, and chooses the next source to fill that gap before I have to ask. The web offers a way back to the present world. Pretrained weights offer an enormous space of things worth checking. AI can already reach a great many places. Binding all of that into one line of reasoning takes one more thing. Memory gives an AI somewhere to return. Reasoning must decide when to return — and where. References [1] N. F. items.summary_html:
Memory, files, search, and enormous pretraining. What ties them together is the ability to notice what the current reasoning is missing.

Recently I was using GPT to work out where one of my academic papers stood in peer review.

A status message had arrived from the editorial office, and I wanted to understand what it meant. I went through it with GPT.

The first answer was careful. It read the wording of the email, avoided claiming to know the sender’s intentions, and kept several possibilities open. That isn’t the wrong posture.

But something was missing.

I told it to stop reading the email in isolation and look at the whole timeline of the submission. Then I told it to compare against how peer review normally runs. Then I pointed it to the documents I had saved and to the history of the revisions.

Each time, its explanation changed.

What matters here is not which reading turned out to be right. What I noticed sat further upstream.

GPT had a lot of what it needed. It had the earlier conversation. It had the files. It could search the web if it chose to.

And yet in its first answer, it didn’t really ask itself: what do I need to look at next before I can judge this?

I wasn’t handing it conclusions.

I was telling it where to look before it concluded.

I think that gap matters more than it seems to in today’s AI.

(I’m not reproducing any private correspondence or review content here. The subject is the information-selection problem that surfaced while I worked through it with GPT.)

The Next Problem for Memory Is What Drives Retrieval

Memory has quickly become one of the big themes in AI: long context windows, persistent memory, project-level files, external databases, RAG. All of it is useful.

But storing more does not, by itself, make judgments better.

Liu and colleagues’ “Lost in the Middle” showed that even when the needed information sits inside a long context, models can fail to use it well depending on where it appears [1]. That result concerns the models and tasks studied at the time, not every model in use today. It is still a good reason to separate “can be put in the input” from “can be used when it’s needed.”

In my case, too, the information existed.

What was weak was the move of working backward from the current question to call up the relevant timeline, the saved documents, the normal process, and the right points of comparison.

Owning a large library is different from knowing which book to open right now.

Beyond capacity, the next problem for AI memory may be what drives retrieval.

Humans Don’t Replay Their Whole Memory Before They Think

We don’t unfold our entire life’s memory into awareness every time we make a judgment either.

The current situation acts as a cue, and related memories and knowledge get called up from there.

Teyler and DiScenna’s hippocampal memory indexing theory treats the hippocampus as an index for re-accessing the distributed cortical representations that were active during an experience [2]. In that view, memory is less a box that holds each event whole and more a mechanism for reconstructing the needed patterns of activity later.

In a free-recall study, Polyn and colleagues found that cortical activity corresponding to a category (people, places, objects) appeared several seconds before participants recalled and said aloud an item from that category [3]. In human memory search, the context and cues active at the moment are related to what gets pulled up next.

Badre and colleagues, working with semantic memory tasks, separately examined the control involved in retrieving information from weak cues and the control involved in selecting what’s needed among competing candidates, and reported that the two corresponded to different activity in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex [4].

There’s no need to copy brain regions over to AI. What’s interesting is how the functions are divided.

The current object becomes the cue. Related past material gets called up. Among the candidates, the ones that matter this time get selected. If that still isn’t enough, you go looking for the next piece.

AI memory may need more than topic-based archives like “work,” “family,” and “papers.”

If memories carried return paths, such as which assumption I got wrong last time, what I checked that changed the judgment, and under what conditions an old conclusion stops holding, then memory could work less like a warehouse for replaying the past and more like an index for correcting present reasoning.

The Information That Changes the Decision

Search systems usually look for information related to the question.

In reasoning, related isn’t always enough.

If explanation A and explanation B are competing, what you really want is information that can change which one survives. Something that resembles both won’t do that.

Markant and Gureckis compared active learning, where learners choose their own examples, with a condition in which the same examples are handed to learners passively [5]. In their analysis, what mattered was not only the act of choosing but that learners could pick the next example according to the hypotheses they currently held.

With causal inference the stakes rise. Steyvers and colleagues showed that learning a causal structure improved when participants could choose their own interventions and observe the results, compared with observation alone [6]. Deciding which intervention would tell competing causal hypotheses apart becomes part of the problem itself.

A web search is not an experimental intervention, and piling up search results doesn’t prove causation.

The design question carries over all the same:

What information could change the current explanation, rather than merely reinforce it?

I think this is one of the lines between an AI that can search and an AI that can investigate.

AI Has an Unusual Combination of Strengths

Look at the AI side, and something interesting is happening.

Modern LLMs carry knowledge and patterns acquired through large-scale pretraining. Petroni and colleagues examined how much relational factual knowledge can be drawn out of pretrained language models and showed that knowledge captured in the parameters can be queried [7]. That doesn’t make a language model a complete or accurate database.

Combining that internal knowledge with external retrieval is the basic direction of RAG. Lewis and colleagues combined a pretrained model’s parametric memory with a retrievable, non-parametric memory [8].

Now add long-term memory, user-specific projects, files, web search, and a range of tools.

At that point, AI can become more than a system that answers from what it already knows.

It can think of a field to compare against from general knowledge. It can go back to an earlier correction through its own memory. It can pull the original wording from a file. If current information is needed, it can go to the web. If the current state only lives in an external service, it can check with a permitted tool.

I’m not simply saying this beats human memory. People have bodies, experience, purposes, meaning-making, and an ongoing relationship with the world around them.

AI has a different kind of strength:

It can use broad learned knowledge as a cue, then go out into the world on the spot to fetch what it’s missing.

With that combination, the bottleneck may shift from how much was stored to what to go and get next.

Yes, This Research Already Exists

If I wrote here that AI research hasn’t noticed this idea, this article would fail its own test.

Research that alternates between reasoning and retrieval is already well along.

ReAct interleaved a language model’s reasoning with actions in an external environment. The model gains information through actions and uses the results in later problem solving [9].

IRCoT is even closer to what I’m describing. In multi-step knowledge questions, what to retrieve depends on the reasoning so far, and that reasoning depends on what was retrieved earlier. Trivedi and colleagues built on this interdependence by interleaving retrieval with chain-of-thought reasoning [10].

Self-RAG introduced a mechanism for the model to assess when to retrieve, whether retrieved passages are relevant, and whether its output is supported by them [11]. Search-R1 uses reinforcement learning to train reasoning that includes multiple rounds of interaction with a search engine [12].

In 2025, Geng and colleagues studied tasks that reverse-engineer black-box programs and formulas [13]. They compared an active condition, in which the model chose its own inputs and observed the outputs, with a condition in which it passively received examples. Performance improved in the active condition, and passing the same data passively to a separate run did not produce the same performance. These are controlled tasks that return reliable input-output pairs, and the conditions differ in more than who does the choosing. Still, the result makes a case for evaluating the process of selecting information while updating hypotheses, alongside the information collected.

So I’m not claiming to have invented a new search algorithm.

What bothers me is a more practical gap.

Search, memory, files, and tools can all be available. If the user still has to keep saying “now look at this,” an important part of information selection is still being done by the human.

There is still a distance between what’s possible in research and what fires spontaneously, at the moment it’s needed, in an actual conversation.

So How Should the Reasoning Flow Work?

Working backward from this failure, the following flow seems natural to me:

Current Object → Initial Causal Model → Missing Evidence → Source Routing → Evidence Typing → Causal Update → Commit or Continue

First, pin down what you’re actually trying to judge.

Next, build several candidate explanations from the current information and learned knowledge instead of betting on one.

Then ask:

What would change the ranking of these candidates?

Only then decide where to go.

If past exchanges or corrections are needed, go back to memory or the project. If you need the fine detail of the original material, read the files. If current rules, research, or product information may have changed, search the web. If the current state only exists in an external service, use a tool. Whatever can’t be obtained stays marked as unknown, or goes back to the human as a question.

After retrieving, keep track of where each piece came from.

General knowledge that surfaces from pretraining is a strong prior for deciding what to look into. On its own, it proves nothing about this particular case. Memory can bring back the past, but it can’t guarantee that an old state still holds. Secondary sources on the web help with comparison, but they don’t carry the weight of primary documents.

Then update the causal model with the retrieved evidence.

This is the important part.

Search is there to test the first answer as much as to support it. New evidence is allowed to flip the ranking of explanations. And if the question was framed wrongly to begin with, the causal model itself can be rebuilt.

Finally, if missing evidence that could still change the judgment remains, keep going. When further retrieval is unlikely to change much, answer, and say what uncertainty remains.

These seven functions don’t need to be exposed to the user as a step-by-step trace. What matters is that the system performs them when the task requires them.

This also suggests that caution should act at the point of commitment, not by weakening the reasoning from the start.

Build strong candidates from the available material, and then be strict about what gets committed as fact.

If you can’t know what someone was thinking, mark only their intentions as unknown. If you haven’t confirmed the current state, mark only that as unconfirmed. Uncertainty on the outside doesn’t justify thinning out the causality you can observe on the inside.

Thinking boldly and asserting boldly are two different things.

More Searching Isn’t the Answer Either

There’s an opposite failure.

Being able to search doesn’t mean heading to the web every time a question comes up.

In a decision task where participants could pay for information, Kobayashi and Hsu showed that the value of information includes its instrumental value, which comes from improving choices, and also the value of knowing an outcome in advance [14]. They also examined neural signals related to that value in the striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.

People sometimes gather information because they want to know, not because it helps.

AI can fall into the same trap if the number of searches becomes the measure of performance.

Collect ten articles that agree with your explanation, and if they all trace back to a single source, you have one piece of evidence, not ten. If your search terms are phrased to confirm your hypothesis from the start, the world you find will be skewed as well.

So before searching, I think this is the question to ask:

What would change my current judgment?

And after searching, one more:

Is what I just retrieved evidence for that question, or just something on the same topic?

When those questions stop getting answers, the volume of searching may be rising while the reasoning gets no deeper.

What We Should Actually Measure

Evaluating this idea doesn’t have to be complicated.

Scatter the important information across several places: some in memory, some in files, some in current web information. Mix in outdated information and irrelevant material.

The user doesn’t say which source to look at.

Then see whether the AI reaches the sources it needs on its own.

The number of searches is one thing to measure, and only one.

Did it find the needed material before a human pointed to it? Did it put current evidence ahead of outdated memory? Did it choose information that separates competing explanations? Did new evidence actually update its judgment? Did it avoid unnecessary searching? And how many times did a human have to step in with “now look at this” before it reached the same quality?

This one episode is not an experiment proving the method works.

But it did make clear, at least to me, what I was frustrated about.

What I wanted is easy to say and hard to build: an AI that notices what its own reasoning is missing, and chooses the next source to fill that gap before I have to ask.

The web offers a way back to the present world. Pretrained weights offer an enormous space of things worth checking. AI can already reach a great many places. Binding all of that into one line of reasoning takes one more thing.

Memory gives an AI somewhere to return. Reasoning must decide when to return — and where.

items.title: The CEO of a $55 billion conglomerate explains why the Japanese concept of 'kosoryoku' is so important in the AI age
items.summary: Sumitomo Corporation CEO Shingo Ueno says AI can analyze the past, but humans should still envision the future. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sumitomo CEO Shingo Ueno believes 'kosoryoku' is a key skill in business. The term translates as 'the ability to envision futures that do not yet exist'. Ueno says AI can be a helpful research tool, but cannot yet conceptualize the future well. A little-known Japanese term about imagining the future helps explain both the role — and the limits — of AI in the workplace, according to the CEO of one of the country's largest conglomerates. Speaking to Business Insider in early September, Shingo Ueno, the head of Sumitomo Corporation, a Japanese multi-industry powerhouse with a market capitalization of around $55 billion, said that AI is a powerful research tool but lacks a crucial human capability: kosoryoku. Pronounced koh-soh-ryoh-koo, the Japanese term essentially means the power to conceptualize or formulate a vision for the future that has not yet been imagined, something Ueno says AI does not currently have. "Generative AI is helping me a lot to improve my efficiency. I'm fully utilizing it," Ueno said. One of its biggest advantages is its ability to retrieve information quickly . "If I want to find information about something the company did before, I might have previously spent a day searching for that experience. Now, the answer comes immediately," he said. That speed helps Ueno, who has spent over 40 years working for Sumitomo Corporation, follow his preferred management style : resolving issues quickly instead of allowing them to linger. "My method is to make decisions on the spot," he said. "I try to avoid the back-and-forth — having the same issue come back the next day." Still, Ueno has found that AI cannot make every decision for him . "I once tried to make a decision using AI, and I just got rubbish answers," he said. "It wasn't usable at all." The problem, he said, is that AI depends on information from the past. It can identify patterns and suggest possible directions, but it is less capable when it comes to envisioning a future that does not yet exist. "AI analyzes past data to show us a direction. But it is still based on the past," Ueno said. "It can't create the future. It can't really show the vision." Developing kosoryoku does not require employees to come up with revolutionary ideas from scratch, he said. "We don't need to be inventors. We don't need to come up with something completely new," Ueno said. "We can start with something that already exists, improve it, and make it our own." Separately, Ueno said taking time away from work is important because it allows him to rest and return with new ideas. "At the weekend, I basically spend my time without thinking about work," he said. "That is extremely important, just resting my head. Then, when I go back to work, I can come up with new ideas." AI may help executives understand the past in seconds. Ueno's message is that humans must still decide what the future should look like. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The Week in AI Careers: Workers Expect Job Losses, Executives Say Otherwise, + More
items.summary: The clearest careers signal from the week came from Pew Research Center, which found that across most of the world people now expect AI to shrink the number of jobs rather than grow it. A companion Pew release showed the worry has flipped along party lines in the United States, with Democrats now more concerned about AI and jobs than Republicans, a reversal from two years ago. Running against that public mood, executives on stage at Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference spent the week arguing the opposite, that AI expands what people do rather than eliminating them. The two evergreen ODSC events close out the issue. It was a quiet week for scheduled labor-market data, so the issue is built around sentiment and the widening gap between how the public and how AI’s sellers describe the same technology. Build AI Workflows That Actually Work Join the ODSC AI NYC: AI for Work Summit in New York, Dec 2–3, for hands-on AI workshops focused on AI agents, workflow automation, evaluation, governance, and enterprise AI deployment . 🎟️ Explore the AI for Work Summit & Register → Build practical AI skills, work on real workflows, and leave with ideas you can put to work right away. Worker sentiment and workplace policy Most countries expect AI to cost jobs, Pew finds across 37 markets What happened: Pew Research Center published a 37-market study on September 17 finding that in 34 of the 37 places surveyed, people lean toward believing AI will lead to fewer jobs rather than more. Concern runs highest in wealthier countries: around seven in ten adults or more in places such as the United States, Australia, and South Korea say AI will result in job loss over the next 20 years, and in the United States that share has risen 7 percentage points in two years. Respondents were also more likely to say AI will widen the gap between rich and poor than to say it will narrow it, with four in ten or more holding that view in high-income countries. The findings draw on surveys of 42,151 people across 36 countries fielded between February 8 and May 13, 2026, plus separate United States surveys, and are reported in Pew’s write-up . Why it matters: This is one of the broadest reads yet on how workers themselves expect AI to hit employment, and the direction is consistent across very different labor markets. The finding that pessimism climbs with national income cuts against the assumption that wealthier, more digitally fluent workforces feel more secure, and suggests exposure to AI at work raises concern rather than easing it. For anyone building AI tools or leading teams that use them, a workforce that expects job loss is a workforce that reads every deployment through that lens, which shapes adoption, trust, and appetite for reskilling. In the United States, Democrats are now more worried than Republicans about AI and jobs What happened: A same-week Pew Research Center analysis, released September 16, found that 75 percent of Democrats and 68 percent of Republicans now expect AI to lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years. The gap reflects a two-year shift: Democrats’ expectation of AI-driven job losses rose 17 percentage points since 2024 while Republican views held roughly steady, reversing an earlier pattern in which Republicans were the more worried group. On AI in daily life more broadly, 56 percent of Democrats and 49 percent of Republicans said they are more concerned than excited. The figures come from a survey of 3,488 US adults conducted June 22 to 28, 2026, on Pew’s American Trends Panel, detailed in Pew’s short read . Why it matters: A 17-point swing in two years is fast for a question about a technology’s effect on work, and it signals that AI and employment is becoming a partisan issue rather than a shared economic worry. That matters for how AI workforce policy gets debated, from training subsidies to disclosure rules, because positions that track party lines tend to move differently than positions rooted in a person’s own job. For employers, it is a reminder that internal messaging about AI lands on a workforce whose baseline expectations are shifting and no longer uniform. The ODSC West Keynote Lineup Is Live 🎤 See who’s taking the stage in San Francisco, Oct 27–29, and hear from leading voices shaping what’s next in AI, agents, machine learning, and more. 🎟️ Save 40% with Fall Savings — register before this pricing round ends. Roles and hiring At Dreamforce, Salesforce and Nvidia chiefs argue AI expands work rather than cutting it What happened: Speaking at Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference in San Francisco during the week of September 15, Marc Benioff pushed back on fears that AI is hollowing out payrolls, telling Fortune on September 16 that “we have more employees now than we’ve ever had” and putting Salesforce’s headcount at more than 83,000. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, on stage the same week, dismissed the idea that AI will destroy jobs and argued the technology will broaden what people do at work. The remarks are reported in Fortune and in wire coverage of the two executives’ joint appearance . The optimism sits alongside Benioff’s own earlier 2026 statement that Salesforce had cut about 4,000 customer-support roles as AI agents took on that work, reducing support headcount from roughly 9,000 to about 5,000, as he told Yahoo Finance . Why it matters: The Dreamforce messaging is close to the mirror image of the Pew findings above, with the public increasingly expecting AI to shrink employment while the executives selling the tools insist it grows the work. Both can be partly true at the task level, since a company can add net headcount while automating specific functions, which is what “more employees than ever” and “4,000 support roles cut” describe at the same firm. The reconciliation is the story worth watching, because how leaders frame that mix sets the tone for reskilling programs and for whether workers treat AI adoption as a threat or a tool. AcademyAI raises £1.65 million to close the workplace AI skills gap What happened: AcademyAI, a UK-based startup, raised a £1.65 million pre-seed round backed by Nexus Family Office and Panthera Family Office, according to Tech.eu , published September 15. The company’s platform evaluates employees’ AI capabilities against a six-axis framework built with the Alan Turing Institute, then delivers five-minute training modules targeted at the gaps it finds, with dashboards for leadership to track capability development across teams. Why it matters: This is a funding signal on the training side of the same gap the Pew data above describes from the worker side. Co-founder Alex Packham put the problem plainly: most employers have rolled out tools like ChatGPT and Copilot but have no way to tell whether their people can actually use them. A pre-seed round this specific, assessment first and training second, is a bet that the bottleneck is measuring and closing individual skill gaps inside existing teams, not hiring new AI specialists around them. Registration and schedule are at odsc.ai/west . ODSC AI NYC, the AI for Work Summit, runs December 2 to 3 at the Jay Conference Center at Bryant Park, focused on applied enterprise AI: agents and copilots, deployment, evaluation, governance, and production workflows. Details are at summit.ai .

items.title: From admin to architect: Jamf’s vision for the autonomous Apple enterprise
items.summary: Now a private company , Jamf opened its big annual event for Apple enterprise management teams, JNUC , by taking big steps to exploit artificial intelligence in the management of Apple fleets. During her keynote speech at the Kansas City event, CEO Beth Tschida shared some of the details of the platform-scale overhaul the company has set in motion. “IT teams are managing more endpoints and more complexity than ever,” she said. “We want Jamf to handle more of that routine work automatically… because AI runs better on Apple, and Apple runs better on Jamf.” Tschida — and Jamf — have been consistent on the value of AI to IT, which played a major focus at last year’s JNUC also. When I spoke with her, she was resolute on the need for IT to engage with the tech, telling me, “AI is happening whether organizations know it or not. That’s the problem. You can try to block it, but that’s very hard to do well. It’s far better to build visibility and governance around it.” As you’ll see, this is very much part of what Jamf at JNUC 2026 is working to achieve. AI, Apple, and IT The combination is about exploiting AI support inherent to Apple’s platforms to help reduce time-consuming IT tasks. It means that Apple device management in the future will be less about management and more about creating autonomous enterprise ecosystems in which the tech handles the routine tasks, while humans handle the strategy. Jamf’s offerings now include a new AI-powered self-service diagnostics system. Employees will be able to troubleshoot their own devices by asking Jamf questions on their device, such as “Why are my video calls lagging?” and receive an immediate explanation and a one-click fix. These improvements aren’t confined to routine task automation. They also extend into AI governance. The company introduced its AI Governance suite earlier this year, and at JNUC announced new capabilities to help IT take control of shadow AI across their networks. A response to shadow AI These include a centralized AI control panel which shows admins which AI systems are running across their fleet and lets them enforce usage policies and also generate audit-ready reports. The company is extending this into the Safari, Chrome, and Edge browsers, which means organizations can prevent the upload of corporate files to personal AI accounts through browsers on managed devices. It means that IT doesn’t just see AI is being used but can identify which models are running and what the token costs are, while also being able to block corporate files from being uploaded to a personal account in Safari or Chrome. For security-conscious firms, Jamf is also enabling the deployment of local inference engines. That support means companies can run AI workloads directly on Apple hardware, ensuring that prompts and sensitive data never, ever leave the device. IT as a service The transformation of IT means IT itself is becoming an application, and Jamf seems to be embracing this approach with a new Platform API Gateway and a Terraform provider. Together, these make it possible for IT teams to manage their entire Apple environment using “Infrastructure as Code.” Think GitOps for admins, in which a change to the fleet becomes a peer-reviewed pull request, and a rollback becomes as simple as a click. Jamf also introduced Jamf Tap, its NFC/RFID system that lets frontline workers simply tap an ID badge to instantly assign the device and sign into necessary apps, aimed at streamlining things like shift changes in warehouses. Final announcements from the company included Ring Deployments, a rollout system that tests updates with a pilot group before expanding to the wider fleet, and a curated catalog that automatically installs and updates popular Mac apps. items.summary_html:
Now a private company, Jamf opened its big annual event for Apple enterprise management teams, JNUC, by taking big steps to exploit artificial intelligence in the management of Apple fleets. During her keynote speech at the Kansas City event, CEO Beth Tschida shared some of the details of the platform-scale overhaul the company has set in motion.

“IT teams are managing more endpoints and more complexity than ever,” she said. “We want Jamf to handle more of that routine work automatically… because AI runs better on Apple, and Apple runs better on Jamf.”

Tschida — and Jamf — have been consistent on the value of AI to IT, which played a major focus at last year’s JNUC also. When I spoke with her, she was resolute on the need for IT to engage with the tech, telling me, “AI is happening whether organizations know it or not. That’s the problem. You can try to block it, but that’s very hard to do well. It’s far better to build visibility and governance around it.”

As you’ll see, this is very much part of what Jamf at JNUC 2026 is working to achieve.

AI, Apple, and IT

The combination is about exploiting AI support inherent to Apple’s platforms to help reduce time-consuming IT tasks. It means that Apple device management in the future will be less about management and more about creating autonomous enterprise ecosystems in which the tech handles the routine tasks, while humans handle the strategy.

Jamf’s offerings now include a new AI-powered self-service diagnostics system. Employees will be able to troubleshoot their own devices by asking Jamf questions on their device, such as “Why are my video calls lagging?” and receive an immediate explanation and a one-click fix. 

These improvements aren’t confined to routine task automation. They also extend into AI governance. The company introduced its AI Governance suite earlier this year, and at JNUC announced new capabilities to help IT take control of shadow AI across their networks. 

A response to shadow AI

These include a centralized AI control panel which shows admins which AI systems are running across their fleet and lets them enforce usage policies and also generate audit-ready reports. The company is extending this into the Safari, Chrome, and Edge browsers, which means organizations can prevent the upload of corporate files to personal AI accounts through browsers on managed devices. 

It means that IT doesn’t just see AI is being used but can identify which models are running and what the token costs are, while also being able to block corporate files from being uploaded to a personal account in Safari or Chrome.

For security-conscious firms, Jamf is also enabling the deployment of local inference engines. That support means companies can run AI workloads directly on Apple hardware, ensuring that prompts and sensitive data never, ever leave the device.

IT as a service

The transformation of IT means IT itself is becoming an application, and Jamf seems to be embracing this approach with a new Platform API Gateway and a Terraform provider. Together, these make it possible for IT teams to manage their entire Apple environment using “Infrastructure as Code.” 

Think GitOps for admins, in which a change to the fleet becomes a peer-reviewed pull request, and a rollback becomes as simple as a click.  

Jamf also introduced Jamf Tap, its NFC/RFID system that lets frontline workers simply tap an ID badge to instantly assign the device and sign into necessary apps, aimed at streamlining things like shift changes in warehouses.

Final announcements from the company included Ring Deployments, a rollout system that tests updates with a pilot group before expanding to the wider fleet, and a curated catalog that automatically installs and updates popular Mac apps.

JNUC 2027 takes place in Anaheim, California, from October 26–28, 2027. It will mark the company’s 25th anniversary.

items.title: After multiple deaths and injuries, NHTSA is investigating comma.ai
items.summary: Aftermarket devices that can boost or augment a vehicle’s native advanced driver assistance systems are the target of a new federal investigation this week. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation says it knows of five crashes in which drivers using devices from comma.ai crashed into stopped or slow-moving cars. Two of the crashes resulted in three deaths, and 11 people were injured in four of the five crashes, some seriously. Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz, who rose to prominence at the start of the last decade by jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations. In 2015, Hotz turned his attention to partially automated driver assists, which were gaining attention following Tesla’s exploits with its Autopilot system. Hotz first modified his own Acura to give it a more advanced driver assist that let him take his hands off the wheel, with the goal of selling his system to Tesla and replacing Mobileye as the company’s supplier. (Mobileye dropped Tesla as a customer the following year after becoming unhappy with the way the car company was using Mobileye products in unintended ways.) Read full article Comments

items.title: Mathematicians Can’t Make Sense of How OpenAI’s Agents Solved One of the Toughest Math Problems Because the AI’s “Proof” Is Borderline Incomprehensible
items.summary: Earlier this month, OpenAI announced that it had found a solution for one of the biggest unsolved problems in math, the Navier-Stokes equations, by directing 10,000 of its powerful AI agents to work on the enigma for 88 hours straight. It was an occasion fraught with controversy , however, as mathematicians accused the company of essentially stealing their work. That controversy is still rippling through the math world. But what has the AI’s solution taught us? Not a lot, as it turns out, because the proof it wrote, while technically correct, is borderline incomprehensible. “So far it’s been very difficult to really extract any human understanding from this new AI proof,” James Maynard, an Oxford mathematician, told NPR . “The paper is not written for humans,” echoed Javier Gómez-Serrano, a mathematician at Brown University who uses AI in his own research. The AI’s proof could help the field after “some serious re-writing,” he added, but “as of today, the paper doesn’t teach us much.” The Navier-Stokes equations mathematically describe how fluids, ranging from a rush of wind to the churn of ocean currents, move and behave. They’ve been used for nearly two centuries with reliable results, but why they work remains something of a mystery. Scientists have been eager to push the equations to their limits and see if their predictions could reach a breaking point where they describe a scenario that makes no sense in the real world. Reifying the equation’s importance, the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000 listed the Navier-Stokes as one of its six Millennium Problems, with the prize for solving it at $1 million. OpenAI claimed that its swarm of AI agents identified a scenario in which the fluids accelerate to an infinite velocity, creating a “blow up” or singularity — something, of course, that’s impossible in the physical universe. Hours before the announcement, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, who had been working on the Navier-Stokes problem for years, accused OpenAI of jumping on his work without notice or permission, and thereby essentially pilfering his ideas by pushing them over the finish line. He claimed that OpenAI’s work followed a similar path to his own, which he says that no one else in the field was pursuing. Because he’d been using OpenAI’s Codex tool to help with his research , he insinuated, OpenAI may have secretly accessed his notes. When he approached OpenAI about this, he claims that the company said it would credit him on its paper if he dropped his collaborator, Levent Alpöge, who was working at Anthropic. OpenAI denied the allegations but admitted that it “cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.” There’s also some groaning about the Navier-Stokes problem OpenAI says it solved. To earn the Clay Institute’s Millennium prize, mathematicians could solve either the “forced” or “unforced” version of the problem. The forced version involved an external force like gravity applied to the fluids. As laid out in a recent Scientific American piece , experts are chiefly interested in finding a purer scenario where the equations “blow up” without an external force and only with the forces within the fluid. OpenAI’s solution, however, relies on an external force. More than that, a recent proof posted by mathematicians contends that OpenAI’s solution can never lead to solving the full problem. “The most important problem is unsolved,” Luis Silvestre, a mathematician at the University of Chicago, told SciAm . “The Clay problem is settled, but the main problem for the Navier-Stokes equations is not.” Still, mathematicians are in agreement that, however technical it may be, OpenAI’s solutions are valid, even if it’ll take many more weeks to unpack the AI’s ramblings. More on AI: Fearing No Repercussions, OpenAI Admits That Its Rogue AI Agents Performed a Bunch of Other Terrifying Actions
