items.title: Software Engineer Says AI Is Causing Chaos Among Coders Who Now Just “Press Enter” All Day, Have Stopped Thinking or Understanding Software
items.summary: The advent of powerful AI coding tools has quickly made programmers heavily reliant on the tech, with experts warning that they’re slowly but surely losing the ability to write code by hand. It’s a growing existential crisis that’s significantly raising the chance of errors or security issues in AI code that hasn’t been properly vetted. Experts are warning of a “ class divide ” between those, who are over relying on AI tools and more experienced coders, or “craftsmen,” who are left wading through the former’s group’s output and applying any necessary fixes. Meanwhile, coders who’ve been instructed to use nothing but AI in a race to the bottom are losing their minds, saying they’re relegated to pushing buttons instead of taking pride in their work and building meaningful products themselves. As a user who goes by “v0xium” argued on X , the situation is getting out of hand. In a post that’s been viewed over seven million times and liked tens of thousands of times, the user warned that “it is over.” “The state of engineering right now is horrible,” the user wrote. “It has been half a month since I started a new role at a big company. Nobody knows anything here.” The engineer explained that everything at the unnamed company is being made by Anthropic’s coding assistant Claude Code. And while everybody is “being forced to ship as much as they can,” and pushing code isn’t a “bottleneck,” operations are still “slow.” “People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter,” v0xium wrote. “Everyone, literally everyone, from an L1 to an L7 engineer here is doing the same thing. Talk to Claude.” That means there’s “no sense of victory” and “nobody is resolving bugs.” “In reality, nobody is thinking anymore,” the engineer concluded. “Everything is done by LLMs. It is so soul-sucking.” The concerning tweet thread drew a somber reaction. Even X owner Elon Musk chimed in with a “ yikes .” “We are turning an entire generation of technical experts around the world into the equivalent of retirees pushing a button in front of casino slot machines,” podcast host and venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya responded . “Essentially the brain rot of doom scrolling social media is coming for your development team…” The comments highlight an alarming fundamental shift, with AI tools effectively stripping engineers of the cognitive tasks they once found fulfilling. That tedium could result in companies pushing uninspired and buggy products. “The value of automated software is not making the software faster,” Palihapitiya added. “It is understanding your intention and making the software BETTER.” A recently-coined term perfectly describes this behavior: “ meat proxies ,” or people who regurgitate the output of AI chatbots verbatim without ever critically engaging with it. “Most software engineers are facing an identity crisis bordering on depression,” VC firm Menlo Ventures partner Deedy Das tweeted earlier this year. “The craftsmen are tired. Day after day, their workload grows. Bugs seep into production. No one seems to care. Another round of AI is thrown at it. Their animosity to their colleagues rises.” “Eventually, they give up,” he added. “The craft they loved is dead.” More on AI coding: Software Engineers Are Facing an Existential Crisis As They Drown In Horrendous AI Code
items.summary_html:
The advent of powerful AI coding tools has quickly made programmers heavily reliant on the tech, with experts warning that they’re slowly but surely losing the ability to write code by hand.

It’s a growing existential crisis that’s significantly raising the chance of errors or security issues in AI code that hasn’t been properly vetted. Experts are warning of a “class divide” between those, who are over relying on AI tools and more experienced coders, or “craftsmen,” who are left wading through the former’s group’s output and applying any necessary fixes.

Meanwhile, coders who’ve been instructed to use nothing but AI in a race to the bottom are losing their minds, saying they’re relegated to pushing buttons instead of taking pride in their work and building meaningful products themselves.

As a user who goes by “v0xium” argued on X, the situation is getting out of hand. In a post that’s been viewed over seven million times and liked tens of thousands of times, the user warned that “it is over.”

“The state of engineering right now is horrible,” the user wrote. “It has been half a month since I started a new role at a big company. Nobody knows anything here.”

The engineer explained that everything at the unnamed company is being made by Anthropic’s coding assistant Claude Code.

And while everybody is “being forced to ship as much as they can,” and pushing code isn’t a “bottleneck,” operations are still “slow.”

“People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter,” v0xium wrote. “Everyone, literally everyone, from an L1 to an L7 engineer here is doing the same thing. Talk to Claude.”

That means there’s “no sense of victory” and “nobody is resolving bugs.”

“In reality, nobody is thinking anymore,” the engineer concluded. “Everything is done by LLMs. It is so soul-sucking.”

The concerning tweet thread drew a somber reaction. Even X owner Elon Musk chimed in with a “yikes.”

“We are turning an entire generation of technical experts around the world into the equivalent of retirees pushing a button in front of casino slot machines,” podcast host and venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya responded. “Essentially the brain rot of doom scrolling social media is coming for your development team…”

The comments highlight an alarming fundamental shift, with AI tools effectively stripping engineers of the cognitive tasks they once found fulfilling. That tedium could result in companies pushing uninspired and buggy products.

“The value of automated software is not making the software faster,” Palihapitiya added. “It is understanding your intention and making the software BETTER.”

A recently-coined term perfectly describes this behavior: “meat proxies,” or people who regurgitate the output of AI chatbots verbatim without ever critically engaging with it.

“Most software engineers are facing an identity crisis bordering on depression,” VC firm Menlo Ventures partner Deedy Das tweeted earlier this year. “The craftsmen are tired. Day after day, their workload grows. Bugs seep into production. No one seems to care. Another round of AI is thrown at it. Their animosity to their colleagues rises.”

“Eventually, they give up,” he added. “The craft they loved is dead.”

items.title: Reddit is ramping up its war on marketing slop
items.summary: Adam Collins, Reddit's chief communications officer, wants to preserve the platform's human qualities. Reddit Reddit is ramping up its crackdown on marketing slop. It'll limit the distribution of suspected spam so it doesn't appear in the home feed. Reddit also found a big network that violated its rules requiring disclosure of marketing activity. Reddit is ratcheting up its war on marketing slop. The company exclusively told CMO Insider that it's taking new steps to combat spam and keep human conversations at the center of its platform. First, it'll prevent suspected spam from appearing in the main home feed while it's under review. Reddit said in testing, this approach cut spam in the home feed by 28%, user reports of spam in the feed by 11%, and push notifications with spam by 7%. It plans to test this approach in search results next. Reddit is also taking a few other steps: It plans to start explaining to users why it suspects certain content is spam, rather than just showing "Removed by Reddit" It won't recommend posts or comments from accounts that have been asked to verify they're human or register their automation, but haven't yet done so "What's made Reddit really unique over the last 21 years, and special, is the humanity that you see on Reddit every day," said Adam Collins, Reddit's chief communications officer. "Our goal is to preserve that for the future as well. That's really what these efforts are about." Reddit said it had uncovered a coordinated network of 485 accounts that created more than 44,000 pieces of content across the platform, often about work and productivity. These accounts presented themselves as regular users but were, in fact, connected to businesses, violating Reddit's rules requiring marketing activity to be disclosed. Reddit said it reversed the potential benefit of the coordinated behavior by removing karma and votes that resulted from the manipulation. Karma is a score on Reddit that measures a user's reputation. The spam problem is a particular threat to Reddit, which considers its human-moderated communities to be its greatest advantage over other social platforms. Reddit vs. AI After going public in 2024, Reddit increased advertising on its forums and entered into partnerships with OpenAI and Google. Marketers took note and have been racing to create content for Reddit. Brands particularly hope their efforts will help them show up in AI search , where Reddit is highly cited. The problem: Self-promotional content from brands, especially if they use AI to make it, risks harming the human quality that Reddit sees as setting itself apart from other platforms. A July report from the AI detection firm Pangram found that Reddit was the least affected by AI among five platforms, with 3% of its short-form content flagged as AI. LinkedIn was at the high end at 30%. Reddit has been proactive. In July, Reddit announced tools to combat AI-enabled promotional content and spam. Reddit said at the time that these tools helped catch 23 million spam views per day and cut users' exposure to spam by about 20% in the period from January to March 2026, compared to the prior three months. Collins said that while some commercial spam is obvious to users, these tools were able to catch subtler instances, such as spam accounts that appeared to be people interacting with each other. Moderation is an ongoing Whac-A-Mole game, though, and as long as spammers keep finding workarounds, Reddit's work will continue. "The conversations that are happening on Reddit have value," Collins said. "We have to continue to adjust and continue to improve our efforts to remove that kind of content to make sure that it continues to be that great value of a place for users." What marketers are saying Agency execs who spoke with CMO Insider said brands that use Reddit as intended — by listening to their consumers and being useful to them — won't be affected by the spam crackdown. "The brands that win will earn participation by being transparent, useful, and native to each community, while giving customers genuine reasons to talk about them," said Joe Gagliese, co-CEO of Viral Nation. Brian Yamada, chief innovation officer at VML, said the sugar rush some brands got by manipulating Reddit would be short-lived. Slop isn't going away, though, he added. "It's not just a Reddit problem," Yamada said. "The flood of generative AI slop is likely to continue as brands or companies are looking for shortcuts or cheats to get visible." Collins said Reddit has an appeals process to correct false positives and that it's letting suspected spam remain while it's under review. Moderators and users play an important gatekeeping role on Reddit, and Collins said that wouldn't change. Moderators can still review and approve content for their communities, but limiting suspected spam during a review period would help prevent users from being exposed to it, he said. Reddit is also taking a few other steps:

  • It plans to start explaining to users why it suspects certain content is spam, rather than just showing "Removed by Reddit"
  • It won't recommend posts or comments from accounts that have been asked to verify they're human or register their automation, but haven't yet done so

"What's made Reddit really unique over the last 21 years, and special, is the humanity that you see on Reddit every day," said Adam Collins, Reddit's chief communications officer. "Our goal is to preserve that for the future as well. That's really what these efforts are about."

Reddit said it had uncovered a coordinated network of 485 accounts that created more than 44,000 pieces of content across the platform, often about work and productivity. Reddit said it reversed the potential benefit of the coordinated behavior by removing karma and votes that resulted from the manipulation. Karma is a score on Reddit that measures a user's reputation.

The spam problem is a particular threat to Reddit, which considers its human-moderated communities to be its greatest advantage over other social platforms.

Reddit vs. AI

After going public in 2024, Reddit increased advertising on its forums and entered into partnerships with OpenAI and Google.

Marketers took note and have been racing to create content for Reddit. Brands particularly hope their efforts will help them show up in AI search, where Reddit is highly cited. The problem: Self-promotional content from brands, especially if they use AI to make it, risks harming the human quality that Reddit sees as setting itself apart from other platforms.

A July report from the AI detection firm Pangram found that Reddit was the least affected by AI among five platforms, with 3% of its short-form content flagged as AI. LinkedIn was at the high end at 30%.

Reddit has been proactive. In July, Reddit announced tools to combat AI-enabled promotional content and spam.

Reddit said at the time that these tools helped catch 23 million spam views per day and cut users' exposure to spam by about 20% in the period from January to March 2026, compared to the prior three months.

Collins said that while some commercial spam is obvious to users, these tools were able to catch subtler instances, such as spam accounts that appeared to be people interacting with each other.

Moderation is an ongoing Whac-A-Mole game, though, and as long as spammers keep finding workarounds, Reddit's work will continue.

"The conversations that are happening on Reddit have value," Collins said. "We have to continue to adjust and continue to improve our efforts to remove that kind of content to make sure that it continues to be that great value of a place for users."

What marketers are saying

Agency execs who spoke with CMO Insider said brands that use Reddit as intended — by listening to their consumers and being useful to them — won't be affected by the spam crackdown.

"The brands that win will earn participation by being transparent, useful, and native to each community, while giving customers genuine reasons to talk about them," said Joe Gagliese, co-CEO of Viral Nation.

Brian Yamada, chief innovation officer at VML, said the sugar rush some brands got by manipulating Reddit would be short-lived.

Slop isn't going away, though, he added.

"It's not just a Reddit problem," Yamada said. "The flood of generative AI slop is likely to continue as brands or companies are looking for shortcuts or cheats to get visible."

Collins said Reddit has an appeals process to correct false positives and that it's letting suspected spam remain while it's under review.

Moderators and users play an important gatekeeping role on Reddit, and Collins said that wouldn't change. Moderators can still review and approve content for their communities, but limiting suspected spam during a review period would help prevent users from being exposed to it, he said.

items.title: Adtech vet Brian O'Kelley's startup is pivoting to AI agents and rebranding with a new name
items.summary: Apostra cofounders Brian O'Kelley and Anne Coghlan Franco Vogt Pivot! Adtech veteran Brian O'Kelley's Scope3 startup is rebranding. Apostra wants to become a leader in agentic AI advertising. The startup acts as an "orchestration layer" connecting advertiser agents with publisher agents. Adtech veteran Brian O'Kelley , once described as the "master of the hard pivot," is pushing the reset button again. O'Kelley and his cofounder, Anne Coghlan, exclusively told CMO Insider that they are renaming their company from Scope3 to Apostra as they aim to make the startup a leader in agentic AI advertising. They describe Apostra as a platform that connects advertisers' AI agents with AI agents representing media sellers, so that marketers don't have to build separate integrations with potentially thousands of publishers, platforms, and other media providers. O'Kelley told CMO Insider that advertising has been constrained by a fragmented media infrastructure, manual processes, and a programmatic advertising landscape organized around real-time bidding but not optimized for the most highly valued ad placements. "You can't buy anything that's not a rectangle with a cookie," O'Kelley said. Apostra is designed to let AI agents handle the work of negotiating and managing ad campaigns across various publishers, including online placements, linear TV, and in-store audio, and to connect brands with creators and clippers. The advertiser agent makes the media owner's agent aware of the marketer's goals, while the media owner's agent can bring forward details about the publisher's audience and potential ad opportunities. Apostra uses AdCP, a protocol created last year by a consortium of adtech companies, including Scope3, that provides a common language for agents to interact. Apostra said this makes it easier for marketers to place ads in channels such as "walled garden" social platforms , podcasts, or out-of-home advertising, which are traditionally harder to reach through programmatic ad buying. Unlike traditional programmatic advertising , this doesn't involve software bidding on individual ad impressions in real time. Instead, the agents can automate parts of the slower process of discovering, negotiating, approving, and executing media deals. The company says it's working with 40 media partners and has built AdCP adapters for major ad platforms, including Google, Meta, Amazon, Reddit, and ChatGPT Ads. Apostra said it is already running seven-figure campaigns through the system. O'Kelley said an unnamed major brand began with a $1 million US campaign in April, then expanded the experiment into several other markets and channels. While it may sound like an ad network, Apostra said it functions more like a neutral gateway. It doesn't charge transaction fees or a percentage of media spend like other adtech platforms, but will instead sell add-on "intelligence capabilities" such as campaign proposal evaluation, negotiation support, catalog integration, and currency handling. Apostra says that by using its technology, marketers could discover media they wouldn't otherwise access through traditional sales channels, and publishers could gain access to more advertiser demand and reduce the costs of selling ad space. The process isn't necessarily fully autonomous. Publishers can still require human approval for campaigns, while brands can retain control over things like how the creative looks and the broader strategy. O'Kelley gave the example of a media partner whose AI agent posts proposed ads to a Slack channel for a human employee to review. 'Master of the hard pivot' The launch of Apostra marks another twist in O'Kelley's long adtech career. items.title: Legal AI startup Spellbook hired a new CMO — and she has strong opinions on avoiding 'creepy' AI marketing
items.summary: Meltem Kuran-Berkowitz has joined Spellbook as its chief marketing officer. Meltem Kuran Berkowitz Legal AI startup Spellbook has appointed Meltem Kuran-Berkowitz as its CMO. Kuran-Berkowitz wants Spellbook's marketing to help it hit the $100 million mark. Spellbook is embracing AI, but she draws the line at using it to impersonate human communication. The new CMO of a legal tech startup has a message for marketers: Stop using AI to pretend to be human. Spellbook, which offers AI tools for drafting and analyzing legal contracts, exclusively told CMO Insider that it had appointed Meltem Kuran-Berkowitz as its chief marketing officer. She is taking the top marketing role full time after a brief stint freelancing for the company. Kuran-Berkowitz previously spent five and a half years as head of growth at the payroll and workforce platform Deel, overseeing the company's growth to $1 billion in annual recurring revenue. Kuran-Berkowitz joins Spellbook as it, too, is leveling up. In October 2025, the company raised $50 million in Series B funding at a $350 million valuation, led by Khosla Ventures. In March, the company secured a $40 million debt facility, which it said it would put toward acquiring rival generative AI companies. The legal tech space is booming. Investors poured $2 billion into startups building for the legal sector in the first half of this year, per the market research firm Crunchbase, as AI has transformed one of Silicon Valley's sleepier corners into one of its hottest. Legal AI specialists like Harvey and Legora are competing alongside tech giants like OpenAI as law firms and corporate legal teams race to adopt tools that promise to automate grunt work. Kuran-Berkowitz said an early measure of her success will be helping the company hit $100 million in revenue by the end of this year. Getting there, she said, means making far more potential customers aware of the company. She doesn't plan to flood them with AI-generated marketing, though. "If we're going to get somebody's eyeballs, whether it's in an email or an Instagram post, we're going to be honest with you about it: it's going to be made from another human, and we're not going to waste your time," Kuran-Berkowitz said. There are places where Kuran-Berkowitz thinks AI can be useful in marketing, from mining sales calls for insights to building internal presentation decks . She draws the line when it starts to impersonate human interaction. "My inbox has blown out with cold emails because now everybody can write them. Now, everybody finds the one niche thing we have in common," Kuran-Berkowitz said. She gave the example of AI-personalized cold emails that manufacture tenuous connections with lines like: "I was in Italy once." She said that kind of AI-generated familiarity "feels creepy." "I feel very strongly towards those things, and I just don't want to do that to people," Kuran-Berkowitz said. Spellbook CEO Scott Stevenson also has strong opinions on his employees' use of AI. Earlier this month, he wrote a memo encouraging staffers to write the rough, " D+ version " of their ideas first, before leaning on AI to polish their proposals. Spellbook's marketing plan Kuran-Berkowitz said she doesn't want to follow legal tech startups like Harvey and Legora in going down the celebrity-sponsorship marketing route. Instead, she wants "every single touchpoint with the customer to be meaningful," and explain what the product does. Her media strategy involves showing up in the places where Spellbook's potential customers already spend their time — from closed communities to newsletters — without, as Kuran-Berkowitz puts it, "ruining the vibes." "Where can we fit ourselves nicely without ruining the vibes? And then what can we produce and add to the vibes?" she said. This summer, for example, Spellbook created a $1 million fellowship fund for law students to help them streamline wonky legal workflows. Ultimately, Kuran-Berkowitz wants to expand perceptions of Spellbook beyond the redlining tool that made its name. She wants Spellbook to be the default brand people associate with managing contracts. "The world runs on contracts," she said. "That's just a fact, and the contracts run on Spellbook." items.title: Anthropic made Opus 5.5 cheaper. Then it broke four things your agent depends on.
items.summary: Anthropic made Claude Opus 5.5 , released on Tuesday, cheaper than its predecessor , cutting the price from $5 to $4 per million input tokens and from $25 to $20 per million output tokens. The 1 million-token context window and 128,000-token maximum output are unchanged. On paper, that makes upgrading an easy decision. In practice, it may not be as simple as changing the model ID. Anthropic’s migration guide flags four breaking changes that can cause requests built for Opus 5 to return 400 errors after switching to Opus 5.5. Several other changes won’t trigger an error but could still change how an existing agent behaves. Anthropic’s migration guide flags four breaking changes that can cause requests built for Opus 5 to return 400 errors after switching to Opus 5.5. Thinking is always on The first change involves thinking controls. Opus 5.5 returns a 400 error when a request sets thinking to disabled or uses enabled with budget_tokens , leaving effort as the way to control how much reasoning the model does. Agents that previously switched thinking off for simple steps to save time and tokens will need to assign those steps a lower effort level instead. Because thinking is now always on, responses begin with thinking blocks, so code that assumes the first content block is text will also need to change. The default effort level has also dropped from high on Opus 5 to medium on Opus 5.5, so requests that omit the parameter will quietly run at a lower setting. Anthropic recommends setting effort explicitly and re-running effort evaluations, since the right level for each step may have shifted along with cost and latency. No more forced tool calls Forced tool use no longer works either, as setting tool_choice to any or tool returns a 400 error, including on the token counting endpoint, where cost estimates built on those settings will fail along with the requests they were meant to price. Many agent loops force a call when a step has to query a database, run code, or reach another service, and Anthropic’s replacement is auto -combined with strict tool use or structured outputs, with the prompt stating when the tool applies. Routing and conversation history Thinking blocks are now tied to the model and conversation that produced them. On the Claude API, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 are the only other models that can read Opus 5.5 thinking blocks, so a router or fallback that hands a conversation to any other model will run those turns without the earlier reasoning instead of returning an error. That adds another layer for teams already watching whether their agent calls are quietly being routed to an older model . Opus 5.5 can read thinking blocks from Opus 5 and earlier Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku models, but not from Fable or Mythos. Conversations must also stay append-only for those blocks to remain valid. Trimming old messages, changing tool definitions, summarizing earlier context on the client side, or rewriting the system prompt mid-conversation invalidates existing thinking blocks, and for accounts created on or after August 31, 2026 , at midnight UTC, replaying a thinking block after one of those edits returns a 400 error by default. Older accounts get no error, but the invalid blocks still reach the model, and Anthropic says future models will enforce the check for all accounts. Integrations that never edit earlier turns need no code change, and Anthropic says Claude Code, claude.ai, Claude Managed Agents, and the Claude Agent SDK already work this way, while agents that compact their own context should follow the company’s preserved thinking documentation. The fourth change affects computer-use agents on the Claude API and Google Cloud, where Opus 5.5 rejects the computer_20251124 tool and accepts computer use only through the computer_toolset_20260801 toolset. The request itself gets simpler because the beta header goes away and the toolset entry takes no name or display dimensions, but the agent loop needs more work. Each action now arrives as its own tool_use block identified by the block’s name rather than input.action , a single turn can contain several of them, and every result has to echo toolset_name . The older tool still works on Amazon Bedrock, and Anthropic directs developers on other platforms to the computer use tool’s compatibility documentation. …a router or fallback that hands a conversation to any other model will run those turns without the earlier reasoning instead of returning an error. Changes that won’t throw errors The change most likely to go unnoticed doesn’t produce an error at all. On Opus 5, text Claude writes between tool calls comes back as text blocks, but on Opus 5.5 that narration arrives as progress-update thinking blocks, and at the default thinking.display setting of omitted those blocks are empty. Any agent interface that streams that narration to users will go silent between tool calls until developers set display to updates, a beta option that returns progress updates while keeping reasoning hidden, or to summarized, which returns both, and then render each non-empty thinking block ahead of the tool call it precedes. Opus 5.5 also ships with broader safety classifiers. It can return a stop_reason of refusal with stop_details categories that now include bio and reasoning_extraction alongside cyber, and Anthropic’s server-side fallback won’t retry requests declined under reasoning_extraction, handing the refusal back to the application instead. Agents that don’t handle refusals will stop mid-task, a problem developers have already run into with OpenAI’s safety system cutting off API responses . The change most likely to go unnoticed doesn’t produce an error at all. Upgrading from older models Teams coming from Opus 4.8 need to work through the Opus 5 migration first, which covers thinking being on by default and the response-shape changes that follow, before applying the Opus 5.5 changes. Teams on Opus 4.7 or earlier have more ground to cover, and those on models older than Opus 4.7 also face rejected sampling parameters, rejected manual extended thinking, removed prefill, and a newer tokenizer. Claude Managed Agents users only need to change the model name. Developers working in Claude Code can run /claude-api migrate to apply the model ID swap, parameter changes, prefill replacement, and effort calibration across a codebase before reviewing a checklist of items to verify by hand. Anthropic recommends testing the migration in a development environment before switching production traffic. Developers maintaining their own integrations will need to test the pieces around the model, too. Tool calls, model handoffs, conversation history, and user-facing progress updates can all behave differently after the switch, because agent failures often originate outside the model itself .

items.title: I’m a travel influencer who works every day while building my own business. Here are 4 ways I avoid burnout.
items.summary: The offers and details on this page may have updated or changed since the time of publication. See our article on Business Insider for current information. Rhiannon Wood, 26, started her journey as a solo-traveler and 'micro influencer' by first taking odd jobs around the world. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood Rhiannon Wood, 26, is a travel influencer with about 60,000 Instagram followers. She works without an agent, preferring the freedom that comes with managing her own content. Here are the ways she avoids burnout from the extra workload an agent would normally absorb. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rhiannon Wood , a 26-year-old travel micro influencer who runs a social media business and leads group tours around the world. It has been edited for length and clarity. I built my social media following from the ground up as a postgrad student working odd jobs around the world. Today, my work as a travel influencer continues to grow by the day, both in my following and in the number of brand deals I secure. I also partner with tourism companies to earn money leading adventure group trips around the world, though I'm building my own travel agency to launch next year. I take pride in doing everything myself, but there's a downside to taking on all the work: it sometimes feels like I'm skirting on the edge of burnout. I work almost every day negotiating deals, planning trips, scheduling posts, and engaging with my audience. While some influencers hire a social media agent to reduce their workload, I choose to work without one. Earlier this year, several agencies offered to take 25% to 30% of my earnings in exchange for potentially securing more brand deals — and income — for me. Ultimately, I declined. It's unclear whether working without an agent earns me more or less money, but, for now, I prefer the freedom and control of handling the work myself. I can post and interact with my followers exactly when and how I want. I also have a highly engaged account , which I've used to build trust with the online and offline communities I've cultivated over the years. One bad interaction could jeopardize that trust. Still, I've had to learn that working every day isn't sustainable. I've gotten better at stepping away from my work and making time to rest, rather than feeling like I always need to be doing something. Here's how I stay on top of my work while ensuring I have a life outside it. Learn how to say no to plans Rhiannon Wood is a social media influencer who leads travel group trips around the world. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood I'm normally the sort of person who says yes to everything . But for the first time, I'm saying no to travel plans later this year and instead am choosing to stay in one place for longer. I think it's important to recognize that rest — as much as work, travel, and having fun — is a priority, too. I'm still learning how to say no to plans, or at least how to schedule in no plans at all. I scheduled a rest period for myself this summer because I signed up for a lot of group trips from late last year through the end of this September, and I am so glad I was able to rest for a week to reset my mind and body. Understand what rest looks like for you Rhiannon Wood emphasizes taking rest when needed and to not feel bad about doing so. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood For me, rest involves stopping, sitting, and doing nothing for an entire day without feeling bad about it. I'm a big believer that taking the time to rest will eventually make you more productive. Working out can also be a form of rest for some, including me. Going to the gym and the climbing gym is a big hobby of mine, and I never film content or do work there. Instead, I see it as personal gain: I'm able to go at my own pace, on my own time. Adopt a positive frame of mind Rhiannon Wood has amassed over 60,000 followers on Instagram. Analytics aren't the only measure of success, she said, pointing also to the community she has made over the years. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood If I keep telling myself I'm burned out from work, I'll believe it. The same goes for telling myself that I'm rested, have a lot of time to myself, and am excited about what's next: positive affirmations often lead me to positive results in my life and work. I take this mindset into how I look at my account's engagement analytics, too. While it is healthy to validate your emotions, feel them fully, and understand what is causing you stress, it's also healthy to find a silver lining in whatever is causing it. If I see a decrease in engagement or my follower count, I try to look at my work from an external frame of mind and be grateful for the number of spots for a group trip I've sold, for example, which means that the people who are going on them want to spend time with my community and me. That's arguably more important than my follower count, anyway. Have delusional self-belief in yourself Rhiannon Wood said she can count on her strong work ethic and positive mindset to carry her through the ups and downs of her career. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood I try to remind myself that taking risks is necessary if I want to be rewarded in my line of work. Nothing comes easily, and most goals require you to chip away at them little by little. When work feels more stressful than usual, I focus on chipping away at my tasks in a sensible order. Even if I can't yet see exactly how my career path will unfold, I believe in myself and my ability to get where I want to go because I know I'm ambitious and have a strong work ethic. It's a sort of delusional self-belief, but it's served me well. I might not have enough money or all the answers right now, but I believe I'll find a way to make it happen. Somehow, it usually works out. Read the original article on Business Insider

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rhiannon Wood, a 26-year-old travel micro influencer who runs a social media business and leads group tours around the world. It has been edited for length and clarity.

I built my social media following from the ground up as a postgrad student working odd jobs around the world.

Today, my work as a travel influencer continues to grow by the day, both in my following and in the number of brand deals I secure. I also partner with tourism companies to earn money leading adventure group trips around the world, though I'm building my own travel agency to launch next year.

It's unclear whether working without an agent earns me more or less money, but, for now, I prefer the freedom and control of handling the work myself.

I can post and interact with my followers exactly when and how I want. I also have a highly engaged account, which I've used to build trust with the online and offline communities I've cultivated over the years. One bad interaction could jeopardize that trust.

Still, I've had to learn that working every day isn't sustainable. I've gotten better at stepping away from my work and making time to rest, rather than feeling like I always need to be doing something.

Here's how I stay on top of my work while ensuring I have a life outside it.

Learn how to say no to plansRhiannon Wood is a social media influencer who leads travel group trips around the world.

Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood

I'm normally the sort of person who says yes to everything.

But for the first time, I'm saying no to travel plans later this year and instead am choosing to stay in one place for longer. I think it's important to recognize that rest — as much as work, travel, and having fun — is a priority, too.

I'm still learning how to say no to plans, or at least how to schedule in no plans at all. I scheduled a rest period for myself this summer because I signed up for a lot of group trips from late last year through the end of this September, and I am so glad I was able to rest for a week to reset my mind and body.

Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood

For me, rest involves stopping, sitting, and doing nothing for an entire day without feeling bad about it. I'm a big believer that taking the time to rest will eventually make you more productive.

Working out can also be a form of rest for some, including me. Going to the gym and the climbing gym is a big hobby of mine, and I never film content or do work there.

Instead, I see it as personal gain: I'm able to go at my own pace, on my own time.

Adopt a positive frame of mindRhiannon Wood has amassed over 60,000 followers on Instagram. Analytics aren't the only measure of success, she said, pointing also to the community she has made over the years.

Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood

If I keep telling myself I'm burned out from work, I'll believe it.

The same goes for telling myself that I'm rested, have a lot of time to myself, and am excited about what's next: positive affirmations often lead me to positive results in my life and work.

I take this mindset into how I look at my account's engagement analytics, too. While it is healthy to validate your emotions, feel them fully, and understand what is causing you stress, it's also healthy to find a silver lining in whatever is causing it.

If I see a decrease in engagement or my follower count, I try to look at my work from an external frame of mind and be grateful for the number of spots for a group trip I've sold, for example, which means that the people who are going on them want to spend time with my community and me.

That's arguably more important than my follower count, anyway.

Have delusional self-belief in yourselfRhiannon Wood said she can count on her strong work ethic and positive mindset to carry her through the ups and downs of her career.

Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood

I try to remind myself that taking risks is necessary if I want to be rewarded in my line of work. Nothing comes easily, and most goals require you to chip away at them little by little.

When work feels more stressful than usual, I focus on chipping away at my tasks in a sensible order.

Even if I can't yet see exactly how my career path will unfold, I believe in myself and my ability to get where I want to go because I know I'm ambitious and have a strong work ethic.

It's a sort of delusional self-belief, but it's served me well. I might not have enough money or all the answers right now, but I believe I'll find a way to make it happen.

Somehow, it usually works out.

items.title: When AI disagrees, people change how they perceive the technology—not their original view
items.summary: When an AI chatbot agrees with our reasoning in resolving a social dilemma, we may become more confident in our opinions. But when the chatbot disagrees, we may simply dismiss the challenge rather than reconsider our views. That's according to new research from the University of Michigan examining how people respond when artificial intelligence weighs in on personal and interpersonal dilemmas.

items.title: OpenAI is enlisting an influencer army to make it look 'good for the world'
items.summary: OpenAI; Getty Images; Alyssa Powell/BI OpenAI is ramping up its influencer strategy as AI hate spikes. It's asking creators to share how ChatGPT is improving their lives and is "good for the world." Not on the messaging agenda: killer robots or noisy data centers. AI's reputation is in hot water. Can influencers save it? OpenAI has been ramping up its creator marketing efforts as AI safety concerns take center stage. The company isn't asking influencers to assuage fears that a rogue AI could destroy humanity . Instead, it's prompting them to showcase why ChatGPT is "cool , " per one influencer talent manager , or how it can support work that's "good for the world," according to one campaign pitch viewed by Business Insider. OpenAI doubled the number of sponsored Instagram posts promoting ChatGPT from 61 in June to 122 in July, and then increased it further to 141 in August, according to data compiled by the influencer marketing platform HypeAuditor. Business Insider reviewed dozens of sponsored posts for OpenAI's ChatGPT product, and spoke with six managers and creators who had worked with the company. The company is casting a wide net, reaching out to parenting and fitness influencers as well as tech-savvy creators to broaden its user base and grow its advertising business. The message: ChatGPT can help you parent, run a business, create content, plan a workout, and be a good person. OpenAI's influencer strategy can be split into two buckets: getting businesses to pay for enterprise tools and keeping millions of consumers coming back to ChatGPT. Working with OpenAI can be risky for creators. Some influencers who post sponsored content for AI companies are getting dragged by their audiences. A small group of creators who attended an OpenAI brand trip in August were told their content was "morally bankrupt" and "dystopian" in their comments sections. That hasn't stopped companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Higgsfield AI from pitching influencers. "In the five inboxes that I manage alone, every single day, I would say at least 15 emails are from an AI company or some AI feature," Amanda Acevedo, a talent manager at G&B Digital Management, told Business Insider. Creator Natasha Badger, who makes content about marketing and tech, said it was a "big war" between AI companies over "who can get the most market share and work with the most influencers." Influencers are painting OpenAI's portrait Creators are a crucial part of OpenAI's public relations. They're "how people get information and learn about our products," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Founders-turned-influencers have been the cream of the crop for OpenAI's #ad strategy. Acevedo said the company is keen on working with creators who can tell a vivid story about how they're strategically using AI to "build an actual business." Badger, for instance, worked with OpenAI in July to promote its ChatGPT Work tools. She's one of many influencer-entrepreneurs the AI company is casting in short-form video ads across Instagram and TikTok. In the sponsored post, Badger walks through how she used ChatGPT to build a presentation. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Natasha Badger (@natashabadger) "Most people following any of us have ChatGPT already," Badger said. "They don't need to convert users. It's more getting people to continue going to ChatGPT as your go-to LLM." OpenAI has been open to hearing influencers' content ideas rather than pushing a narrow script, insiders who've worked on campaigns said. "They want it to be catered to a specific use case that resonates with our lives and day-to-day," Badger said. OpenAI's influencer strategy, however, is growing well beyond B2B marketing. At the start of September, The Shade Room — a meme page with over 28 million Instagram followers — shared a sponsored post with ChatGPT. It wasn't a demo of how AI could streamline your workflow. It was a word search puzzle generated by ChatGPT. One talent manager said OpenAI representatives had expressed interest in working with fitness creators, since health and running questions are such common use cases for ChatGPT. HypeAuditor's analysis of hundreds of Instagram posts promoting ChatGPT found these were the core topics: Coding Productivity Career development Health Travel Education Content creation Shopping Home projects In a recent back-to-school partnership, Martha Dove, a mother of five, shared how she's using ChatGPT to help her kids with their math homework. The ad specifically promotes tools like ChatGPT's "study mode" and teen safety features. Acevedo said there's one key message AI brands across the board are pushing with creators: AI is an assistant, "not a replacement." "I'm still her mom and her teachers are still her teachers — this isn't replacing any of that," Dove emphasized in her video. OpenAI is beefing up its influencer resources As OpenAI hires more influencers, it's building a team of tech veterans who know the inner workings of creator partnerships. OpenAI has hired a handful of talent from platforms like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and Snapchat, according to a review of OpenAI staffers' LinkedIn profiles. Most visibly, in February, OpenAI poached Charles Porch, Instagram's longtime head of partnerships. Charles Porch joined OpenAI after leaving Meta in 2026. Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Vanity Fair The AI company has also tapped the influencer marketing agency Viral Nation — which has worked with major tech companies like Meta, Google, and Uber — to handle elements of its creator campaigns. One job of these longtime influencer marketers is to make creators feel like AI isn't the enemy. "There is so much tension between AI and the creator economy," Acevedo said. She sees commissioning sponsored posts as a way for OpenAI to "help bridge that gap — that we're not against each other." Read the original article on Business Insider

  • Productivity
  • Career development
  • Health
  • Travel
  • Education
  • Content creation
  • Shopping
  • Home projects

As OpenAI hires more influencers, it's building a team of tech veterans who know the inner workings of creator partnerships.

OpenAI has hired a handful of talent from platforms like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and Snapchat, according to a review of OpenAI staffers' LinkedIn profiles. Most visibly, in February, OpenAI poached Charles Porch, Instagram's longtime head of partnerships.

Charles Porch joined OpenAI after leaving Meta in 2026.

Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Vanity Fair

The AI company has also tapped the influencer marketing agency Viral Nation — which has worked with major tech companies like Meta, Google, and Uber — to handle elements of its creator campaigns.

One job of these longtime influencer marketers is to make creators feel like AI isn't the enemy.

items.summary_html:
Patreon co-founder Sam Yam is joing OpenAI to lead Creator Product. | Image: The Verge

OpenAI has hired three former Patreon execs to anchor its product strategy for creators. items.title: The Emerging M&A Map For AI Agent Security
items.summary: AI agents are quickly becoming part of the enterprise. They browse the web, write code, access files, trigger APIs and interact with internal systems. That creates enormous productivity potential, but it also creates a new security problem: Companies now need to protect not only users, devices and applications, but software actors that can take actions on their behalf. AI agents are becoming a new class of enterprise identity An agent may access corporate files, query databases, send emails or execute code. Once it has that level of access, it needs permissions, monitoring and governance. Companies will need to know which agent accessed what information, which systems it connected to, and whether the actions it took were authorized. As enterprises move from experimenting with a few agents to deploying hundreds of them, agent identity will become another important layer of cybersecurity. The challenge is that these identities are not passive. Agents can move between systems, invoke tools and make decisions, which makes controlling them more complex than managing traditional users or service accounts. The value will sit in specific control points This market will probably not develop as one broad category called “AI security.” The real opportunity will be around specific control points. One company may protect agent identity, another may control the data an agent can access, while others may focus on prompts, MCP servers, plug-ins, traffic or auditability. We are already seeing activity around these areas. Kiteworks recently acquired Israeli startup Bonfy.AI, which focuses on real-time data classification and policy enforcement. Israeli cybersecurity startup Huskeys , meanwhile, raised a $27 million Series A led by Blackstone and focuses on understanding and securing increasingly complex internet traffic, including traffic generated by autonomous systems. These companies are solving different problems, but together they show how the market may begin to separate into distinct security layers. These control points are creating a new M&A map Identity providers may extend identity governance to autonomous agents. Data-security vendors may need to control what information agents can access. Cybersecurity platforms, cloud companies and enterprise software vendors may eventually need agent-security capabilities embedded directly into their products. For entrepreneurs, this means that “AI security” may already be too broad a positioning. The more important question is what exactly the company controls. Itay Sagie is a strategic adviser to tech companies, investors, CEOs and boards, specializing in strategy, growth and M&A. He is a guest contributor to Crunchbase News and a university lecturer on strategy, finance and entrepreneurship. Learn more at SagieCapital.com and connect with him on LinkedIn . items.title: Mozilla is plastering New York with posters mocking tech billionaires as part of a new marketing campaign
items.summary: The Mozilla Foundation is putting up posters in New York calling out Big Tech execs as part of a new marketing campaign promoting its fellowship program. Courtesy of the Mozilla Foundation. The Mozilla Foundation is coming after Big Tech in a new ad campaign launching Wednesday. The ads criticize execs like Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk and praise Mozilla's own tech fellows. The campaign features a series of posters hung near the United Nations and tech-worker hot spots. The Mozilla Foundation isn't holding back its disdain for Big Tech leaders. This week, it's hanging up posters around New York calling out tech executives like Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk and hyping up its own class of technology fellows as part of a new ad campaign. The campaign is meant to juxtapose the work of Musk, Zuckerberg, and Jeff Bezos with lesser-known projects from technologists like Rose Njeri Tunguru, a member of Mozilla's fellowship program who is building infrastructure to help Kenyans independently verify election results. "What we really wanted to do was poke a hole in the mythology that tech innovation happens in one particular way," said Ziyaad Bhorat, Mozilla's vice president of imagination and strategic growth. Society is "hyper-focused on one idea of tech genius" and "a lot of people are working on better things and alternatives," he said. The goal is to build awareness of the work of Mozilla's fellow class and, hopefully, drive additional online attention as passersby spot the posters and share them on social media. The Mozilla Foundation is a nonprofit that owns Mozilla Corporation, a for-profit subsidiary that makes the web browser Firefox and other products. It works with techies, researchers, and others to fund projects that support an open internet, ethical data practices, and trustworthy AI tools. Mozilla doesn't pull its punches in the ads when attacking tech's billionaire class. Its poster of Zuckerberg, for example, references troubles his company, Meta, has run into with its camera glasses, which some wearers have used to harass strangers and prank store workers . "Mark gets into eyewear" and "makes creepers, peepers," it reads. Meta executives have acknowledged bad behavior tied to their glasses, with Instagram's CEO, Adam Mosseri, writing in July that the company would take down footage if users were "surreptitiously taking videos of other people and harassing them and then posting them on our platform." A Meta spokesperson said the company disables the cameras on any glasses where a user has removed the LED light that indicates a photo or video is being taken. The company said it ran an awareness campaign to help educate people about how the glasses work in communities where they are prevalent. Jeff Bezos is featured on a poster from Mozilla's new ad campaign. His company, Blue Origin, paused its space tourism program in January. Courtesy of the Mozilla Foundation. Mozilla has done other anti-establishment ad campaigns to promote its work, enlisting an anonymous creative collective called Basement Freaks to make videos for its annual tech report in January. Its latest campaign arrives at a moment when many Americans are wary of Big Tech and its leaders. Americans worry about potential job losses tied to artificial intelligence, and the arrival of new surveillance technologies like Flock cameras . Half of US adults said they were more "concerned than excited" about the increased use of AI in daily life, according to a June survey from the Pew Research Center. Billionaires are also unpopular among US adults. In a March poll by the University of Massachusetts Lowell and YouGov, Musk's net favorability was -16%, while Zuckerberg's was -43%. "The general population feels a little bit of a loss of what they can do personally, and they feel as though they're resigned to this future that is dictated by Silicon Valley or the most powerful in these Big Tech companies," said Emma Bates, a fractional CMO at Mozilla who served as a strategic advisor and collaborator on the campaign. "They don't just have to resign to the fact that AI and robots are going to take over the world. It's not the only way." Mozilla is running what's called a "wild postings" campaign, a street-level advertising tactic where posters are slapped onto the sides of buildings or barricades rather than placed at traditional billboard sites. The organization is strategically placing its posters. It's putting some near the United Nations building that is currently hosting its General Assembly, as well as in tech-worker hubs like Hudson Yards, NoHo, and Dumbo. It's also hiring influencers to visit the poster sites and make content about them for social media. "We know that this campaign will be a little bit provocative, and we're hoping that then leads to more people sharing it and getting the message out," Bates said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: OpenAI cut GPT-6 token prices in half. The bigger lever may be the cache.
items.summary: OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol and Luna on Tuesday, essentially more affordable versions of GPT-6 Astra that come closer to Astra on alignment than GPT-5.6 Sol did , but still fall short of the flagship model. Most notably, the AI company slashed token prices, making the new GPT-6 models significantly cheaper to use. Beyond token prices, though, OpenAI says better caching can also help developers push costs down even more. Per OpenAI : “Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost,” with API prices for Sol and Luna down 50% compared to their GPT-5.6 counterparts (58% lower for Luna output tokens). What improvements? Namely, higher cache-hit rates by default, the ability to preserve earlier context even when reasoning effort and tool availability change, and new tools to monitor and diagnose caching performance. Reuse context without starting over Prompt caching isn’t, of course, novel to the new GPT-6 models themselves. But the upgraded Sol and Luna come with improvements designed to keep more previously processed context reusable as the agent moves forward on a task. “We’ve improved prompt caching for GPT‑6 to deliver higher cache hit rates by default, helping agents reuse more context, respond faster, and benefit from discounts of 90% on cached input-token reads.” That adds another opportunity to lower the already low API price tag, though the 90% cached-input discount matches GPT-5.6 pricing; what’s new is how often the cache gets hit. By using cached context to reuse work it’s already done, the model doesn’t have to process the same context again from scratch for every single call, thereby reducing latency — and token costs. Beyond this higher default cache-hit rate, OpenAI says the new GPT-6 models offer more flexibility to optimize caching performance. The new models let developers adjust reasoning effort and tool availability without having to break the cache. This way, an agent can scale reasoning effort up and down based on how difficult a step is, then make different tools available depending on what the task requires without disturbing earlier cached context — again, a win for both speed and cost. See what gets cached and what doesn’t GPT-6 Sol and Luna also arrive with a Prompt Caching Dashboard, where OpenAI says developers can view caching performance to understand how much context is reused. Specifically, they can see how much input is cached and how that amount changes over time. The diagnostics tool then flags missed caching opportunities to help developers understand what could use more efficient caching. Rather than keeping cache performance largely hidden behind the scenes, the idea is to make it more visible so developers can actively measure and optimize cache reuse. Altogether, OpenAI says these caching improvements are already making a difference. Per the AI company, GitHub reports, “these improvements have reduced the share of prompt tokens requiring fresh processing by more than 50% across billions of requests to OpenAI models.” These results span the past “several months.” Token prices aren’t the only way to make agents cheaper OpenAI’s pricing cuts for GPT-6 Sol and Luna made the biggest splash, with the AI company significantly dropping API prices from GPT-5.6 levels. Compared to the current prices for GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna , which stand at $4 and $0.20 per million input tokens and $20 and $1.20 per million output tokens, respectively (GPT-5.6 Sol’s rates are promotional pricing), the new GPT-6 models come in at just $2 and $0.10 per million input tokens and $10 and $0.50 per million output tokens, respectively. With GPT-6 Sol and Luna’s caching improvements and lower token pricing, OpenAI is making the case for tackling agent costs from both sides: charging less for fresh processing and reducing how often the same context needs to be reprocessed. But as more AI model providers compete aggressively on pricing, it’s becoming clearer that cheaper models alone won’t save your AI budget — and lower token prices aren’t the only way to make agents cheaper. With GPT-6 Sol and Luna’s caching improvements and lower token pricing, OpenAI is making the case for tackling agent costs from both sides: charging less for fresh processing and reducing how often the same context needs to be reprocessed. As agents continue to work on longer and more complex tasks, there will likely be more pressure to do both.

items.title: Which spiritual and political issues will be the focus of Pope Leo XIV’s visit to France?
items.summary: KEY TAKEAWAYS The Catholic Church of France will welcome Pope Leo XIV from September 25 to 28 2026. The Pope will address young people at the Stade de France, thus following in the footsteps of his predecessor John Paul II in 1980. This trip will provide the Pope with an opportunity to speak on artificial intelligence, and pay tribute to social Catholicism and the legacy of Robert Schuman, a leading figure in European and Christian democracy. Pope Leo XIV is due to visit France from September 25 to 28. The planned tour itinerary for the papal visit – which has been the subject of prior consultation – and the main topics expected to be discussed are significant from both a political and a religious standpoint. This is an “apostolic journey” , not a “state visit”: it is first and foremost as the head of the Catholic Church, the successor to the Prince of the Apostles , that the Pope is coming to France to meet with members of the Catholic community. Admittedly, he is also a head of state – of Vatican City – and, as such, he will be received by French president Emmanuel Macron and several other political leaders : his visit therefore also has an official dimension. Leo XIV’s interest in France may stem from his personal history, as his paternal grandmother was from Le Havre and his father took part in the landings in Normandy and Provence. Like all popes up to Benedict XVI, and unlike his predecessor Francis, he speaks French, one of the Vatican’s official languages, and had visited France even before his pontificate. But broader considerations must also be taken into account. The timing is favourable, with a papal visit taking place well in advance of the campaign for the presidential election, as was the case with John Paul II’s first trip to France , in June 1980. This should make it possible, if not to prevent, then at least to limit attempts to exploit the visit for political gain, particularly by candidates hoping to win the Catholic vote. Reaching out to young people of France For Leo XIV, the youth debate is primarily religious. France was once regarded as “the Eldest Daughter of the Church’ , according to a popular adage hailing back to the late 19th century. In this respect French Catholicism undoubtedly exerted a significant influence through its pastoral, liturgical and intellectual initiatives that were rolled out from the 1930s up until the 1960s . Admittedly, for over half a century, the Catholic Church has been experiencing a collapse , which Pope Francis implicitly criticised it for, considering Europe to be "a little weary” : this might explain his decision not to visit France as such, even though he had been there on three occasions (visiting Strasbourg, Marseille and Corsica). But Pope Leo XIV sees things differently. On May 28 2025, three weeks after his election, he wrote to the bishops of France to mark the centenary of the canonisation of three of his compatriots, Jean Eudes , Thérèse of Lisieux and Jean-Marie Vianney , in the hope that this anniversary might inspire “a new missionary zeal”. This reflects the Pope’s view of the importance of France’s spiritual heritage. Despite the difficulties facing the Church in France and the crisis triggered by the sexual abuse scandals, the threefold increase in the number of adult baptisms points to a relative resurgence of Catholicism since 2022. The reasons behind this development, which appears to run counter to the trend observed until then, and despite its limitations – the number of these adult baptisms does not offset the decline in the number of infant baptisms – are raising questions as far afield as Rome. The catechumens are mainly young people, aged between 18 and 40. Rome Reports – March 2026. This section of the population remains a pastoral priority for the popes. John Paul II launched the World Youth Days (WYD) and, during his travels, would meet with young people, as he did in 1980 at the Parc des Princes stadium. Leo XIV is upholding this tradition by organising a vigil at the Stade de France , where 80,000 people are expected (50,000 congregated there in 1980). Addressing the challenges of AI The shrine at Lourdes is another symbol of the vitality and influence of Catholicism in France, even though visitor numbers to the spiritual destination are tending to fall slightly. The Pope visited the site while he was still a seminarian. The Pope intends to honour this major place of pilgrimage by meeting with the sick – whose care is one of the sanctuary’s defining features – and with victims of sexual violence. With foreigners representing 60 % of visitors , Lourdes lies at the crossroads of the national and international dimensions that characterise the Pope’s journey. The speech he will deliver at Unesco is primarily part of this global perspective. No Pope has spoken from this platform since John Paul II in 1980. Benedict XVI addressed ‘the world of culture’ at the Collège des Bernardins in 2008. Accepting an invitation from the Director-General of Unesco, Pope Leo XIV will speak there about the challenges associated with the use of artificial intelligence, particularly in the fields of education, information and artistic creation. This statement echoes his first and recent encyclical letter, Magnifica Humanitas , “on the protection of the human person in the age of AI”. In this regard, the Pope and Unesco share the same cultural concerns. Paying tribute to Robert Schuman, a leading figure of Europe and Christian democracy The Pope’s stop in Metz , with its focus on Europe , is another aspect of the papal visit bearing an international dimension. Popes John Paul II, in 1988, and Francis, in 2014, had delivered speeches to MEPs in Strasbourg, within an institutional setting. Pope Leo XIV opted for a symbolic visit to the Moselle Prefecture. This department, neighbouring Belgium and bordering two countries, was tossed back and forth between France and Germany from 1870 to 1945, through a series of wars, before being dubbed the “crossroads of Europe”. But it is first and foremost to Robert Schuman that the Pope, who shares the same first name , intends to pay tribute. The politician, one of the “Fathers of Europe” , is buried in Scy-Chazelles, near Metz, where he lived for many years. A process for his beatification is underway, and Pope Francis has recognised him as “venerable” . A member of the Popular Republican Movement, Robert Schuman was associated with Christian democracy . This movement stemmed from social Catholicism, which Leo XIII (1878–1903) promoted in his encyclical Rerum Novarum (1891). However, at that time, the Pope envisaged it solely as “beneficial Christian action amongst the people” (encyclical Graves de Communi, 1901 ). Having become a genuine political movement, Christian democracy has continued to draw on the principles of social Catholicism (subsidiarity, solidarity, participation), the legacy of which Pope Leo XIV, through his choice of name, embodies. Konrad Adenauer and Alcide De Gasperi came from this background, as did Schuman. It was they who began to build Europe with the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC). The aim was to reconcile the former belligerents by drawing on shared interests. Peace is therefore at the heart of the European project. Pope Leo XIV’s planned address at the Robert Schuman Centre , following an interfaith meeting, will, in fact, be entitled “At the roots of Europe for peace and unity”. During the Pope’s visit to France, peace, Europe and the implications of AI for human dignity may well be the most political and international aspects of the trip, while developments in French Catholicism and youth issues bear more directly religious significance. However, these various aspects are complementary in the Holy See’s vision to encourage Catholics – and young people in particular – to become involved in building a world of peace and promoting human dignity. items.title: I wanted to live in the US, then had a game-changing visit to Europe. Here's why I chose Germany.
items.summary: Ishansh Gupta, an Indian national, works at BMW and lives in Munich. Courtesy of Aditya Sharma Ishansh Gupta dreamed of studying in the US — until he heard about free education in Europe. Drawn by Germany's manufacturing strengths, he did his master's degree there instead of the US. Gupta now works at BMW. He's glad he didn't take the risk on an expensive US education. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ishansh Gupta, 29, who lives in Munich. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Growing up in India , I knew I wanted to live in the US one day. I had relatives who'd moved there, and the way Bollywood movies portrayed the American dream resonated with me. I was interested in technology, and some of the biggest opportunities were there. While completing my bachelor's degree in computer science and engineering in India, I applied for internships around the world to increase my chances of getting accepted by a US university for a master's degree. I interned in Poland for two six-week stints in 2017 and 2018. After spending time in Europe, instead of applying to US colleges, I went to university in Germany and now work at BMW. I got a taste of life in America in 2022, when I did an assignment in South Carolina. I left feeling glad that I built my life in Germany and didn't pay for an expensive US education . Learning that international students could get free tuition in Germany was game-changing During a trip to Berlin, I met a group of Indian people in a restaurant, who told me it was possible for international students to get free tuition at public universities in Germany. It was a game-changing moment for me. Even attending a private university in Germany felt more affordable than studying in the US, where I expected to pay around $100,000 for a master's degree , including tuition and living costs. While interning in Poland and visiting Germany, I had a really positive experience with European people and culture, and I was excited to explore different European countries . I was also impressed by Germany's manufacturing and engineering strengths, and the level of technical knowledge people had. In 2019, I started a master's degree in data engineering at a private institution in Germany. A partial scholarship meant tuition cost me 8,000 euros ($9,000) instead of 20,000 euros. I learned very basic German in India, but it was a very international, English-speaking university, so I didn't really struggle with a language barrier. In my last semester, I completed a six-month internship at BMW, and was accepted onto a three-year PhD program there. In 2023, I got a full-time job as a digitalization specialist at BMW, and in 2026, I moved into a HR role leading AI initiatives for senior executives. I'm still learning German, partly because I'm big on networking and want to understand inside jokes when connecting with people. I do have some meetings in German, and I'm able to understand a lot of the context, but if I don't understand something, people are always happy to explain in English. Gupta continues to learn the German language. Courtesy of Aditya Sharma I worked for BMW in the US for a few months, and noticed some differences with Germany In my experience and that of friends in Germany, there is a strong culture of work-life balance in Germany . When I worked on-site at BMW in South Carolina for three months in December 2022, I got the impression from friends and contacts at different companies that a person's brand, ambition, and network seemed to matter a lot more in the US than in Germany. The corporate culture in the US encourages people to talk about their work, build visibility, and take big career bets early on, like changing companies more frequently or joining a startup. In Germany, it's common for people to stay with the same company for a long period, I think due to factors like labor protections and indefinite contracts. I don't think people are less ambitious in Germany, they just talk about it less. I'm open to future opportunities in the US, perhaps with an expat contract at BMW, but I'm happy to stay in Germany too. I'm glad that I experienced the US without risking paying for an expensive education Earlier in my life, taking a large loan or asking my parents to finance an expensive US education when I didn't have an established career, professional network, or financial security would have been very risky. Today, the situation is very different. I have more professional experience and personal savings. If I took an opportunity in the US and things didn't work out as planned, I think I'd have a realistic path back into the European job market. Germany and Europe gave me opportunities that I could hardly have predicted when I first arrived. I've worked at BMW, pursued an industrial PhD program, and built my career while still having time for other interests like fitness and travel. I don't feel at a disadvantage compared to people in America when it comes to the quality of my education or experiences. I always imagined I might live and work in the US one day, and I'm glad that I could experience that without taking on the financial risk of an expensive US education. I wouldn't do things differently. Do you have a story to share about deciding on the right place to grow your career? Contact this reporter at ccheong@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

I've worked at BMW, pursued an industrial PhD program, and built my career while still having time for other interests like fitness and travel. I don't feel at a disadvantage compared to people in America when it comes to the quality of my education or experiences.

I always imagined I might live and work in the US one day, and I'm glad that I could experience that without taking on the financial risk of an expensive US education. I wouldn't do things differently.

I had the opportunity to check in with Google ahead of the announcement, ask some questions, and get some inside info about all of the many unknowns surrounding these systems. In practical terms, what that means is that you get an expanded desktop that’s designed to feel like Android but with a variety of enhancements to better take advantage of the added screen space. Amusingly enough, that results in something that brings to mind the short-lived large-screen-optimized Android 3.0 Honeycomb era of 2010 — with notifications and Quick Settings living in one corner of the interface, the clock and date in another corner, and a dock along the the bottom-center. The Googlebook desktop, as seen during a Google press demo. Google Unlike with Chromebooks, Googlebooks do give you a fully customizable home screen, where you can add any number of widgets and shortcuts you want. They also allegedly include the new Gemini-powered Create My Widget option for building your own custom widgets from simple natural-language prompting, though we’ve been hearing about that since May with promises of an appearance on Pixel phones, too, and it’s yet to show up anywhere so far. A demo of the Googlebook Create My Widget system, which was also announced for Pixel phones in May.
