items.title: OpenAI Launches GPT-6 Sol and Luna With 50% Lower API Pricing Than GPT-5.6
items.summary: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna to its GPT-6 range, which are faster and more affordable versions of the models trained using methods similar to those used with GPT-6 Astra, as OpenAI has stated. The company is cutting the API prices for Sol and Luna by 50% when compared to the promotional rates of GPT-5.6. GPT-6 Astra, which was launched this month, is still OpenAI's best model in all respects. The new models are now available today to paid users in ChatGPT Work and Codex , and Luna is also accessible to free users through the desktop app. The benchmark comparisons are something that OpenAI has carried out themselves, while the figures for the competitors have been obtained from public reports. GPT-6 Sol and Luna Pricing, Factuality, and Performance OpenAI has stated that the improvements in caching and inference have allowed it to provide the models at a lower cost, the savings from which it is passing on to its customers. On a per million tokens basis: For GPT-6 Sol the cost is $2 in input and $10 in output, as compared to $4 and $20 for GPT-5.6 Sol, which represents a 50% reduction. For GPT-6 Luna the cost is $0.10 for input and $0.50 for output, as compared to $0.20 and $1.20 for GPT-5.6 Luna, which represents a 50% reduction. OpenAI makes Astra the option for the most demanding types of work, while Sol and Luna are directed at ordinary tasks and at large-scale applications. OpenAI states that GPT-6 Sol is able to carry out difficult work tasks at higher usage limits and at a lower cost. In the AutomationBench test of business workflows across various applications, OpenAI finds that GPT-6 Sol, when running at xhigh effort, outperforms Claude Opus 5 running at max effort at only 9% of Opus 5's cost per task. Furthermore, at high effort GPT-6 Luna achieves an improvement of 5.4 percentage points at a cost per task that is 58% lower than that of its predecessor. In the final assessment of the Agents, where complex professional workflows are evaluated, GPT-6 Sol achieves a score of 56.4% at maximum effort, this being at a cost per task that is 60% lower than that of Claude Opus 5. OpenAI states that it is still making progress in terms of factual reliability. In its internal assessment of factuality, which is based on de-identified real-world conversations in which users have pointed out errors, GPT-6 Sol commits about half as many mistakes as its predecessor and is approaching the level of reliability seen with Astra but at a much lower cost. GPT-6 Luna also shows improvements, reaching the performance of GPT-5.6 Sol at higher effort levels but at about one hundredth of the cost. OpenAI adds that these conversations which cause errors are not typical of normal use. OpenAI states that coding agents are now dealing with tasks that are more complex and longer in duration, which is why the cost of sustained use has become more important. items.title: Adobe Premiere Comes to Android for Free With Full Video Editing Tools
items.summary: Adobe has made a fully featured Adobe Premiere app for Android available on the Google Play Store, as Adobe has stated. The app provides complete video editing on a mobile device, with the ability to edit and export videos up to 4K, support for multi-track timelines, and optional generative AI features. It is free to use, does not require a login, includes no upgrade prompts, and does not add any watermarks; only the AI features and cloud storage involve a cost. Adobe Premiere for iOS was launched a year ago. More than fifty thousand downloads have been recorded for the app. Adobe Premiere for Android Features and Premiere Rush Comparison Adobe presents the app as being designed for "creators" and says it can be used to produce TikToks and Instagram Reels, to turn moments from video podcasts into clips, and to edit vlogs; it provides access to a full range of mobile video tools. The application allows users to begin with templates created by other users, edit and export videos in up to 4K resolution, and deal with effects, transitions, creative assets, and music taken from Adobe Stock, their own files, or audio that has been extracted. Video, music, voiceovers, and effects can be layered on a multi-track timeline, and there is an Enhance Audio function to achieve studio-quality sound. There are also optional features relating to generative AI, such as Generative Fill, Image-to-Video, and Generate Sound Effects. Adobe has stated that it intends to include Adobe Fonts, improved captions, keyframes, cropping, beat detection, and the ability to carry on editing in Premiere on desktop. Adobe Premiere was represented in the Play Store between 2019 and 2025 through Premiere Rush CC, a more simplified version designed for use on mobile devices. This app offered fewer features than the new version and carried a monthly fee of $9.99, or could be obtained as part of the complete Adobe Creative Cloud Suite, which cost more than $50 per month. The Android Police points out that offering the full version of Adobe Premiere for free will reduce the growing competition that Adobe is facing from apps such as Canva and CapCut. Adobe Premiere for Android Requirements, Pricing, and Availability The app is free with no login required and no watermarks: It is compatible with devices that run Android 13 or a later version and needs a minimum of 5GB of RAM. Editing features, such as 4K export and the use of multiple tracks, are provided free of charge. What you need to pay for are the AI features and cloud storage. Adobe Premiere can now be found on the Google Play Store and has already received more than 50,000 downloads. The company has mentioned further features it plans to add in the future, such as Adobe Fonts, improved captions, keyframes, and beat detection, but has not stated when these features will be introduced. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: AI Agents Are Becoming a New Malware Distribution Channel
items.summary: By Farukh Rakhimov, Head of Compliance, Data Protection and Information Security at AdTech Holding Roughly 7,600 fake GitHub repositories, 6,600 fraudulent profiles and more than 14 million downloads: that is the scale of FakeGit, a malware campaign documented by Island in July 2026. Over 800 repositories impersonated AI skills and MCP servers, distributing SmartLoader and the StealC infostealer. Fake repositories are nothing new. The surprise was who recommended them. Gemini and ChatGPT independently suggested the same malicious walmart-mcp repository. The agents found the attacker’s project and handed users installation instructions. Attackers no longer need to deceive users directly. They can deceive the assistants users trust. Why Agents Are Vulnerable Two architectural characteristics make these attacks possible. First, agents process instructions and external information as text. A malicious instruction hidden in a README, webpage or tool description may be interpreted as something to obey rather than analyze. This is indirect prompt injection. Second, agents can act on those instructions. Security researcher Simon Willison calls the combination of three conditions the lethal trifecta: access to valuable information, exposure to untrusted external content and the ability to send data outside the system. Together, these conditions turn malicious text into a potential data breach. Other attacks exploit something simpler: fabricated trust signals. Stars, downloads, contributor histories and registry listings can make malicious software appear legitimate. Here are eight ways these weaknesses are being exploited. 1. AgentBaiting: When an Agent Recommends Malware AgentBaiting targets the assistant rather than the user. In the FakeGit campaign, attackers created convincing repositories with realistic documentation and distributed them through public registries. Gemini and ChatGPT independently recommended the same fake Walmart MCP connector because it appeared relevant and credible. The repositories distributed SmartLoader, which downloaded StealC to steal browser credentials, cookies, active sessions and cryptocurrency wallet data. The agents were not compromised. They simply recommended software whose apparent credibility had been manufactured. 2. Tool Poisoning: Instructions Hidden in Tool Descriptions MCP servers provide agents with textual descriptions of available tools. Attackers can hide instructions inside those descriptions. In April 2025, Invariant Labs demonstrated how instructions embedded in a malicious calculator tool could manipulate a separate, trusted email connector into copying outgoing messages to an attacker. The user never sees the malicious instructions. Tool poisoning remains a demonstrated threat model rather than a publicly confirmed real-world incident. 3. When Agents Conceal Their Actions Some malicious skills explicitly instruct agents not to disclose what they have done. A 2026 academic study examined 98,380 skills from two registries and confirmed 157 as malicious, identifying 632 vulnerabilities and 13 attack techniques. One recurring instruction gave the research its title: “Do Not Mention This to the User.” An agent could therefore report that a task was completed while omitting unauthorized actions, including the transmission of sensitive information. 4. Rug Pull: Trusted Software Changes After Installation A package may behave legitimately for months before introducing malicious functionality. In September 2025, Koi Security uncovered postmark-mcp, a connector impersonating the legitimate Postmark email service. Versions through 1.0.15 appeared harmless. Version 1.0.16 introduced a hidden BCC recipient that copied outgoing emails to an attacker-controlled domain. The package potentially exposed password-reset messages and authentication links associated with approximately 300 organizations. Postmark confirmed that the connector was not its product and that its own service had not been compromised. The attack exploited trust accumulated by earlier versions. Automatic updates allowed malicious functionality to arrive without renewed user approval. 5. Malicious Changes Can Happen Outside the Package Reviewing source code cannot detect everything when external dependencies change independently. In August 2025, Check Point disclosed MCPoison, a vulnerability in Cursor that allowed attackers to modify previously approved project configurations and execute commands without renewed approval. Cursor 1.3 addressed the issue. Another 2026 experiment demonstrated how a skill distributed to approximately 26,000 agents could initially link to legitimate documentation before the external page changed to malicious installation instructions. The package itself remained unchanged, allowing the threat to escape scanners examining only submitted files. 6. Opening an Untrusted Repository Can Execute Code AI-enabled development environments introduce risks even before users deliberately install additional software. Check Point found that Claude Code could execute repository-controlled configuration commands before users completed its trust-confirmation process. The vulnerabilities included arbitrary command execution (CVE-2025-59536) and API credential exposure through a manipulated server endpoint (CVE-2026-21852). Anthropic subsequently patched the reported vulnerabilities. The implication is straightforward: opening an unfamiliar project inside an agent-enabled development environment may create execution paths that ordinary file inspection would not. 7. ClickFix: Users Install Malware Themselves ClickFix requires no sophisticated prompt injection. Attackers disguise malicious commands as installation prerequisites inside README or SKILL.md files. Users follow the instructions and execute the commands themselves. During the ClawHavoc campaign in early 2026, researchers discovered malicious skills masquerading as cryptocurrency and productivity tools in the OpenClaw ecosystem. Koi Security identified 341 malicious skills among 2,857 available during its audit. Antiy CERT subsequently tracked 1,184 malicious skills associated with just 12 accounts. The malware targeted cryptocurrency wallets, browser credentials, API keys, SSH keys and Telegram sessions. 8. When the Agent Becomes the Attacker Agents can also coordinate offensive operations. In November 2025, Anthropic reported GTG-1002, a cyberespionage campaign in which attackers connected penetration-testing tools to Claude Code through MCP. According to Anthropic, the model independently performed approximately 80–90% of tactical operations, while human operators established objectives and made major strategic decisions. Anthropic attributed the campaign to a state-sponsored group. That assessment has not been independently confirmed in public threat-intelligence repositories. The case illustrates how existing offensive tools can be assembled into autonomous workflows. The Economics of Fake Reputation Many attacks depend on artificially manufactured credibility. An April 2026 investigation found GitHub stars advertised for $0.03–$0.10 each. Researchers also identified approximately six million suspicious stars across 15,835 repositories. In another case, attackers cloned an Oura MCP connector and spent three months creating fake contribution histories before distributing the malicious version through legitimate registries. A separate malicious Solidity extension displayed artificially inflated download counts, eventually approaching two million. One blockchain developer reportedly lost approximately $500,000. Popularity determines discoverability, not security. Code reviews and scanners also have limitations: malicious functionality can hide in dependencies, tool descriptions, subsequent updates or external webpages. What This Means for AdTech The open-source ecosystem has faced similar supply-chain threats before. Mandatory two-factor authentication, trusted publishing and verified package provenance eventually strengthened established registries. AI skill marketplaces are developing much faster, while their security infrastructure remains comparatively immature. The consequences are also broader: an AI skill may operate with access to email, repositories, databases and credentials. For AdTech, the same risk extends directly to advertising accounts. Media buyers and AdOps teams increasingly connect agents, reporting assistants and campaign tools to DSPs, advertising platforms and advertiser data. A poisoned reporting or creative-generation skill could expose campaign information, compromise account credentials or put advertising budgets at risk. The underlying deception is familiar: buying fake stars and downloads to make malicious software appear trustworthy follows the same logic as using fake engagement and bot traffic to make fraudulent advertising inventory look legitimate. As AI agents gain more authority, verifying the software and signals they trust becomes as important as securing the systems they operate.

items.title: AI Agents Are Coming to Enterprise Software. The Hard Part Is Integration
items.summary: As AI agents move from experimental pilots into enterprise software, businesses are looking for practical ways to introduce intelligent automation without rebuilding the platforms they already depend on. Existing SaaS products often sit across complex technology environments involving APIs, databases, identity systems, legacy applications, and multiple business workflows. Integrating an AI agent into this environment requires more than connecting an application to an LLM. It requires an architecture that supports security, governance, scalability, reliability, and a consistent customer experience. GeekyAnts helps businesses integrate AI agents and intelligent capabilities into existing SaaS products through its AI Product Engineering services, connecting AI with existing products, workflows, APIs, data sources, and enterprise systems. For technology leaders, the central question is not “How can we add an AI chatbot?” but “Where can an AI agent safely improve an existing workflow, and what architecture is required to make that capability production-ready?” Why Enterprise SaaS Products Are Adding AI Agents Large SaaS platforms already contain extensive customer, operational, financial, and workflow data. The challenge is that users often have to navigate multiple interfaces and systems to turn that information into an outcome. An AI agent can provide an intelligent interaction layer over these existing capabilities. Instead of manually locating information, interpreting it, and executing several steps, users can describe the desired outcome in natural language. For example, an enterprise service platform could allow an operations manager to ask an agent to identify unresolved high-priority incidents, analyze their business impact, summarize the relevant history, and prepare recommended remediation steps. The value comes from connecting intelligence to existing workflows rather than creating another isolated AI experience. Start With Enterprise Workflows, Not AI Models For a VP of Engineering or Head of Digital Transformation, selecting the AI model should not be the first architectural decision. The starting point should be the workflow. High-value candidates often involve repetitive knowledge work, require information from multiple systems, contain clearly defined business rules, or consume significant employee time. Common enterprise use cases include customer service operations, sales intelligence, financial analysis, IT operations, employee support, document processing, compliance workflows, product analytics, and enterprise knowledge management. A useful assessment should examine the current workflow, its cost, cycle time, error rate, system dependencies, security requirements, and potential business impact. This creates a measurable baseline against which the AI implementation can be evaluated. items.summary_html:
As AI agents move from experimental pilots into enterprise software, businesses are looking for practical ways to introduce intelligent automation without rebuilding the platforms they already depend on. Existing SaaS products often sit across complex technology environments involving APIs, databases, identity systems, legacy applications, and multiple business workflows. Integrating an AI agent into this environment requires more than connecting an application to an LLM. It requires an architecture that supports security, governance, scalability, reliability, and a consistent customer experience. GeekyAnts helps businesses integrate AI agents and intelligent capabilities into existing SaaS products through its AI Product Engineering services, connecting AI with existing products, workflows, APIs, data sources, and enterprise systems.

For technology leaders, the central question is not “How can we add an AI chatbot?” but “Where can an AI agent safely improve an existing workflow, and what architecture is required to make that capability production-ready?”

Why Enterprise SaaS Products Are Adding AI Agents

Large SaaS platforms already contain extensive customer, operational, financial, and workflow data. The challenge is that users often have to navigate multiple interfaces and systems to turn that information into an outcome. An AI agent can provide an intelligent interaction layer over these existing capabilities. Instead of manually locating information, interpreting it, and executing several steps, users can describe the desired outcome in natural language. For example, an enterprise service platform could allow an operations manager to ask an agent to identify unresolved high-priority incidents, analyze their business impact, summarize the relevant history, and prepare recommended remediation steps. The value comes from connecting intelligence to existing workflows rather than creating another isolated AI experience.

Start With Enterprise Workflows, Not AI Models

For a VP of Engineering or Head of Digital Transformation, selecting the AI model should not be the first architectural decision. The starting point should be the workflow. High-value candidates often involve repetitive knowledge work, require information from multiple systems, contain clearly defined business rules, or consume significant employee time. Common enterprise use cases include customer service operations, sales intelligence, financial analysis, IT operations, employee support, document processing, compliance workflows, product analytics, and enterprise knowledge management. A useful assessment should examine the current workflow, its cost, cycle time, error rate, system dependencies, security requirements, and potential business impact. This creates a measurable baseline against which the AI implementation can be evaluated.

Integrate the Agent With the Existing Architecture

Enterprise SaaS environments rarely operate as a single application. They typically include APIs, microservices, data platforms, identity providers, third-party SaaS applications, event systems, and legacy platforms. An AI agent should therefore be treated as another architectural layer rather than an independent application. A controlled tool and API layer can allow the agent to interact with approved business capabilities. For example, an enterprise CRM agent could have separate tools for retrieving account information, analyzing customer activity, creating follow-up tasks, and updating records. GeekyAnts handles this type of AI integration by connecting agent capabilities with existing application APIs, backend services, data sources, and business workflows, allowing enterprises to introduce AI into their existing SaaS architecture without replacing the underlying platform. This approach also creates a clearer boundary between the probabilistic behavior of the AI layer and the deterministic behavior of core enterprise services.

Build Around Identity and Access Management

Enterprise AI agents should inherit the organization’s existing security model. If a user cannot access certain customer records through the primary SaaS application, the AI agent should not create an alternative path to those records. Integration should therefore account for identity providers, single sign-on, role-based access control, attribute-based access control, tenant isolation, API authorization, and audit requirements. Authorization should also apply to individual agent actions. Reading information, generating recommendations, modifying records, initiating transactions, and communicating externally may require different permission levels. For sensitive workflows, a human approval step can be introduced before an agent executes an irreversible or high-impact action.

Use RAG and Enterprise Data Carefully

Enterprise AI agents frequently need information that is not available within a foundation model. This may include internal documentation, product information, customer records, support histories, policies, technical documentation, or operational data. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, can allow an agent to retrieve relevant information from approved enterprise sources before generating an answer or taking an action. However, enterprise RAG should not be treated simply as a vector database implementation. Architecture teams need to consider document permissions, data freshness, metadata, indexing pipelines, source-of-truth systems, tenant isolation, retention requirements, and access controls. The retrieval layer should preserve the same governance standards applied to the underlying enterprise data.

Design for Human Oversight

Fully autonomous execution may not be appropriate for every enterprise workflow. A more practical approach is to define different autonomy levels based on business risk. An agent might automatically summarize information or classify a support request. It could recommend a financial or operational action that requires approval. A low-risk workflow might eventually be automated after sufficient validation. This creates a controlled path from AI assistance to AI-driven execution. For digital product leaders, this approach can also improve user trust because employees remain able to understand what the system recommends, why it recommends it, and when it is taking an action.

Enterprise AI Requires Observability

Traditional application monitoring is not enough for agentic systems. Engineering teams need visibility into the complete agent workflow, including model calls, retrieved context, tool calls, failures, latency, token consumption, and final outcomes. If an agent fails to complete a customer-support workflow, engineering teams should be able to determine whether the problem came from retrieval, model reasoning, authorization, an unavailable API, malformed tool input, or a downstream service. Agent observability should therefore become part of the production architecture. Useful metrics include task completion rate, tool-call success rate, escalation frequency, latency, model usage, cost per task, retrieval quality, and user feedback.

Control AI Costs at Enterprise Scale

AI costs can behave differently from conventional application infrastructure. A single agent interaction may trigger multiple model calls, retrieval operations, API requests, and validation steps. At enterprise volume, small inefficiencies can become significant operational costs. Technology leaders should establish AI FinOps practices early. Model routing can allocate simple tasks to smaller models while reserving more capable models for complex reasoning. Caching can reduce repeated computation, while context management can limit unnecessary tokens. Tool selection and workflow design can also reduce redundant calls. Cost should be measured at the workflow level rather than simply by model usage. Knowing the cost of completing a specific business task provides a more useful metric for determining whether an AI capability is delivering sufficient value.

Secure the Agent Against New Attack Surfaces

AI agents introduce security considerations that do not exist in conventional application workflows. Prompt injection, indirect prompt injection, sensitive-data exposure, malicious tool instructions, unauthorized actions, and compromised data sources can all affect agent behavior. Enterprise security teams should therefore test not only the model but the entire agent architecture. Security controls can include input validation, output validation, tool allowlists, least-privilege access, sandboxing where appropriate, data-loss prevention controls, audit logging, human approval gates, and continuous security testing. The goal is to ensure that the agent cannot turn a natural-language instruction into an unauthorized enterprise action.

Modernize Without Replacing the Existing SaaS Platform

One reason AI agents are attractive to large enterprises is that they can add a new interaction layer without requiring an immediate replacement of the underlying platform. An existing SaaS product can retain its core services, databases, APIs, authentication, and business logic while an agent introduces a more intelligent way to access those capabilities. This is particularly relevant for organizations with significant investments in legacy applications or complex digital platforms. Rather than replacing a mature system simply to introduce AI, architecture teams can expose selected capabilities through APIs and gradually introduce agentic workflows around them. This approach can support incremental modernization while reducing the operational risk associated with large-scale platform replacement.

Where AI Development Services Fit Into the Architecture

Once the use case and architecture have been defined, implementation requires more than model integration. Enterprise teams need capabilities spanning model integration, RAG pipelines, agent orchestration, API integration, backend engineering, data processing, evaluation, security, and deployment. GeekyAnts provides AI Development Services that include building and integrating AI capabilities into business applications and existing digital products. This can involve connecting AI models with enterprise APIs, databases, knowledge sources, authentication systems, and application workflows so that the resulting AI functionality operates as part of the existing product. For enterprise teams, the implementation should remain aligned with the broader technology architecture rather than creating a separate AI stack that becomes difficult to maintain.

A Practical Enterprise Roadmap

A large-scale AI agent initiative can be approached in stages. First, identify a business workflow where the expected value can be measured. Establish baseline metrics such as processing time, operational cost, employee effort, or customer resolution time. Next, map the existing technology architecture. Identify the systems, APIs, data sources, identity controls, and business rules that the agent will need to interact with. Then define the agent’s boundaries. Determine what it can read, what it can recommend, what it can execute, and which actions require human approval. The engineering team can then build a controlled pilot around one workflow. The pilot should be tested against normal scenarios, ambiguous requests, incorrect inputs, permission restrictions, malicious instructions, and high-volume conditions. Once the workflow demonstrates sufficient reliability, it can be expanded gradually across additional users, business units, or processes.

What Enterprise Leaders Should Evaluate

Before integrating an AI agent into an existing SaaS product, technology leaders should ask several practical questions: Does the use case produce measurable business value? Can the agent operate within existing identity and authorization controls? Which APIs and enterprise systems will it need to access? What information needs to be retrieved, and where does that information originate? Which actions can be automated and which require human approval? How will agent behavior be monitored in production? How will AI costs be measured and controlled? What happens when the model, retrieval system, API, or downstream service fails? How will the architecture scale across customers, tenants, regions, and business units? These questions move the conversation from AI experimentation toward enterprise engineering.

The Future of AI-Enabled SaaS

For large organizations, the next stage of SaaS innovation is likely to involve AI becoming part of the operating layer of digital products rather than existing as a standalone chatbot. Users will increasingly expect software to understand intent, retrieve relevant information, coordinate actions, and reduce the number of manual steps required to complete a task. For engineering and digital-platform leaders, the opportunity is to introduce these capabilities without compromising the architecture that already supports the business. The strongest implementations will combine AI capabilities with disciplined API design, enterprise security, observability, governance, and human oversight. The objective is not maximum autonomy. It is controlled automation that produces measurable improvements while fitting naturally into the organization’s existing technology environment.

FAQsCan an AI agent be integrated into an existing enterprise SaaS platform?

Yes. An AI agent can be integrated through existing APIs, backend services, identity systems, data platforms, and business workflows. GeekyAnts integrates AI capabilities with existing SaaS products and their underlying technology infrastructure, without requiring a complete platform replacement.

What does AI agent integration involve?

AI agent integration can involve connecting AI models with APIs, databases, enterprise knowledge sources, authentication systems, business rules, and application workflows. The exact architecture depends on the use case and existing SaaS environment.

Should an enterprise AI agent have direct database access?

Generally, direct unrestricted database access should be avoided. Controlled APIs and tools provide a clearer security and governance boundary and allow teams to determine exactly which operations an agent can perform.

How can enterprises protect sensitive data used by AI agents?

Organizations can apply identity controls, authorization policies, tenant isolation, encryption, data-loss prevention, audit logging, access restrictions, and controlled retrieval mechanisms to AI workflows.

Is RAG suitable for large enterprise SaaS applications?

RAG can be useful when an agent needs access to proprietary or frequently changing enterprise information. Its implementation should account for data permissions, freshness, indexing, metadata, source systems, and tenant isolation.

How can companies control AI costs at scale?

Organizations can use model routing, caching, context optimization, usage monitoring, structured workflows, and limits on unnecessary model and tool calls. Measuring cost per completed business workflow can provide a clearer view of AI economics.

Should enterprise AI agents be fully autonomous?

Not necessarily. The appropriate autonomy level depends on the risk and business impact of the workflow. Low-risk activities can potentially be automated, while sensitive financial, operational, or customer-facing actions may require human approval.

What should engineering teams monitor after launching an AI agent?

Teams should monitor task completion, model and tool failures, latency, retrieval performance, token consumption, cost per task, escalations, user feedback, security events, and downstream service performance.

How should enterprises move from an AI proof of concept to production?

A practical path is to start with a measurable workflow, validate the architecture and security model, build a controlled pilot, test failure and security scenarios, establish observability, and then scale gradually across users and workflows.

items.title: Fine-Tuning a Small Model to Triage Kubernetes Alerts
items.summary: A step-by-step recipe for teaching Qwen3–1.7B to triage your cluster’s alerts, on a free GPU. It beat Opus 5 by 12 points and never sends your data outside the cluster. Lately I’ve been working with agents pretty much every day, and one of the jobs I keep seeing companies hand to agents is troubleshooting. An alert fires, someone has to work out what broke, and that someone is usually expensive and tired. I’ve built a couple of agents for this myself, and all of them called a large model behind an API. That works, but a few things kept me wondering whether it really scales: Cost. Every call is billed, and on a noisy night you pay for the same PodNotReady a few hundred times, per cluster. Privacy. Every alert leaves the cluster, together with the logs, events and config around it, and lands on someone else’s servers. Accuracy. The large models aren’t even that good at it: on IBM’s ITBench , agents powered by state-of-the-art models resolved only 13.8% of the SRE scenarios. So in this experiment I wanted to see how far a small model can go. I took Qwen3–1.7B, a model small enough to run on two CPU cores inside the cluster, and taught it one narrow job: read an alert and the state around it, and name the fault that caused it. On 124 alerts it had never seen, the tuned model scored 79.8%, against 67.7% for Claude Opus 5. This article is the recipe, step by step, so you can do the same with your own cluster. Each step explains the concept first, then shows the code I used. Everything runs on a laptop plus a free Colab GPU. The full harness is on GitHub , and the trained model is on Hugging Face if you want to try it before training your own. Where the model lives: one small model per cluster, and only verdicts leave The framework at a glance The recipe has nine steps in three groups: decide and collect, train and measure, then ship. Most of the work is in the first group. The training run itself took nine minutes. The nine steps in three groups The arrows only go forward here, but in practice step 7 sends you back to step 3 more than once. The evaluation is where you find out what the dataset is missing. Step 1: Choose the approach There are three ways to make a general model good at your task, and they solve different problems. Pick by asking what the model is missing. Four ways to adapt a model, and where your data goes The short version: RAG adds facts, fine-tuning adds skills. Triage is a skill. The model doesn’t need to look anything up. It needs to learn that ServiceHasNoEndpoints with every pod healthy usually means the Service's selector is wrong, and that the same alert with a crashing pod means something else. I tried prompting first. The untuned model, given the full list of faults and clear instructions, answered none to almost everything and scored 10.5%. No retrieved document would teach it that pattern either, so I fine-tuned. These also combine. A fine-tuned triage model can later get a RAG step that attaches the right runbook to its verdict. That’s a separate problem, and I left it out here. Agent skills , an open format now read by many agent tools, sound close to fine-tuning, but they sit on the prompting side. A skill never changes the weights: it’s instructions and code that get loaded into the context when the task calls for them, so it can teach an agent a procedure but not a pattern the model can’t already see. The two fit together well. A skill could tell a large troubleshooting agent to ask the small in-cluster model for a fault id first, then follow the matching runbook. Privacy is the strongest argument in that last column. Prompting, RAG and agent skills all still run on a large model, so whatever they read to troubleshoot, your logs, configs, topology and code, ends up on a third party’s servers. The risk isn’t theoretical. In July 2026 a researcher found that xAI’s Grok Build coding agent uploaded entire Git repositories to xAI’s cloud storage , including unredacted .env credentials and files the agent had been told not to open: 5.1 GiB sent for a task that read about 192 KiB. Production troubleshooting is exactly the case where the context is your most sensitive data, and a model running inside the cluster keeps all of it there. Code: the system prompt, the prompt builder and the scorer used for the untuned baseline and the API models are in eval/baseline.py . Step 2: Choose and size the base model There’s no official line between small and large models. NVIDIA’s position paper on small models for agents defines a small model as one that fits on a common consumer device and answers fast enough to serve one user, and counts most models under 10 billion parameters. It’s the same Transformer architecture as a frontier model, trained the same way, just sized for hardware you own. For an in-cluster job I looked at four things: Size. It has to run on a CPU node next to everything else, without a GPU. License. It has to be open enough to fine-tune and ship inside your own infrastructure. Instruction following. A base that already follows a system prompt learns a narrow task from far fewer examples. Context length. The prompt carries the alert, the pods, the services and recent events, which comes to about 700 tokens. I picked Qwen3–1.7B , the second-smallest model in Alibaba’s Qwen3 family . It’s Apache 2.0, it handles a 40,960-token context, and it’s recent enough to follow instructions well. Qwen3 also has a thinking mode, where it writes out its reasoning before answering. For a one-word answer that only burns time, so I turned it off everywhere: in training, in scoring and in the server. How much memory it needs A model’s weights take the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter. Qwen3–1.7B has 1,738,007,552 parameters, so: Memory for Qwen3–1.7B’s weights at each precision Serving needs more than the weights. The KV cache stores the attention keys and values for every token in the context, so the model doesn’t recompute them for each new token. Its size per token is: 2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes = 2 × 28 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 114,688 bytes At a 2,048-token context that’s about 224 MiB. A common rule of thumb adds 20% on top of the weights for the cache and runtime buffers. In practice the 8-bit model peaked at 4.14 GiB in its container, well above what the arithmetic predicts, so measure your own and set limits from the measurement. For training, a 16-bit copy of the model (3.2 GiB) plus LoRA’s gradients and optimizer state fits comfortably on the free Colab T4, which has 16 GB. Code: the whole pipeline, from cluster to serving, is summarised in the repo’s README . Step 3: Build a labelled dataset by breaking a cluster Fine-tuning needs examples of the input and the right answer. For alert triage, the hard part is the right answer: someone has to decide what caused each alert, and doing that by hand is slow and inconsistent. So I made the answers known in advance. I broke a cluster on purpose, one fault at a time, and labelled every alert that fired with the fault I had just injected. Start from what you already have In this example I used a local kind cluster, because I needed labels I could trust and a cluster I was free to break. In your own environment you probably don’t need to break anything to get started. You already have most of the raw material: Alerts you’ve already seen. Prometheus keeps every firing alert as the ALERTS series, and Alertmanager can forward every notification to a webhook you control. That gives you the inputs. Incidents you’ve already resolved. Tickets and postmortems usually record the root cause. Joining them to the alerts that fired during the incident gives you the labels. Logs and events. Kubernetes events, pod status and application logs from around each alert are the context the model reads, the same way a person on call would. Runbooks. Your runbook names are often a good starting label set, because they’re already the categories your team thinks in. Where your history has gaps, inject faults on purpose in a staging cluster, either with a small harness like the one below or with a chaos tool such as Chaos Mesh or LitmusChaos . Real incidents give you realism, and injected faults give you clean labels and enough examples of the rare classes. A mix of both is a good place to be. The setup A local kind cluster with three nodes. kube-prometheus-stack for Prometheus and Alertmanager. A small demo app: an nginx frontend that proxies to a backend, plus a load generator so the services see traffic. A fault catalogue, where each fault has an injector and an undo. Each injector is a couple of kubectl calls that return their own undo. Here is the one that breaks a Service selector: if fid == "wrong_service_selector": kubectl("patch", "service", workload, "-n", namespace, "--type=merge", "-p", '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"nothing-matches-this"}}}') return [["patch", "service", workload, "-n", namespace, "--type=merge", "-p", '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"' + workload + '"}}}']] The collection loop Wait until the cluster is healthy and no alerts are firing. Record which fault is about to be injected, and when. Inject it. For five minutes, capture every alert that fires, together with the context an engineer would open first: the pods in the namespace, their phase, readiness, restarts and waiting reasons, the Services and their selectors, and the recent events. Revert, and wait for healthy again. Every alert inside a window gets that window’s fault as its label. The noise class, none, comes from windows where nothing was injected, so the model also learns what routine churn looks like. Fifteen minutes of real capture: three injection windows and their alerts Make the alerts fire fast The default rules in kube-prometheus-stack wait up to fifteen minutes before firing. That’s sensible in production and slow for collecting data, so I wrote my own rules that fire after one to two minutes. Check that each rule can actually fire. A Service whose selector matches nothing doesn’t report zero endpoints, its series simply disappears, so a rule written as == 0 never triggers. This one subtracts the Services that have ready endpoints from the Services that exist: - alert: ServiceHasNoEndpoints expr: > kube_service_info{service!="kubernetes"} unless on (namespace, service) label_replace( sum by (namespace, endpointslice) (kube_endpointslice_endpoints{ready="true"}), "service", "$1", "endpointslice", "(.*)-[a-z0-9]+" ) for: 1m labels: { severity: critical } What the data looks like The same alert name can mean very different things, and the context is what tells them apart. Here are two real captured records: Two real alerts: a crashlooping pod explains itself, a broken Service hides behind healthy pods In the first, the pod has restarted five times with an error exit, so the answer is on the pod. In the second, every pod is healthy, and the only thing wrong is one line in the Service. The event log even shows leftover warnings from an earlier fault. This is why the capture records Services and selectors, and not only pods. The catalogue I ended up with twelve faults plus the noise class, and 426 alerts from 156 injection windows: The twelve faults and the noise class Check the data before you train on it A labelled dataset built by automation is only as good as its checks. These four caught real problems in mine: Filter to the namespace you broke. Alertmanager sees the whole cluster. An alert from the monitoring stack that happens to fire during a window will otherwise get that window’s label. Confirm each fault actually broke something. Probes aimed at a missing path look like a failure, but nginx answers 200 on every path. Aim them at a closed port, and check that the expected symptom shows up before you keep the window. Keep one list of labels. The label list builds the prompt, and it’s used again when scoring. Define it once and import it everywhere, so a new fault can’t be silently dropped. Read samples by hand. Pick a few records per class and ask yourself whether you could answer them from what’s in the record. If you can’t, the model can’t either. Code: the cluster is harness/kind-cluster.yaml , the monitoring stack harness/prometheus-values.yaml , the fast alert rules harness/alert-rules.yaml and the demo app harness/demo-app.yaml . The faults are in faults/catalogue.yaml and faults/inject.py . Capture is harness/capture.py , the resumable collection loop harness/collect.py , and the steps to run it all harness/RUN.md . Step 4: Split the data by incident A model has to be judged on examples it never trained on, or the score only tells you how well it memorized. So the data is split before any training: Training set. The examples the model learns from. Validation set. An optional slice used while you tune settings such as the learning rate or the number of epochs, and for stopping training early. Test set. Held back until the end and used once, to report the result. If you make decisions by looking at it, it stops being a fair exam. Two more rules matter for this kind of data. Stratify by class. A plain random split can leave a rare class with no test examples at all, and then nobody notices the model never learned it. Stratifying keeps each class’s share the same on both sides. Every class here has at least 18 training examples. Group by incident. This is the rule that’s easy to miss. One injected fault produces several alerts within a few minutes, and they describe the same pods with nearly the same events. If you split alert by alert, the test set ends up full of alerts whose near-twins are in training, and the score measures recall rather than understanding. The unit of independence is the injection window, not the alert. Split by alert versus split by window The window key is the fault, its target and the minute it started, which you can recover from each alert’s capture time and its delay after injection: def window(row: dict) -> tuple: """One injection: its alerts share a fault, a target and a start time.""" seen = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(row["captured_at"].replace("Z", "+00:00")) start = seen - dt.timedelta(seconds=float(row.get("seconds_since_injection") or 0)) return (row["fault"], str(row.get("fault_target")), start.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M")) Whole windows go to one side or the other, drawn per class so the test set stays stratified. The result was 302 training alerts and 124 test alerts, from 42 test windows, with no window on both sides. The export script asserts that last part every time it runs, because a split that leaks gives you a good-looking number and nothing else. If you’d rather not write the grouping yourself, scikit-learn’s StratifiedGroupKFold does stratified, grouped splits with the window key as the group. What about the validation set? I didn’t keep one. With 426 alerts, a third slice would have left some classes with very few training examples. Instead I fixed the training recipe up front, using the defaults the tooling recommends, and never adjusted it after looking at test results. That keeps the test score honest, at the cost of not knowing whether other settings would do better. With more data, hold out 10 to 15% of the training windows for validation and use it for early stopping or a small hyperparameter search. Code: the grouped, stratified split is eval/make_grouped_split.py , and the check that no window lands on both sides is in models/export_training.py . Step 5: Format the data as chat An instruction-tuned model was trained on conversations, so the easiest way to teach it something new is to write your examples as conversations too. Each example becomes three messages: system : the job and the rules, the same for every example; user : one alert and its context; assistant : the answer, a single fault id. Here is one real example. The system message lists every allowed answer, so the model only has to choose, and the user message is built from the captured record in the order an engineer would read it: One training example: system, user and assistant messages And the three together are one line of a JSONL file: def chat(row: dict) -> dict: return {"messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": prompt_for(row)}, {"role": "assistant", "content": row["fault"]}, ]} One rule saves a lot of trouble: build the prompt in one function and import it everywhere, in the training export, in the evaluation and in the service that runs in the cluster. If the model is trained on one wording and served another, you’re measuring a model you don’t deploy. Chat templates and tokens The model doesn’t read messages, it reads one long string of tokens , the word pieces a model works with. Every model family has a chat template that flattens the messages into that string, with special markers for where each turn starts and ends. For Qwen3 it looks like this: The chat template flattens the messages into one string of tokens Never write this by hand. The tokenizer ships the template, and tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False) produces it. The empty block is what Qwen3's template writes when thinking is turned off, and the same template has to be used at serving time, or the model sees a format it wasn't trained on. A typical example here is about 700 tokens of prompt and a few tokens of answer. During training, the model learns to predict each next token of that string. You can mask the loss so it only learns from the answer; I trained on the whole string, which is the default and worked fine for a task this narrow. Code: models/export_training.py writes train.jsonl and eval.jsonl, importing SYSTEM and prompt_for from eval/baseline.py . Step 6: Fine-tune with LoRA Full fine-tuning keeps training a pretrained model on your examples and updates every weight. For 1.7 billion weights that needs a lot of GPU memory for gradients and optimizer state, and every version you train is another full copy of the model. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning updates only a small part of the model. The model already knows the language, so a small change is enough to teach it a narrow task. The most common method is LoRA , low-rank adaptation . How LoRA works LoRA freezes every original weight matrix W and trains two small matrices beside it, B and A. Their product is a correction added to W’s output: h = W x + (α/r) B A x If W is d × d, then B is d × r and A is r × d, where r, the rank , is small. B starts at zero, so at the first step the model behaves exactly like the base, and training moves it only as far as the data asks. α (alpha) scales the correction. Full fine-tuning updates the whole matrix; LoRA trains two thin matrices beside a frozen one For one attention matrix in Qwen3–1.7B, 2048 × 2048, full fine-tuning updates 4,194,304 weights. LoRA at rank 16 trains 2048 × 16 + 16 × 2048 = 65,536 of them. The original LoRA paper reported 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters when adapting GPT-3 175B. At 1.7B the ratio is smaller, but the idea is the same. Where to put the adapters Each Transformer layer has two parts. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter, using four projections: query, key, value and output (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj). The MLP then transforms each token, using three more (gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj). I put an adapter on all seven, in all 28 layers. That comes to 17,432,576 trainable weights out of 1,738,007,552, or 1.00% . The trained adapter is about 66 MB. A 16-bit base or a 4-bit one QLoRA loads the frozen base in 4 bits to save memory and trains the adapter on top. It’s the right choice when the base won’t fit in your GPU otherwise. But the adapter then learns corrections to rounded 4-bit weights, and if you later merge it into the ordinary 16-bit model for deployment, those corrections land on weights they weren’t meant for. In one comparison I ran, a QLoRA adapter lost 41 points of accuracy when merged. The same data trained over a 16-bit base lost nothing, and the run was faster. A 1.7B model fits on a T4 in 16 bits, so train in 16 bits if you plan to merge. The training code I used Unsloth , which wraps Hugging Face’s PEFT and TRL libraries and makes LoRA training faster and lighter on a small GPU. In a Colab notebook with a T4 runtime, after pip install unsloth and uploading train.jsonl: from unsloth import FastLanguageModel from datasets import Dataset from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer import json model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Qwen3-1.7B", max_seq_length=4096, load_in_4bit=False) model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=16, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, bias="none", target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"], use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth", random_state=7) rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("train.jsonl")] texts = [tokenizer.apply_chat_template(r["messages"], tokenize=False) for r in rows] trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model, tokenizer=tokenizer, train_dataset=Dataset.from_dict({"text": texts}), args=SFTConfig( dataset_text_field="text", max_seq_length=4096, per_device_train_batch_size=1, gradient_accumulation_steps=8, num_train_epochs=3, learning_rate=2e-4, warmup_steps=5, lr_scheduler_type="linear", optim="adamw_8bit", weight_decay=0.01, logging_steps=5, seed=7, output_dir="out", report_to="none")) trainer.train() model.save_pretrained("qwen3-1.7b-triage-lora") tokenizer.save_pretrained("qwen3-1.7b-triage-lora") What each setting does What each training setting does With 302 examples and an effective batch of 8, that’s about 38 updates per epoch and about 114 in total. On the free Colab T4 the run took 541 seconds, about nine minutes. Training is still not fully deterministic on a GPU. I trained the same data with the same seed twice and got 79.8% and 82.3% on the test set. Report the spread, not only the best run. Code: the full training script, with scoring before and after and the q8_0 export, is models/train_colab.py . Model: the trained adapter is published at jcanizalez/qwen3–1.7b-k8s-alert-triage-lora , with a model card covering the prompt format, how to load it with PEFT, and how to serve it with llama.cpp at q8_0. Step 7: Evaluate against baselines A score means little on its own. It needs baselines, and the same test for everyone. I scored four contenders on the same 124 test alerts, with the same system prompt and the same user messages: the untuned Qwen3–1.7B, the tuned one, and two API models, a frontier model and a cheap fast one. Generate, then parse The model generates greedily (always the most likely next token), with a short output limit, and the answer is parsed back to one of the known ids. Evaluating in the task’s own terms is simple here, because the answer is a label. If the reply contains several ids, the last one mentioned wins, and a reply with none counts as wrong. def parse(text: str) -> str: low = (text or "").lower() hits = [f for f in FAULTS if re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(f)}\b", low)] return max(hits, key=lambda f: low.rfind(f)) if hits else "unparseable" prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( row["messages"][:-1], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False) ids = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda") out = model.generate(**ids, max_new_tokens=48, do_sample=False) answer = parse(tokenizer.decode(out[0][ids["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)) Scoring the API models The two API models were scored through OpenRouter , which serves many providers behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so a single script and a single key cover both. Each test alert gets exactly the same system and user messages the small model saw, with temperature 0, and the reply goes through the same parse function: OPENROUTER = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" body = json.dumps({ "model": model, # "anthropic/claude-opus-5" or "google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite" "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": prompt_for(row)}, ], "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 2000, }).encode() req = urllib.request.Request(OPENROUTER, data=body, headers={ "Content-Type": "application/json", "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}", }) with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120) as res: text = json.loads(res.read())["choices"][0]["message"]["content"] answer = parse(text) Two details matter. The output limit is generous, 2,000 tokens, because a model that reasons before answering can spend a small limit before it writes anything, and an empty reply would score as wrong. And a failed request is retried, and aborts the run if it keeps failing, rather than counting as a wrong answer, so a network problem can’t pass for a bad model. The script records every answer and its latency per alert, which is where the p95 figures come from. To score another model, run eval/baseline.py --model . Two metrics Accuracy is the share of alerts labelled correctly. It’s easy to read, but a model can look good by getting the common classes right and ignoring the rare ones. Macro F1 fixes that. For each class, precision is how often the model is right when it names that class, and recall is how many of that class’s alerts it finds. F1 combines the two, and macro F1 averages F1 over the classes, so every class counts the same no matter how many alerts it has. The results Results on 124 held-out alerts The tuned 1.7B model beats Opus by 12 points. A second training run with the same data and settings scored 82.3%, so the lead is well outside the run-to-run spread. Read the untuned row carefully. It answers none to almost everything: 8 of 8 on real noise and zero on ten of the other twelve classes. So its 10.5% is close to what you'd get by always saying nothing is wrong, and the useful comparison is against Opus, not against the untuned model. Look at every class Correct answers per fault for the tuned model, Opus and Flash-Lite, on 124 held-out alerts The per-class view shows what the totals hide. The top row is the case for fine-tuning: when the backend is scaled to zero, the frontend’s pods look healthy while its requests fail, and from outside that looks like several other faults. The tuned model gets 8 of 9, Opus 2 and Flash-Lite none. That’s knowledge about this cluster, and a general model can’t have it. The bottom rows show where the small model is weaker. dns_broken needs the model to notice that a Service is an ExternalName pointing at a host that doesn't resolve, and Opus reads that better, 5 of 8 against 3. On real noise the tuned model raises false alarms, 3 of 8 against Flash-Lite's 6. Those are the first two classes I'd send to a larger model, and they tell you what data to collect next. Code: the API models are scored by eval/baseline.py , the local model by the score function in models/train_colab.py . Every answer, per model and per alert, is in results/headtohead . Step 8: Merge, quantize and package Training leaves you with a base model and an adapter that run in Python on a GPU. The cluster wants one file that runs on a CPU. Getting there takes three moves: merge the adapter into the base, reduce the precision, and write the result as GGUF. Each one can cost accuracy, so score the model again after each. Merging Merging computes W + (α/r)BA once for every adapted matrix and saves the result as an ordinary model, so inference no longer needs the adapter. With a 16-bit base the arithmetic is exact. In my runs the merged model scored 80.6% against 82.3% for the adapter loaded separately, two alerts out of 124, which is within the spread between training runs. model.save_pretrained_merged("merged", tokenizer, save_method="merged_16bit") You can also skip merging. llama.cpp can load the base and the adapter side by side with --lora adapter.gguf, which suits a design where many clusters share one base and each gets its own small adapter. Precision Every weight is a number, and precision is how many bits it gets: Number formats Quantization, worked by hand Quantization stores weights as small integers plus a scale. The simplest scheme, absmax , takes a block of weights, finds the largest absolute value, and maps it to the largest integer available. Take four weights: 0.2, −1.3, 4.1 and 0.05. At 8 bits the integers run from −127 to 127, so the scale is 127 / 4.1 ≈ 30.98. The weight 0.2 becomes round(0.2 × 30.98) = 6, which reads back as 6 / 30.98 ≈ 0.19. The weight 0.05 becomes 2, which reads back as 0.065. Both are close. At 4 bits the integers run from −7 to 7, so the scale is 7 / 4.1 ≈ 1.71. Now 0.2 becomes round(0.34) = 0, and so does 0.05. Both small weights are gone. The same four weights at 8 and 4 bits That’s the whole trade: fewer bits means a smaller file and faster CPU inference, and coarser steps, so small values get rounded away. Real formats reduce the damage by using small blocks, each with its own scale. q8_0 , llama.cpp’s 8-bit format, uses blocks of 32 weights with one 16-bit scale each. q4_k_m uses 4-bit blocks grouped into super-blocks with their own scales, and keeps a few sensitive tensors at 6 bits. The research is encouraging for large models. LLM.int8() showed 8-bit inference matching 16-bit accuracy on models up to 175B parameters, and GPTQ brought models that size to 3 or 4 bits per weight with little loss. The LLM.int8() work also showed that a few outlier values can wreck simple 8-bit schemes, so whether quantization is cheap depends on what’s in the weights. GGUF GGUF is the file format of llama.cpp . It stores the weights together with typed key-value metadata in a single file : the architecture, the tokenizer, the chat template and every tensor. Here’s what’s inside the file I serve, read from its own header: Inside the GGUF the cluster serves The chat template travels inside the file, so the server formats prompts exactly as training did. To produce it, either let Unsloth do everything: model.save_pretrained_gguf("export", tokenizer, quantization_method="q8_0") or convert the merged model with llama.cpp’s own tools: python convert_hf_to_gguf.py merged --outfile model-f16.gguf --outtype f16 ./llama-quantize model-f16.gguf model-q8_0.gguf Q8_0 Unsloth writes into a sibling directory named export_gguf, not into export, so look there for the file. What it cost The same adapter, run four ways on the same 124 test alerts: One adapter run four ways, against Opus 8-bit costs about five points and still beats Opus comfortably. 4-bit drops to 30.6%. q4_k_m is the default most tools suggest, and for many models it's a fine choice, but for this fine-tune it throws away most of what training taught. Always score the quantized file itself, not the model you trained. My working explanation, which I haven’t tested directly, is the one from the worked example: the adapter changes each weight by a small amount, and at 4 bits many of those changes round back to the original value, like the two small weights above. Code: the merge test is models/score_merged.py , the export and scoring of each quantization models/score_quantizations.py , and the GGUF header reader behind the figure is in diagrams/figures.py . Step 9: Serve it inside the cluster The deployment is two small workloads in their own namespace: llama-server runs the model, and a triage service turns alerts into prompts and prompts into verdicts. One alert, from webhook to verdict The model server llama-server from llama.cpp serves an OpenAI-compatible API from a single GGUF, which sits on a volume so a retrain is a file copy rather than a new image: containers: - name: llama-server image: ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server args: ["-m", "/models/model.gguf", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080", "-c", "2048", "--reasoning", "off", "-np", "1", "-t", "2"] resources: requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi } limits: { cpu: "2", memory: 5Gi } readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 } llama-server flags The triage service Alertmanager sends firing alerts to the service by webhook: receivers: - name: triage webhook_configs: - url: http://triage.triage.svc.cluster.local:8080/alert send_resolved: false For each alert, the service reads the namespace, builds the same prompt used in training, and asks the model: body = { "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": prompt_for(labels, annotations, ctx)}, ], "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 48, } answer = await http.post(LLAMA_URL, json=body) fault = parse(answer.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]) verdict = {"alert": labels.get("alertname"), "namespace": namespace, "object": workload, "fault": fault, "escalate": fault == "unparseable"} It reads the cluster through a service account bound to this role, and nothing more: kind: ClusterRole metadata: name: triage-reader rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods", "services", "events"] verbs: ["get", "list"] How it performs On two CPU cores the 8-bit model answers in about 6 seconds on average, with a p95 under 10 seconds. That’s slower than Flash-Lite and faster than Opus, and each call costs nothing. In an end-to-end test I injected a crashloop into the demo app, and the first correct verdict came back 128 seconds later. Most of that is the alert rule waiting to fire, not the model. Security Alerts, pod state and events never leave the cluster. Only the verdict does. The service can get and list pods, services and events. It can't change anything it reads. Nothing the model outputs gets executed. The verdict is a label for a person or another system to read. No third party sees your topology, image names or error messages, which matters in regulated environments. An answer the service can’t parse is marked for escalation instead of being guessed. Code: the deployment, RBAC and model volume are serve/manifests.yaml , the service is serve/triage.py with its Dockerfile , and the Alertmanager receiver is in harness/prometheus-values.yaml . The checklist The whole framework on one screen. Each line is something to decide or check before moving on. The checklist What this doesn’t show, and what’s next This is one cluster, one small app and twelve faults I wrote myself. Real clusters have hundreds of alert rules and failures nobody has catalogued, and a model trained on mine knows mine, which is the point, but it means you train your own. With 124 test alerts a 12-point gap is clear, while any single per-class number is only a handful of alerts. I also haven’t measured the escalation path, so I can’t say yet what share of alerts would go to a large model, or what the whole system costs per thousand alerts. The next step is that escalation path. AdaptiveLog does something similar for log analysis, sending a log to the large model when the small one is uncertain. For alerts, I’d let the small model answer when it’s confident, send the rest up, and measure where the line should sit. After that I’d try a public benchmark like ITBench, where I expect a 1.7B model to struggle with open-ended root cause, and a second cluster with different workloads. For the narrow, repetitive first pass of troubleshooting, a small model trained on your own cluster did better than the largest model I could rent, on two CPU cores, without sending anything outside. The hard, new incidents still belong to a bigger model or a person. Fine-Tuning a Small Model to Triage Kubernetes Alerts was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
A step-by-step recipe for teaching Qwen3–1.7B to triage your cluster’s alerts, on a free GPU. It beat Opus 5 by 12 points and never sends your data outside the cluster.

Lately I’ve been working with agents pretty much every day, and one of the jobs I keep seeing companies hand to agents is troubleshooting. An alert fires, someone has to work out what broke, and that someone is usually expensive and tired. I’ve built a couple of agents for this myself, and all of them called a large model behind an API.

That works, but a few things kept me wondering whether it really scales:

  • Cost. Every call is billed, and on a noisy night you pay for the same PodNotReady a few hundred times, per cluster.
  • Privacy. Every alert leaves the cluster, together with the logs, events and config around it, and lands on someone else’s servers.
  • Accuracy. The large models aren’t even that good at it: on IBM’s ITBench, agents powered by state-of-the-art models resolved only 13.8% of the SRE scenarios.

So in this experiment I wanted to see how far a small model can go. I took Qwen3–1.7B, a model small enough to run on two CPU cores inside the cluster, and taught it one narrow job: read an alert and the state around it, and name the fault that caused it. On 124 alerts it had never seen, the tuned model scored 79.8%, against 67.7% for Claude Opus 5.

This article is the recipe, step by step, so you can do the same with your own cluster. Each step explains the concept first, then shows the code I used. Everything runs on a laptop plus a free Colab GPU. The full harness is on GitHub, and the trained model is on Hugging Face if you want to try it before training your own.

Where the model lives: one small model per cluster, and only verdicts leaveThe framework at a glance

The recipe has nine steps in three groups: decide and collect, train and measure, then ship. Most of the work is in the first group. The training run itself took nine minutes.

The nine steps in three groups

The arrows only go forward here, but in practice step 7 sends you back to step 3 more than once. The evaluation is where you find out what the dataset is missing.

Step 1: Choose the approach

There are three ways to make a general model good at your task, and they solve different problems. Pick by asking what the model is missing.

Four ways to adapt a model, and where your data goes

The short version: RAG adds facts, fine-tuning adds skills.

Triage is a skill. The model doesn’t need to look anything up. It needs to learn that ServiceHasNoEndpoints with every pod healthy usually means the Service's selector is wrong, and that the same alert with a crashing pod means something else. I tried prompting first. The untuned model, given the full list of faults and clear instructions, answered none to almost everything and scored 10.5%. No retrieved document would teach it that pattern either, so I fine-tuned.

These also combine. A fine-tuned triage model can later get a RAG step that attaches the right runbook to its verdict. That’s a separate problem, and I left it out here.

Agent skills, an open format now read by many agent tools, sound close to fine-tuning, but they sit on the prompting side. A skill never changes the weights: it’s instructions and code that get loaded into the context when the task calls for them, so it can teach an agent a procedure but not a pattern the model can’t already see. The two fit together well. A skill could tell a large troubleshooting agent to ask the small in-cluster model for a fault id first, then follow the matching runbook.

Privacy is the strongest argument in that last column. Prompting, RAG and agent skills all still run on a large model, so whatever they read to troubleshoot, your logs, configs, topology and code, ends up on a third party’s servers. The risk isn’t theoretical. In July 2026 a researcher found that xAI’s Grok Build coding agent uploaded entire Git repositories to xAI’s cloud storage, including unredacted .env credentials and files the agent had been told not to open: 5.1 GiB sent for a task that read about 192 KiB. Production troubleshooting is exactly the case where the context is your most sensitive data, and a model running inside the cluster keeps all of it there.

Code: the system prompt, the prompt builder and the scorer used for the untuned baseline and the API models are in eval/baseline.py.

Step 2: Choose and size the base model

There’s no official line between small and large models. NVIDIA’s position paper on small models for agents defines a small model as one that fits on a common consumer device and answers fast enough to serve one user, and counts most models under 10 billion parameters. It’s the same Transformer architecture as a frontier model, trained the same way, just sized for hardware you own.

For an in-cluster job I looked at four things:

  • Size. It has to run on a CPU node next to everything else, without a GPU.
  • License. It has to be open enough to fine-tune and ship inside your own infrastructure.
  • Instruction following. A base that already follows a system prompt learns a narrow task from far fewer examples.
  • Context length. The prompt carries the alert, the pods, the services and recent events, which comes to about 700 tokens.

I picked Qwen3–1.7B, the second-smallest model in Alibaba’s Qwen3 family. It’s Apache 2.0, it handles a 40,960-token context, and it’s recent enough to follow instructions well. Qwen3 also has a thinking mode, where it writes out its reasoning before answering. For a one-word answer that only burns time, so I turned it off everywhere: in training, in scoring and in the server.

How much memory it needs

A model’s weights take the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter. Qwen3–1.7B has 1,738,007,552 parameters, so:

Memory for Qwen3–1.7B’s weights at each precision

Serving needs more than the weights. The KV cache stores the attention keys and values for every token in the context, so the model doesn’t recompute them for each new token. Its size per token is:

2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes
= 2 × 28 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 114,688 bytes

At a 2,048-token context that’s about 224 MiB. A common rule of thumb adds 20% on top of the weights for the cache and runtime buffers. In practice the 8-bit model peaked at 4.14 GiB in its container, well above what the arithmetic predicts, so measure your own and set limits from the measurement.

For training, a 16-bit copy of the model (3.2 GiB) plus LoRA’s gradients and optimizer state fits comfortably on the free Colab T4, which has 16 GB.
