Step 3: Build a labelled dataset by breaking a cluster

Fine-tuning needs examples of the input and the right answer. For alert triage, the hard part is the right answer: someone has to decide what caused each alert, and doing that by hand is slow and inconsistent. So I made the answers known in advance. I broke a cluster on purpose, one fault at a time, and labelled every alert that fired with the fault I had just injected.

Start from what you already have

In this example I used a local kind cluster, because I needed labels I could trust and a cluster I was free to break. In your own environment you probably don’t need to break anything to get started. You already have most of the raw material:

  • Alerts you’ve already seen. Prometheus keeps every firing alert as the ALERTS series, and Alertmanager can forward every notification to a webhook you control. That gives you the inputs.
  • Incidents you’ve already resolved. Tickets and postmortems usually record the root cause. Joining them to the alerts that fired during the incident gives you the labels.
  • Logs and events. Kubernetes events, pod status and application logs from around each alert are the context the model reads, the same way a person on call would.
  • Runbooks. Your runbook names are often a good starting label set, because they’re already the categories your team thinks in.

Where your history has gaps, inject faults on purpose in a staging cluster, either with a small harness like the one below or with a chaos tool such as Chaos Mesh or LitmusChaos. Real incidents give you realism, and injected faults give you clean labels and enough examples of the rare classes. A mix of both is a good place to be.

The setup
  • A local kind cluster with three nodes.
  • kube-prometheus-stack for Prometheus and Alertmanager.
  • A small demo app: an nginx frontend that proxies to a backend, plus a load generator so the services see traffic.
  • A fault catalogue, where each fault has an injector and an undo.

Each injector is a couple of kubectl calls that return their own undo. Here is the one that breaks a Service selector:

if fid == "wrong_service_selector":
    kubectl("patch", "service", workload, "-n", namespace, "--type=merge",
            "-p", '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"nothing-matches-this"}}}')
    return [["patch", "service", workload, "-n", namespace, "--type=merge",
             "-p", '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"' + workload + '"}}}']]
The collection loop
  1. Wait until the cluster is healthy and no alerts are firing.
  2. Record which fault is about to be injected, and when.
  3. Inject it.
  4. For five minutes, capture every alert that fires, together with the context an engineer would open first: the pods in the namespace, their phase, readiness, restarts and waiting reasons, the Services and their selectors, and the recent events.
  5. Revert, and wait for healthy again.

Every alert inside a window gets that window’s fault as its label. The noise class, none, comes from windows where nothing was injected, so the model also learns what routine churn looks like.

Fifteen minutes of real capture: three injection windows and their alertsMake the alerts fire fast

The default rules in kube-prometheus-stack wait up to fifteen minutes before firing. That’s sensible in production and slow for collecting data, so I wrote my own rules that fire after one to two minutes. Check that each rule can actually fire. A Service whose selector matches nothing doesn’t report zero endpoints, its series simply disappears, so a rule written as == 0 never triggers. This one subtracts the Services that have ready endpoints from the Services that exist:

- alert: ServiceHasNoEndpoints
  expr: >
    kube_service_info{service!="kubernetes"}
    unless on (namespace, service)
    label_replace(
      sum by (namespace, endpointslice) (kube_endpointslice_endpoints{ready="true"}),
      "service", "$1", "endpointslice", "(.*)-[a-z0-9]+"
    )
  for: 1m
  labels: { severity: critical }
What the data looks like

The same alert name can mean very different things, and the context is what tells them apart. Here are two real captured records:

Two real alerts: a crashlooping pod explains itself, a broken Service hides behind healthy pods

In the first, the pod has restarted five times with an error exit, so the answer is on the pod. In the second, every pod is healthy, and the only thing wrong is one line in the Service. The event log even shows leftover warnings from an earlier fault. This is why the capture records Services and selectors, and not only pods.

The catalogue

I ended up with twelve faults plus the noise class, and 426 alerts from 156 injection windows:

The twelve faults and the noise classCheck the data before you train on it

A labelled dataset built by automation is only as good as its checks. These four caught real problems in mine:

  • Filter to the namespace you broke. Alertmanager sees the whole cluster. An alert from the monitoring stack that happens to fire during a window will otherwise get that window’s label.
  • Confirm each fault actually broke something. Probes aimed at a missing path look like a failure, but nginx answers 200 on every path. Aim them at a closed port, and check that the expected symptom shows up before you keep the window.
  • Keep one list of labels. The label list builds the prompt, and it’s used again when scoring. Define it once and import it everywhere, so a new fault can’t be silently dropped.
  • Read samples by hand. Pick a few records per class and ask yourself whether you could answer them from what’s in the record. If you can’t, the model can’t either.

Step 4: Split the data by incident

A model has to be judged on examples it never trained on, or the score only tells you how well it memorized. So the data is split before any training:

  • Training set. The examples the model learns from.
  • Validation set. An optional slice used while you tune settings such as the learning rate or the number of epochs, and for stopping training early.
  • Test set. Held back until the end and used once, to report the result. If you make decisions by looking at it, it stops being a fair exam.

Two more rules matter for this kind of data.

Stratify by class. A plain random split can leave a rare class with no test examples at all, and then nobody notices the model never learned it. Stratifying keeps each class’s share the same on both sides. Every class here has at least 18 training examples.

Group by incident. This is the rule that’s easy to miss. One injected fault produces several alerts within a few minutes, and they describe the same pods with nearly the same events. If you split alert by alert, the test set ends up full of alerts whose near-twins are in training, and the score measures recall rather than understanding. The unit of independence is the injection window, not the alert.

Split by alert versus split by window

The window key is the fault, its target and the minute it started, which you can recover from each alert’s capture time and its delay after injection:

def window(row: dict) -> tuple:
    """One injection: its alerts share a fault, a target and a start time."""
    seen = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(row["captured_at"].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    start = seen - dt.timedelta(seconds=float(row.get("seconds_since_injection") or 0))
    return (row["fault"], str(row.get("fault_target")), start.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M"))

Whole windows go to one side or the other, drawn per class so the test set stays stratified. The result was 302 training alerts and 124 test alerts, from 42 test windows, with no window on both sides. The export script asserts that last part every time it runs, because a split that leaks gives you a good-looking number and nothing else.

If you’d rather not write the grouping yourself, scikit-learn’s StratifiedGroupKFold does stratified, grouped splits with the window key as the group.

What about the validation set?

I didn’t keep one. With 426 alerts, a third slice would have left some classes with very few training examples. Instead I fixed the training recipe up front, using the defaults the tooling recommends, and never adjusted it after looking at test results. That keeps the test score honest, at the cost of not knowing whether other settings would do better. With more data, hold out 10 to 15% of the training windows for validation and use it for early stopping or a small hyperparameter search.

Code: the grouped, stratified split is eval/make_grouped_split.py, and the check that no window lands on both sides is in models/export_training.py.

Step 5: Format the data as chat

An instruction-tuned model was trained on conversations, so the easiest way to teach it something new is to write your examples as conversations too. Each example becomes three messages:

  • system: the job and the rules, the same for every example;
  • user: one alert and its context;
  • assistant: the answer, a single fault id.

Here is one real example. The system message lists every allowed answer, so the model only has to choose, and the user message is built from the captured record in the order an engineer would read it:

One training example: system, user and assistant messages

And the three together are one line of a JSONL file:

def chat(row: dict) -> dict:
    return {"messages": [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt_for(row)},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": row["fault"]},
    ]}

One rule saves a lot of trouble: build the prompt in one function and import it everywhere, in the training export, in the evaluation and in the service that runs in the cluster. If the model is trained on one wording and served another, you’re measuring a model you don’t deploy.

Chat templates and tokens

The model doesn’t read messages, it reads one long string of tokens, the word pieces a model works with. Every model family has a chat template that flattens the messages into that string, with special markers for where each turn starts and ends. For Qwen3 it looks like this:

The chat template flattens the messages into one string of tokens

Never write this by hand. The tokenizer ships the template, and tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False) produces it. The empty block is what Qwen3's template writes when thinking is turned off, and the same template has to be used at serving time, or the model sees a format it wasn't trained on.

A typical example here is about 700 tokens of prompt and a few tokens of answer. During training, the model learns to predict each next token of that string. You can mask the loss so it only learns from the answer; I trained on the whole string, which is the default and worked fine for a task this narrow.

Step 6: Fine-tune with LoRA

Full fine-tuning keeps training a pretrained model on your examples and updates every weight. For 1.7 billion weights that needs a lot of GPU memory for gradients and optimizer state, and every version you train is another full copy of the model.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning updates only a small part of the model. The model already knows the language, so a small change is enough to teach it a narrow task. The most common method is LoRA, low-rank adaptation.

How LoRA works

LoRA freezes every original weight matrix W and trains two small matrices beside it, B and A. Their product is a correction added to W’s output:

h = W x + (α/r) B A x

If W is d × d, then B is d × r and A is r × d, where r, the rank, is small. B starts at zero, so at the first step the model behaves exactly like the base, and training moves it only as far as the data asks. α (alpha) scales the correction.

Full fine-tuning updates the whole matrix; LoRA trains two thin matrices beside a frozen one

For one attention matrix in Qwen3–1.7B, 2048 × 2048, full fine-tuning updates 4,194,304 weights. LoRA at rank 16 trains 2048 × 16 + 16 × 2048 = 65,536 of them. The original LoRA paper reported 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters when adapting GPT-3 175B. At 1.7B the ratio is smaller, but the idea is the same.

Where to put the adapters

Each Transformer layer has two parts. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter, using four projections: query, key, value and output (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj). The MLP then transforms each token, using three more (gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj). I put an adapter on all seven, in all 28 layers. That comes to 17,432,576 trainable weights out of 1,738,007,552, or 1.00%. The trained adapter is about 66 MB.

A 16-bit base or a 4-bit one

QLoRA loads the frozen base in 4 bits to save memory and trains the adapter on top. It’s the right choice when the base won’t fit in your GPU otherwise. But the adapter then learns corrections to rounded 4-bit weights, and if you later merge it into the ordinary 16-bit model for deployment, those corrections land on weights they weren’t meant for. In one comparison I ran, a QLoRA adapter lost 41 points of accuracy when merged. The same data trained over a 16-bit base lost nothing, and the run was faster. A 1.7B model fits on a T4 in 16 bits, so train in 16 bits if you plan to merge.

The training code

I used Unsloth, which wraps Hugging Face’s PEFT and TRL libraries and makes LoRA training faster and lighter on a small GPU. In a Colab notebook with a T4 runtime, after pip install unsloth and uploading train.jsonl:

from unsloth import FastLanguageModel
from datasets import Dataset
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer
import json
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name="unsloth/Qwen3-1.7B", max_seq_length=4096, load_in_4bit=False)
model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(
    model,
    r=16, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, bias="none",
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
                    "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
    use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth", random_state=7)
rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("train.jsonl")]
texts = [tokenizer.apply_chat_template(r["messages"], tokenize=False) for r in rows]
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model, tokenizer=tokenizer,
    train_dataset=Dataset.from_dict({"text": texts}),
    args=SFTConfig(
        dataset_text_field="text", max_seq_length=4096,
        per_device_train_batch_size=1, gradient_accumulation_steps=8,
        num_train_epochs=3, learning_rate=2e-4, warmup_steps=5,
        lr_scheduler_type="linear", optim="adamw_8bit", weight_decay=0.01,
        logging_steps=5, seed=7, output_dir="out", report_to="none"))
trainer.train()
model.save_pretrained("qwen3-1.7b-triage-lora")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("qwen3-1.7b-triage-lora")
What each setting doesWhat each training setting does

With 302 examples and an effective batch of 8, that’s about 38 updates per epoch and about 114 in total. On the free Colab T4 the run took 541 seconds, about nine minutes.

Training is still not fully deterministic on a GPU. I trained the same data with the same seed twice and got 79.8% and 82.3% on the test set. Report the spread, not only the best run.

Step 7: Evaluate against baselines

A score means little on its own. It needs baselines, and the same test for everyone. I scored four contenders on the same 124 test alerts, with the same system prompt and the same user messages: the untuned Qwen3–1.7B, the tuned one, and two API models, a frontier model and a cheap fast one.

Generate, then parse

The model generates greedily (always the most likely next token), with a short output limit, and the answer is parsed back to one of the known ids. Evaluating in the task’s own terms is simple here, because the answer is a label. If the reply contains several ids, the last one mentioned wins, and a reply with none counts as wrong.

def parse(text: str) -> str:
    low = (text or "").lower()
    hits = [f for f in FAULTS if re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(f)}\b", low)]
    return max(hits, key=lambda f: low.rfind(f)) if hits else "unparseable"
prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    row["messages"][:-1], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True,
    enable_thinking=False)
ids = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
out = model.generate(**ids, max_new_tokens=48, do_sample=False)
answer = parse(tokenizer.decode(out[0][ids["input_ids"].shape[1]:],
                                skip_special_tokens=True))
Scoring the API models

The two API models were scored through OpenRouter, which serves many providers behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so a single script and a single key cover both. Each test alert gets exactly the same system and user messages the small model saw, with temperature 0, and the reply goes through the same parse function:

OPENROUTER = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions"
body = json.dumps({
    "model": model,  # "anthropic/claude-opus-5" or "google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite"
    "messages": [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt_for(row)},
    ],
    "temperature": 0,
    "max_tokens": 2000,
}).encode()
req = urllib.request.Request(OPENROUTER, data=body, headers={
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}",
})
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120) as res:
    text = json.loads(res.read())["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
answer = parse(text)

Two details matter. The output limit is generous, 2,000 tokens, because a model that reasons before answering can spend a small limit before it writes anything, and an empty reply would score as wrong. And a failed request is retried, and aborts the run if it keeps failing, rather than counting as a wrong answer, so a network problem can’t pass for a bad model. The script records every answer and its latency per alert, which is where the p95 figures come from. To score another model, run eval/baseline.py --model .

Two metrics

Accuracy is the share of alerts labelled correctly. It’s easy to read, but a model can look good by getting the common classes right and ignoring the rare ones.

Macro F1 fixes that. For each class, precision is how often the model is right when it names that class, and recall is how many of that class’s alerts it finds. F1 combines the two, and macro F1 averages F1 over the classes, so every class counts the same no matter how many alerts it has.

Step 8: Merge, quantize and package

Training leaves you with a base model and an adapter that run in Python on a GPU. The cluster wants one file that runs on a CPU. Getting there takes three moves: merge the adapter into the base, reduce the precision, and write the result as GGUF. Each one can cost accuracy, so score the model again after each.

Merging

Merging computes W + (α/r)BA once for every adapted matrix and saves the result as an ordinary model, so inference no longer needs the adapter. With a 16-bit base the arithmetic is exact. In my runs the merged model scored 80.6% against 82.3% for the adapter loaded separately, two alerts out of 124, which is within the spread between training runs.

model.save_pretrained_merged("merged", tokenizer, save_method="merged_16bit")

You can also skip merging. llama.cpp can load the base and the adapter side by side with --lora adapter.gguf, which suits a design where many clusters share one base and each gets its own small adapter.

Precision

Every weight is a number, and precision is how many bits it gets:

Number formatsQuantization, worked by hand

Quantization stores weights as small integers plus a scale. The simplest scheme, absmax, takes a block of weights, finds the largest absolute value, and maps it to the largest integer available. Take four weights: 0.2, −1.3, 4.1 and 0.05.

At 8 bits the integers run from −127 to 127, so the scale is 127 / 4.1 ≈ 30.98. The weight 0.2 becomes round(0.2 × 30.98) = 6, which reads back as 6 / 30.98 ≈ 0.19. The weight 0.05 becomes 2, which reads back as 0.065. Both are close.

At 4 bits the integers run from −7 to 7, so the scale is 7 / 4.1 ≈ 1.71. Now 0.2 becomes round(0.34) = 0, and so does 0.05. Both small weights are gone.

The same four weights at 8 and 4 bits

That’s the whole trade: fewer bits means a smaller file and faster CPU inference, and coarser steps, so small values get rounded away. Real formats reduce the damage by using small blocks, each with its own scale. q8_0, llama.cpp’s 8-bit format, uses blocks of 32 weights with one 16-bit scale each. q4_k_m uses 4-bit blocks grouped into super-blocks with their own scales, and keeps a few sensitive tensors at 6 bits.

The research is encouraging for large models. LLM.int8() showed 8-bit inference matching 16-bit accuracy on models up to 175B parameters, and GPTQ brought models that size to 3 or 4 bits per weight with little loss. The LLM.int8() work also showed that a few outlier values can wreck simple 8-bit schemes, so whether quantization is cheap depends on what’s in the weights.

GGUF

GGUF is the file format of llama.cpp. It stores the weights together with typed key-value metadata in a single file: the architecture, the tokenizer, the chat template and every tensor. Here’s what’s inside the file I serve, read from its own header:

Inside the GGUF the cluster serves

The chat template travels inside the file, so the server formats prompts exactly as training did. To produce it, either let Unsloth do everything:

model.save_pretrained_gguf("export", tokenizer, quantization_method="q8_0")

or convert the merged model with llama.cpp’s own tools:

python convert_hf_to_gguf.py merged --outfile model-f16.gguf --outtype f16
./llama-quantize model-f16.gguf model-q8_0.gguf Q8_0

Unsloth writes into a sibling directory named export_gguf, not into export, so look there for the file.

What it cost

The same adapter, run four ways on the same 124 test alerts:

One adapter run four ways, against Opus

8-bit costs about five points and still beats Opus comfortably. 4-bit drops to 30.6%. q4_k_m is the default most tools suggest, and for many models it's a fine choice, but for this fine-tune it throws away most of what training taught. Always score the quantized file itself, not the model you trained.

My working explanation, which I haven’t tested directly, is the one from the worked example: the adapter changes each weight by a small amount, and at 4 bits many of those changes round back to the original value, like the two small weights above.

Step 9: Serve it inside the cluster

The deployment is two small workloads in their own namespace: llama-server runs the model, and a triage service turns alerts into prompts and prompts into verdicts.

One alert, from webhook to verdictThe model server

llama-server from llama.cpp serves an OpenAI-compatible API from a single GGUF, which sits on a volume so a retrain is a file copy rather than a new image:

containers:
  - name: llama-server
    image: ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server
    args: ["-m", "/models/model.gguf", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080",
           "-c", "2048", "--reasoning", "off", "-np", "1", "-t", "2"]
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi }
      limits: { cpu: "2", memory: 5Gi }
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
llama-server flagsThe triage service

Alertmanager sends firing alerts to the service by webhook:

receivers:
  - name: triage
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://triage.triage.svc.cluster.local:8080/alert
        send_resolved: false

For each alert, the service reads the namespace, builds the same prompt used in training, and asks the model:

body = {
    "messages": [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt_for(labels, annotations, ctx)},
    ],
    "temperature": 0,
    "max_tokens": 48,
}
answer = await http.post(LLAMA_URL, json=body)
fault = parse(answer.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
verdict = {"alert": labels.get("alertname"), "namespace": namespace,
           "object": workload, "fault": fault,
           "escalate": fault == "unparseable"}

It reads the cluster through a service account bound to this role, and nothing more:

kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: triage-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "services", "events"]
    verbs: ["get", "list"]
How it performs

On two CPU cores the 8-bit model answers in about 6 seconds on average, with a p95 under 10 seconds. That’s slower than Flash-Lite and faster than Opus, and each call costs nothing. In an end-to-end test I injected a crashloop into the demo app, and the first correct verdict came back 128 seconds later. Most of that is the alert rule waiting to fire, not the model.

Security
  • Alerts, pod state and events never leave the cluster. Only the verdict does.
  • The service can get and list pods, services and events. It can't change anything it reads.
  • Nothing the model outputs gets executed. The verdict is a label for a person or another system to read.
  • No third party sees your topology, image names or error messages, which matters in regulated environments.
  • An answer the service can’t parse is marked for escalation instead of being guessed.

The whole framework on one screen. Each line is something to decide or check before moving on.

The checklistWhat this doesn’t show, and what’s next

This is one cluster, one small app and twelve faults I wrote myself. Real clusters have hundreds of alert rules and failures nobody has catalogued, and a model trained on mine knows mine, which is the point, but it means you train your own. With 124 test alerts a 12-point gap is clear, while any single per-class number is only a handful of alerts. I also haven’t measured the escalation path, so I can’t say yet what share of alerts would go to a large model, or what the whole system costs per thousand alerts.

The next step is that escalation path. AdaptiveLog does something similar for log analysis, sending a log to the large model when the small one is uncertain. For alerts, I’d let the small model answer when it’s confident, send the rest up, and measure where the line should sit. After that I’d try a public benchmark like ITBench, where I expect a 1.7B model to struggle with open-ended root cause, and a second cluster with different workloads.

For the narrow, repetitive first pass of troubleshooting, a small model trained on your own cluster did better than the largest model I could rent, on two CPU cores, without sending anything outside. The hard, new incidents still belong to a bigger model or a person.

items.title: AI Seems to do Everything Impossible. So Where Are We in Time Travel?
items.summary: Every few days, we hear about an AI system discovering a new material, solving a mathematical problem, or finding a scientific pattern humans had missed. At the same time, physics has never completely killed the idea of time travel. Einstein’s equations contain strange solutions involving wormholes and closed timelike curves, while quantum mechanics keeps challenging our everyday intuition about cause and effect. So it is tempting to combine the two trends and ask a very 2026 question: Could AI help us build a time machine? The short answer is that AI may become extremely useful in the search for new physics involving time, gravity and causality. But we are nowhere close to engineering the kind of time travel shown in movies. The biggest obstacle is not simply that the equations are too difficult for humans. We do not yet know whether nature permits the required physical conditions at all. Still, the state of the art is much more interesting than a simple “no.” Time travel already exists… in one direction Before discussing wormholes, there is one misconception worth clearing up. Traveling into the future faster than somebody else is already allowed by established physics. Special relativity tells us that a clock moving very quickly relative to another clock accumulates less elapsed time. General relativity adds another effect: clocks in stronger gravitational fields run more slowly. (Who hasn’t seen interstellar movie, right?) These are measurable engineering effects, not philosophical ideas. Modern atomic clocks have measured gravitational time dilation across millimeter-scale height differences, and GPS requires relativistic corrections to remain accurate. If I could travel sufficiently close to the speed of light and later return to Earth, less time would have passed for me than for the people who stayed behind. In that limited sense, I would have traveled into their future. The problem is scale. Accelerating a human-scale spacecraft to relativistic speed requires extraordinary energy. AI might optimize propulsion, trajectories and materials, but it cannot negotiate with the speed of light. Going backward is where physics gets strange Travel into the past is a completely different problem. General relativity describes gravity as the geometry of spacetime. Surprisingly, some mathematically valid spacetime geometries contain what physicists call closed timelike curves , or CTCs. Roughly speaking, a CTC is a path that always moves locally forward through time but eventually returns to an earlier event. These are not just science-fiction inventions. CTCs arise in serious solutions of Einstein’s equations, including Gödel-type universes, idealized rotating spacetimes, wormhole constructions and some warp-drive geometries. And research on them is still active. In 2025, Achintya Sajeendran and Timothy Ralph published a Physical Review D paper constructing a controlled warp-drive spacetime in which a freely falling particle could follow a closed timelike curve and return to flat spacetime. Importantly, the authors explicitly noted the questionable physical realizability of the metric. In other words, the mathematics provides a time-machine-like geometry. It does not tell us how to build one. Another 2025 Physical Review D study showed how a nonsingular wormhole spacetime containing CTCs could be constructed through a form of topological surgery. But the resulting spacetime violated the standard energy conditions. That somewhat innocent-sounding statement hides one of the biggest problems in the entire subject. Many wormhole or time-machine proposals depend on exotic distributions of energy that we do not know how to create or sustain on useful scales. There is also Stephen Hawking’s famous chronology protection conjecture : perhaps quantum effects prevent time machines from forming in the first place. The question remains unsettled. Work published in 2026 is still examining whether instabilities around chronology horizons could provide such a protection mechanism. Then came a particularly interesting result in June 2026. Kaiyuan Ji, Seth Lloyd and Mark Wilde published a Physical Review Letters paper studying how much information could theoretically be sent backward through a noisy, postselected closed-timelike-curve channel. They derived information-theoretic limits for these hypothetical retrocausal channels. That sounds spectacular, but the distinction is crucial. They did not send information into the past. They studied what communication theory would look like if such a channel existed . That gap between “mathematically describable” and “physically constructible” is basically the entire time-travel problem. So where does AI enter? This is where the question becomes genuinely interesting to me as someone coming from computer science and AI. AI does not need to magically invent a time machine to change this field. Its immediate value is as a search and modeling engine . Einstein’s field equations are nonlinear tensor differential equations, and interesting spacetime geometries occupy an enormous mathematical search space. Traditionally, physicists make simplifying assumptions, choose a form for the spacetime metric, solve the equations and then test whether the solution has sensible physical properties. AI gives us another possibility: searching and representing much larger spaces computationally. We are already seeing early versions of this. A 2025 project called Einstein Fields used neural representations to encode four-dimensional numerical-relativity simulations as implicit neural networks representing the spacetime metric. The researchers reported up to roughly a 4,000-fold reduction in storage on their test cases while preserving high numerical accuracy. Another 2025 project, appropriately named AInstein , used machine learning to numerically solve Euclidean vacuum Einstein equations with a cosmological constant without making the usual symmetry assumptions. Neither project is trying to construct a time machine. That is not really the important part. What matters is the direction of progress: neural methods are beginning to represent and solve complicated geometries that are expensive to explore using conventional numerical techniques. AI is also getting better at discovering equations themselves. Symbolic-regression systems search huge spaces of mathematical expressions and try to recover compact physical laws from data. A recent Nature Computational Science study on parallel symbolic enumeration demonstrated substantial improvements in equation-recovery accuracy and computational efficiency across more than 200 synthetic and experimental problem sets. Now imagine extending this idea to spacetime. Instead of manually proposing one strange metric at a time, researchers could give an AI system a collection of constraints: Find a geometry that satisfies Einstein’s equations, avoids singularities, minimizes violations of energy conditions, remains stable under perturbations and exhibits a desired causal structure. The AI could search candidate geometries, eliminate inconsistent solutions, run numerical simulations and perhaps even derive symbolic descriptions of promising candidates. That would not prove that time travel is possible. But it could search the theoretical design space far faster than humans can today. Photo by NASA Hubble Space Telescope on Unsplash Didn’t a quantum computer already create a wormhole? This is one place where headlines have gotten somewhat ahead of the physics. In 2022, researchers used Google’s Sycamore quantum processor to study a quantum system whose behavior has a dual description resembling a traversable wormhole. The result, published in Nature , was important because it provided an experimental way to study ideas connecting quantum information and gravity. But nobody created a physical tunnel through spacetime. Caltech explicitly clarified that the experiment did not produce a rupture in physical spacetime. Instead, the processor implemented a quantum system whose dynamics could be interpreted through the mathematics of a theoretical wormhole. That distinction is important when discussing AI too. Simulating a wormhole, finding an equation describing one and physically constructing one are three very different achievements. The experiment is nevertheless fascinating because the deepest questions surrounding wormholes and time may require something we still do not possess: a complete, experimentally verified theory combining quantum mechanics with gravity. That is another area where AI might matter enormously. Could a superintelligent AI discover the missing trick? Possibly — if there is a trick to discover. I think discussions about AI and time travel often frame it as an engineering problem. Give a sufficiently intelligent model enough scientific literature, compute and laboratory access, and eventually it will design the machine. But there are two very different possibilities. In one universe, backward time travel is physically possible but hidden behind mathematics or engineering far beyond our current abilities. In that case, advanced AI could be transformative. It might discover completely new spacetime geometries, quantum states, materials or control strategies that humans would never think to test. But consider the other possibility. Perhaps backward time travel is prohibited by a deeper law of nature. Maybe quantum gravity enforces chronology protection. Maybe physically realizable matter can never generate the required geometry. Perhaps causality itself emerges as an unavoidable consistency condition of the universe. If that is true, no amount of intelligence changes the answer. An AI can find a solution that we overlooked, it cannot make an inconsistent universe consistent. This reminds me somewhat of computation itself. Better algorithms can turn previously impractical problems into tractable ones, sometimes spectacularly so. But intelligence does not automatically erase fundamental limits. It helps us explore the space permitted by the rules. So, are we close? As of September 2026, no — not in an engineering sense . We can measure relativistic time dilation with extraordinary precision. We can write mathematically consistent models containing closed timelike curves. We can simulate quantum systems related to wormhole physics. We can calculate how information would behave inside hypothetical retrocausal channels. And AI is rapidly becoming better at representing complicated physical systems, solving equations and discovering new mathematical relationships. What we cannot do is send matter, information or a person into their own past. Still, I would not dismiss the question. Black holes were once strange mathematical consequences of general relativity. Today, we observe their environments and measure gravitational waves produced when black holes collide. That history should make us careful about declaring every exotic mathematical solution physically irrelevant. But there is another lesson hidden in that history. Black holes did not become real because our computers became smarter. They became real because nature contained them. That is probably the most important distinction when thinking about AI and time travel. AI may eventually become the most powerful scientific search engine we have ever built. It could explore solutions to Einstein’s equations that humans would never think to try, uncover unexpected connections between quantum information and spacetime, and perhaps contribute to the theory that finally joins gravity with quantum mechanics. If a route to time travel exists somewhere inside the laws of physics, AI may dramatically improve our chances of finding it. But first, the universe has to have left the door open. AI Seems to do Everything Impossible. So Where Are We in Time Travel? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

At the same time, physics has never completely killed the idea of time travel. So it is tempting to combine the two trends and ask a very 2026 question:

Could AI help us build a time machine?

The short answer is that AI may become extremely useful in the search for new physics involving time, gravity and causality. But we are nowhere close to engineering the kind of time travel shown in movies. The biggest obstacle is not simply that the equations are too difficult for humans. We do not yet know whether nature permits the required physical conditions at all.

Still, the state of the art is much more interesting than a simple “no.”

Time travel already exists… in one direction

Before discussing wormholes, there is one misconception worth clearing up. Traveling into the future faster than somebody else is already allowed by established physics.

Special relativity tells us that a clock moving very quickly relative to another clock accumulates less elapsed time. General relativity adds another effect: clocks in stronger gravitational fields run more slowly. (Who hasn’t seen interstellar movie, right?)

These are measurable engineering effects, not philosophical ideas. Modern atomic clocks have measured gravitational time dilation across millimeter-scale height differences, and GPS requires relativistic corrections to remain accurate. If I could travel sufficiently close to the speed of light and later return to Earth, less time would have passed for me than for the people who stayed behind. In that limited sense, I would have traveled into their future.

The problem is scale. Accelerating a human-scale spacecraft to relativistic speed requires extraordinary energy. AI might optimize propulsion, trajectories and materials, but it cannot negotiate with the speed of light.

Going backward is where physics gets strange

Travel into the past is a completely different problem. General relativity describes gravity as the geometry of spacetime. Surprisingly, some mathematically valid spacetime geometries contain what physicists call closed timelike curves, or CTCs.

Roughly speaking, a CTC is a path that always moves locally forward through time but eventually returns to an earlier event. These are not just science-fiction inventions. CTCs arise in serious solutions of Einstein’s equations, including Gödel-type universes, idealized rotating spacetimes, wormhole constructions and some warp-drive geometries.

And research on them is still active.

In 2025, Achintya Sajeendran and Timothy Ralph published a Physical Review D paper constructing a controlled warp-drive spacetime in which a freely falling particle could follow a closed timelike curve and return to flat spacetime. Importantly, the authors explicitly noted the questionable physical realizability of the metric. In other words, the mathematics provides a time-machine-like geometry. That somewhat innocent-sounding statement hides one of the biggest problems in the entire subject. Many wormhole or time-machine proposals depend on exotic distributions of energy that we do not know how to create or sustain on useful scales.

There is also Stephen Hawking’s famous chronology protection conjecture: perhaps quantum effects prevent time machines from forming in the first place. The question remains unsettled. Work published in 2026 is still examining whether instabilities around chronology horizons could provide such a protection mechanism.

Then came a particularly interesting result in June 2026. Kaiyuan Ji, Seth Lloyd and Mark Wilde published a Physical Review Letters paper studying how much information could theoretically be sent backward through a noisy, postselected closed-timelike-curve channel. They derived information-theoretic limits for these hypothetical retrocausal channels.

That sounds spectacular, but the distinction is crucial. They did not send information into the past.

They studied what communication theory would look like if such a channel existed. That gap between “mathematically describable” and “physically constructible” is basically the entire time-travel problem.

So where does AI enter?

This is where the question becomes genuinely interesting to me as someone coming from computer science and AI. AI does not need to magically invent a time machine to change this field. Its immediate value is as a search and modeling engine.

Einstein’s field equations are nonlinear tensor differential equations, and interesting spacetime geometries occupy an enormous mathematical search space. Traditionally, physicists make simplifying assumptions, choose a form for the spacetime metric, solve the equations and then test whether the solution has sensible physical properties. AI gives us another possibility: searching and representing much larger spaces computationally.

We are already seeing early versions of this.

A 2025 project called Einstein Fields used neural representations to encode four-dimensional numerical-relativity simulations as implicit neural networks representing the spacetime metric. Another 2025 project, appropriately named AInstein, used machine learning to numerically solve Euclidean vacuum Einstein equations with a cosmological constant without making the usual symmetry assumptions.

Neither project is trying to construct a time machine. That is not really the important part. What matters is the direction of progress: neural methods are beginning to represent and solve complicated geometries that are expensive to explore using conventional numerical techniques.

AI is also getting better at discovering equations themselves.

Symbolic-regression systems search huge spaces of mathematical expressions and try to recover compact physical laws from data. A recent Nature Computational Science study on parallel symbolic enumeration demonstrated substantial improvements in equation-recovery accuracy and computational efficiency across more than 200 synthetic and experimental problem sets. Now imagine extending this idea to spacetime.

Instead of manually proposing one strange metric at a time, researchers could give an AI system a collection of constraints: Find a geometry that satisfies Einstein’s equations, avoids singularities, minimizes violations of energy conditions, remains stable under perturbations and exhibits a desired causal structure.

The AI could search candidate geometries, eliminate inconsistent solutions, run numerical simulations and perhaps even derive symbolic descriptions of promising candidates.

That would not prove that time travel is possible. But it could search the theoretical design space far faster than humans can today.

Photo by NASA Hubble Space Telescope on UnsplashDidn’t a quantum computer already create a wormhole?

This is one place where headlines have gotten somewhat ahead of the physics. The result, published in Nature, was important because it provided an experimental way to study ideas connecting quantum information and gravity.

But nobody created a physical tunnel through spacetime. Caltech explicitly clarified that the experiment did not produce a rupture in physical spacetime. Instead, the processor implemented a quantum system whose dynamics could be interpreted through the mathematics of a theoretical wormhole.

I think discussions about AI and time travel often frame it as an engineering problem. Give a sufficiently intelligent model enough scientific literature, compute and laboratory access, and eventually it will design the machine.

But there are two very different possibilities.

In one universe, backward time travel is physically possible but hidden behind mathematics or engineering far beyond our current abilities.

In that case, advanced AI could be transformative. It might discover completely new spacetime geometries, quantum states, materials or control strategies that humans would never think to test.

But consider the other possibility.

Perhaps backward time travel is prohibited by a deeper law of nature. Maybe quantum gravity enforces chronology protection. Maybe physically realizable matter can never generate the required geometry. Perhaps causality itself emerges as an unavoidable consistency condition of the universe.

So, are we close?

As of September 2026, no — not in an engineering sense.

We can measure relativistic time dilation with extraordinary precision.

We can write mathematically consistent models containing closed timelike curves.

We can simulate quantum systems related to wormhole physics.

And AI is rapidly becoming better at representing complicated physical systems, solving equations and discovering new mathematical relationships. What we cannot do is send matter, information or a person into their own past.

Still, I would not dismiss the question. Black holes were once strange mathematical consequences of general relativity. Today, we observe their environments and measure gravitational waves produced when black holes collide. That history should make us careful about declaring every exotic mathematical solution physically irrelevant.

But there is another lesson hidden in that history. Black holes did not become real because our computers became smarter. They became real because nature contained them. That is probably the most important distinction when thinking about AI and time travel.

AI may eventually become the most powerful scientific search engine we have ever built. It could explore solutions to Einstein’s equations that humans would never think to try, uncover unexpected connections between quantum information and spacetime, and perhaps contribute to the theory that finally joins gravity with quantum mechanics.

items.title: Story Points Stopped Working the Day AI Started Writing Code
items.summary: Why estimates now mispredict in both directions, and a framework that measures what actually constrains delivery A few sprints ago I sat in a planning session where the team spent twenty minutes debating whether a story was a 5 or an 8. It was a genuinely tricky piece of matching logic, the kind of story that would have earned its 8 points in any planning poker session over the last two decades. After the meeting, the developer pointed Claude at it and had a working implementation before lunch. The story still took four days to finish, not because the code was hard to write, but because the change touched three services, the diff was large enough that two of us had to review it carefully, and the testing needed a full regression run plus a security sign-off. The 8 points we argued about measured none of that. That planning session convinced me of something I had been suspecting for months: our estimates were not wrong, they were measuring something that no longer costs anything. Coding effort has become cheap, almost free, and yet our entire estimation system is still built around how hard the code is to write. This post is my attempt to work out what we should be estimating instead, and to propose a concrete framework you can run in your next sprint. Why story points worked for twenty years To see what broke, it helps to remember why story points worked in the first place. Classic agile estimation asks the team to size a story relative to other stories, usually on the Fibonacci scale of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Most of us were taught the mantra that points measure complexity rather than time. The real history is more interesting. Story points began on the first XP team as ideal days, literally time, multiplied by a load factor, and the time label was filed off only so that managers would stop hearing estimates as commitments ( Ron Jeffries has told that story himself ). Mike Cohn, whose book taught a generation of teams to estimate, spent years correcting the complexity myth : points estimate effort, and complexity matters only to the degree that it adds effort. His memorable example compares licking a thousand stamps with performing a simple brain surgery: wildly different complexity, similar time, same points. So whether your team practiced the folklore (complexity) or the canon (effort), the estimate tracked the same underlying thing, which was the work of building the software. Complexity became the everyday shorthand for one specific reason: writing the code was the dominant share of a story’s effort, so the harder the code, the bigger the story. A rough split of where that effort went looked like this. When coding is more than half the work, and complex code takes proportionally longer to write, complexity and effort rise and fall together. A 5-point story really did take more time than a 2-point story, because the thing that made it a 5 (trickier logic, more code) was exactly the thing that consumed the hours. The Fibonacci scale made sense too: implementation effort grows roughly exponentially with scope, so the gaps between the numbers widened as the stories grew. It is worth being honest about what the estimate never really counted, even then. Testing, review, and integration were real work in every sprint, but they entered the estimate only implicitly, folded silently into the coding effort: a complex story was assumed to need proportionally more testing, so nobody sized testing separately. Because coding dominated, that shortcut rarely hurt. Keep it in mind, though, because the shortcut is exactly what breaks next. The whole system rested on one quiet assumption: the expensive part of a story is writing the code. Nobody stated it, because for twenty years nobody needed to. Then AI rewrote the split Once your team is using Claude or a similar coding assistant seriously, that quiet assumption collapses. The code that took three days now takes an afternoon, and whether the logic is clever or boring barely changes the wall-clock time, because the AI generates fifty lines and five thousand lines at roughly the same speed. But nothing else about delivering the story got faster. A human still has to review the diff, and there is now more diff to review than ever. A human still has to test the behaviour, coordinate the rollout across services, and clarify what the story actually meant when the acceptance criteria turn out to be fuzzy. The effort didn’t disappear; it moved. The exact percentages will vary by team, and I should be clear that the splits above are illustrative rather than measured. But the direction is showing up in industry data at scale. Faros AI’s 2025 telemetry study of more than ten thousand developers across 1,255 teams found that developers with high AI adoption completed 21 percent more tasks and merged 98 percent more pull requests, while average PR size grew by 154 percent and review time grew by 91 percent (Antonio Pagano has a good discussion of the review-side findings ). Read those numbers together and the story is unmistakable: far more code is shipping, there is far more of it to read per change, and the hours available to read it have not grown at all. In my experience the review slice is the one that surprises teams the most. The more code the AI generates, the more a human has to read, and reading code you didn’t write is slow, careful work. A faster plane does not shorten the journey Here is a metaphor that captured it for me. Think about the last flight you took. The flight itself might have been an hour, but the journey was not. You reached the airport early, queued for check-in, queued again at security, waited at the gate, and on the other side waited for your baggage and then for a cab. Door to door, the one-hour flight cost you five. Now imagine the airline replaces the plane with a supersonic jet that does the hop in ten minutes. Almost nothing changes, because check-in, security, immigration, and baggage do not care how fast the plane is. Your five-hour journey becomes four hours and fifty minutes. And anyone who still estimates journeys by flight duration is now confidently wrong in both directions: the short international hop with two immigration queues takes far longer than its flight time suggests, while the long domestic flight with web check-in and hand luggage takes barely more than its flight time at all. AI is the supersonic jet, and coding is the flight. Story points estimate the flight, but the sprint pays for the journey. A story with a clever algorithm confined to one file gets a big number, but the AI finishes it in a day, so the team under-commits and sandbagging creeps in. A story with a trivial code change that spans four repositories and touches authentication gets a small number, but the review, the security sign-off, and the cross-team testing take a week, so the team over-commits and the sprint spills. Both errors come from the same root: the things that actually consume the sprint (testing, code review, cognitive load on the reviewer, integration effort, coordination between teams) appear nowhere in the estimate. And the Fibonacci scale quietly lost its justification along the way. The fine-grained ladder existed because implementation effort was decomposable and grew exponentially. The human work that remains does not follow that curve, and it resists fine decomposition. Debating 2 versus 3 is now noise dressed up as rigour. Estimate the work AI cannot eliminate So what should we estimate instead? The principle I have landed on is simple to state: Estimate the work AI cannot eliminate. AI has commoditised implementation, but it has not commoditised human judgment. What remains expensive is attention: clarifying intent, choosing between valid strategies, reviewing diffs, testing, and coordinating integration. That residual human attention is the scarce resource on an AI-assisted team, so that is what the estimate should measure. I call the approach Residual Attention Estimation, and it has five moving parts. The clearest way to see the proposal is to compare the question being asked, before and after. Classic points asked about the code, put all their weight on coding complexity, and let testing, review, and integration ride along uncounted. Residual attention asks about the humans instead: six drivers carry the estimate, coding complexity fades out as absorbed by AI, and the answer coarsens from a Fibonacci ladder to three honest sizes. Before the detail, here is the whole framework in one breath. Ambiguous stories get no estimate at all; they get gated back to refinement or into a timeboxed spike. Everything that passes the gate is sized S, M, or L on a single question about human attention rather than code complexity, and disagreements are settled by arguing over six concrete drivers rather than gut feel. Sprints are planned from net person-days and a trailing rate, with a WIP limit where the real constraint now sits: verification. Milestones are forecast from throughput history and reported as confidence levels rather than dates. And once the habit sticks, the AI itself pre-fills the whole assessment during refinement while humans audit it. That is the entire proposal. What follows is the detail of each part, and if the sketch is enough for you, feel free to jump to the adoption plan at the end. 1. A readiness gate instead of padded estimates Before any story gets a size, it must pass two questions. Are the acceptance criteria testable and agreed? And has the team converged on one implementation strategy? A useful operational test for the AI era: the story is ready when the AI could begin implementing it without asking a human another question. If a story fails the gate, it does not get a bigger number; it gets no number at all. Either it goes back for refinement, or it becomes a timeboxed spike of one to three days that answers the open question. Basecamp’s Shape Up calls this fixed budget an appetite, and the word captures the stance well: you decide what the exploration is worth instead of estimating how long discovery takes. This matters because letting ambiguity inflate estimates is how vague stories sneak into sprints. The right response to ambiguity is to resolve it; putting a number on it only hides it. 2. One question, three sizes For each ready story, the team answers a single question: how much focused human attention will this consume end to end, across review, testing, integration, and coordination? Everyone votes S, M, or L, and that is the whole ceremony. S (1 point): one repo, a small diff, existing tests cover it. The AI does nearly everything and a human skims and merges. M (3 points): a diff that needs a real review, new tests to write, or a second service touched. L (8 points): multiple repos or teams, regression or security sign-off, or a high-risk area like auth, payments, or a data migration. XL: not allowed. AI makes thin slicing cheap, so split it. If it seems inconsistent to bury the Fibonacci ladder and then assign 1, 3, and 8 points, the choice is deliberate. The capacity arithmetic later in this post needs sizes with nonlinear weights, because an L genuinely consumes several times the attention of an S, and reusing numbers your existing tooling and velocity charts already understand makes the migration free. What goes away is the fine-grained ladder and the debates between its adjacent rungs, not the idea that sizes should sit far apart. Just as deliberately, the sizes carry no day equivalents. How many days an M costs is a property of your team, of its combined experience and its familiarity with the system, so pinning sizes to durations would bake one team’s abilities into every team’s estimates. The trailing rate in the capacity math learns that conversion from your own sprints, which is exactly where it belongs. Notice what is missing from the question: how hard the code is to write. Algorithmic difficulty, boilerplate volume, and refactoring scale are all absorbed by the AI, so they no longer predict anything. So what does drive the size? Six things, and they are worth spelling out because they are the real content of the estimate. When votes split, the team does not average; it walks these drivers, and each strong answer pushes the size up one step. Review load. How large and how critical is the diff a human must actually read? Five hundred generated lines in a payments service are not five hundred lines of CRUD; the former gets read line by line, the latter gets skimmed. Cognitive load. How much system context must a reviewer hold in their head before they can trust the change? A 50-line edit to a payment service can be a three-hour review, because the reviewer has to reconstruct how retries, refunds, and reconciliation interact before approving anything. The cost lives in that context, and the line count barely hints at it. Blast radius. How many repos, services, and teams does the change touch? Every additional system multiplies the review conversations and the ways a deploy can go sideways. Test burden. Does existing automation already cover the change, do new automated tests need to be written, or does it demand manual, exploratory, or environment-dependent testing? Each step up that ladder is a real jump in human attention. Coordination. Does shipping require another team’s review, a contract change between services, or a release window? Calendar time spent waiting on other people is invisible to complexity but very visible in the sprint. Risk and irreversibility. Data migrations, public APIs, anything security-facing. What does it cost if this is wrong in production? A change you cannot easily roll back earns a slower, more careful verification pass, no matter how simple its code is. A feature toggle to enable disable the feature or to switch between alternative flows. “If someone says ‘I said L because it touches three repos and needs a security review’, you can argue with that and get to an answer. If they say ‘it feels bigger’, you cannot. So keep the rubric as a tiebreaker and a calibration tool. Nobody should be scoring six dimensions per story during planning poker.” The single attention question is the shortcut; the six drivers are what the shortcut compresses. An aside: how to think while estimating residual attention The greatest challenge in embracing this approach lies not in the process itself, but in overriding an ingrained habit. For twenty years, the voice in a developer’s head during planning asked one thing: how complex is this story? When a story comes up, instead of imagining yourself writing the code, imagine yourself shepherding the finished code to production, and ask: How much of the generated code will I actually have to read, and how carefully? How will we prove it works, and does that proof already exist as automation, or does someone have to build or run it? Who will I have to wait for? A reviewer, another team, a release window? items.summary_html:
Why estimates now mispredict in both directions, and a framework that measures what actually constrains delivery

A few sprints ago I sat in a planning session where the team spent twenty minutes debating whether a story was a 5 or an 8. It was a genuinely tricky piece of matching logic, the kind of story that would have earned its 8 points in any planning poker session over the last two decades. After the meeting, the developer pointed Claude at it and had a working implementation before lunch.

The story still took four days to finish, not because the code was hard to write, but because the change touched three services, the diff was large enough that two of us had to review it carefully, and the testing needed a full regression run plus a security sign-off. The 8 points we argued about measured none of that.

That planning session convinced me of something I had been suspecting for months: our estimates were not wrong, they were measuring something that no longer costs anything. Coding effort has become cheap, almost free, and yet our entire estimation system is still built around how hard the code is to write. This post is my attempt to work out what we should be estimating instead, and to propose a concrete framework you can run in your next sprint.

Why story points worked for twenty years

To see what broke, it helps to remember why story points worked in the first place.

Classic agile estimation asks the team to size a story relative to other stories, usually on the Fibonacci scale of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Most of us were taught the mantra that points measure complexity rather than time. The real history is more interesting. Story points began on the first XP team as ideal days, literally time, multiplied by a load factor, and the time label was filed off only so that managers would stop hearing estimates as commitments ( Ron Jeffries has told that story himself ). Mike Cohn, whose book taught a generation of teams to estimate, spent years correcting the complexity myth : points estimate effort, and complexity matters only to the degree that it adds effort. His memorable example compares licking a thousand stamps with performing a simple brain surgery: wildly different complexity, similar time, same points.

So whether your team practiced the folklore (complexity) or the canon (effort), the estimate tracked the same underlying thing, which was the work of building the software. Complexity became the everyday shorthand for one specific reason: writing the code was the dominant share of a story’s effort, so the harder the code, the bigger the story. A rough split of where that effort went looked like this.

When coding is more than half the work, and complex code takes proportionally longer to write, complexity and effort rise and fall together. A 5-point story really did take more time than a 2-point story, because the thing that made it a 5 (trickier logic, more code) was exactly the thing that consumed the hours. The Fibonacci scale made sense too: implementation effort grows roughly exponentially with scope, so the gaps between the numbers widened as the stories grew.

It is worth being honest about what the estimate never really counted, even then. Testing, review, and integration were real work in every sprint, but they entered the estimate only implicitly, folded silently into the coding effort: a complex story was assumed to need proportionally more testing, so nobody sized testing separately. Because coding dominated, that shortcut rarely hurt. Keep it in mind, though, because the shortcut is exactly what breaks next.

The whole system rested on one quiet assumption: the expensive part of a story is writing the code. Nobody stated it, because for twenty years nobody needed to.

Then AI rewrote the split

Once your team is using Claude or a similar coding assistant seriously, that quiet assumption collapses. The code that took three days now takes an afternoon, and whether the logic is clever or boring barely changes the wall-clock time, because the AI generates fifty lines and five thousand lines at roughly the same speed.

But nothing else about delivering the story got faster. A human still has to review the diff, and there is now more diff to review than ever. A human still has to test the behaviour, coordinate the rollout across services, and clarify what the story actually meant when the acceptance criteria turn out to be fuzzy. The effort didn’t disappear; it moved.

The exact percentages will vary by team, and I should be clear that the splits above are illustrative rather than measured. But the direction is showing up in industry data at scale. Faros AI’s 2025 telemetry study of more than ten thousand developers across 1,255 teams found that developers with high AI adoption completed 21 percent more tasks and merged 98 percent more pull requests, while average PR size grew by 154 percent and review time grew by 91 percent (Antonio Pagano has a good discussion of the review-side findings ). Read those numbers together and the story is unmistakable: far more code is shipping, there is far more of it to read per change, and the hours available to read it have not grown at all.

In my experience the review slice is the one that surprises teams the most. The more code the AI generates, the more a human has to read, and reading code you didn’t write is slow, careful work.

A faster plane does not shorten the journey

Here is a metaphor that captured it for me.

Think about the last flight you took. The flight itself might have been an hour, but the journey was not. You reached the airport early, queued for check-in, queued again at security, waited at the gate, and on the other side waited for your baggage and then for a cab. Door to door, the one-hour flight cost you five.

Now imagine the airline replaces the plane with a supersonic jet that does the hop in ten minutes. Almost nothing changes, because check-in, security, immigration, and baggage do not care how fast the plane is. Your five-hour journey becomes four hours and fifty minutes. And anyone who still estimates journeys by flight duration is now confidently wrong in both directions: the short international hop with two immigration queues takes far longer than its flight time suggests, while the long domestic flight with web check-in and hand luggage takes barely more than its flight time at all.

AI is the supersonic jet, and coding is the flight. Story points estimate the flight, but the sprint pays for the journey.

A story with a clever algorithm confined to one file gets a big number, but the AI finishes it in a day, so the team under-commits and sandbagging creeps in. A story with a trivial code change that spans four repositories and touches authentication gets a small number, but the review, the security sign-off, and the cross-team testing take a week, so the team over-commits and the sprint spills. Both errors come from the same root: the things that actually consume the sprint (testing, code review, cognitive load on the reviewer, integration effort, coordination between teams) appear nowhere in the estimate.

And the Fibonacci scale quietly lost its justification along the way. The fine-grained ladder existed because implementation effort was decomposable and grew exponentially. The human work that remains does not follow that curve, and it resists fine decomposition. Debating 2 versus 3 is now noise dressed up as rigour.

Estimate the work AI cannot eliminate

So what should we estimate instead? The principle I have landed on is simple to state:

Estimate the work AI cannot eliminate.

AI has commoditised implementation, but it has not commoditised human judgment. What remains expensive is attention: clarifying intent, choosing between valid strategies, reviewing diffs, testing, and coordinating integration. That residual human attention is the scarce resource on an AI-assisted team, so that is what the estimate should measure. I call the approach Residual Attention Estimation, and it has five moving parts.

The clearest way to see the proposal is to compare the question being asked, before and after.

Classic points asked about the code, put all their weight on coding complexity, and let testing, review, and integration ride along uncounted. Residual attention asks about the humans instead: six drivers carry the estimate, coding complexity fades out as absorbed by AI, and the answer coarsens from a Fibonacci ladder to three honest sizes.

Before the detail, here is the whole framework in one breath. Ambiguous stories get no estimate at all; they get gated back to refinement or into a timeboxed spike. Everything that passes the gate is sized S, M, or L on a single question about human attention rather than code complexity, and disagreements are settled by arguing over six concrete drivers rather than gut feel. Sprints are planned from net person-days and a trailing rate, with a WIP limit where the real constraint now sits: verification. Milestones are forecast from throughput history and reported as confidence levels rather than dates. And once the habit sticks, the AI itself pre-fills the whole assessment during refinement while humans audit it.

That is the entire proposal. What follows is the detail of each part, and if the sketch is enough for you, feel free to jump to the adoption plan at the end.

1. A readiness gate instead of padded estimates

Before any story gets a size, it must pass two questions. Are the acceptance criteria testable and agreed? And has the team converged on one implementation strategy? A useful operational test for the AI era: the story is ready when the AI could begin implementing it without asking a human another question.

If a story fails the gate, it does not get a bigger number; it gets no number at all. Either it goes back for refinement, or it becomes a timeboxed spike of one to three days that answers the open question. Basecamp’s Shape Up calls this fixed budget an appetite, and the word captures the stance well: you decide what the exploration is worth instead of estimating how long discovery takes. This matters because letting ambiguity inflate estimates is how vague stories sneak into sprints. The right response to ambiguity is to resolve it; putting a number on it only hides it.

2. One question, three sizes

For each ready story, the team answers a single question: how much focused human attention will this consume end to end, across review, testing, integration, and coordination? Everyone votes S, M, or L, and that is the whole ceremony.

  • S (1 point): one repo, a small diff, existing tests cover it. The AI does nearly everything and a human skims and merges.
  • M (3 points): a diff that needs a real review, new tests to write, or a second service touched.
  • L (8 points): multiple repos or teams, regression or security sign-off, or a high-risk area like auth, payments, or a data migration.
  • XL: not allowed. AI makes thin slicing cheap, so split it.

What goes away is the fine-grained ladder and the debates between its adjacent rungs, not the idea that sizes should sit far apart.

So what does drive the size? Six things, and they are worth spelling out because they are the real content of the estimate. When votes split, the team does not average; it walks these drivers, and each strong answer pushes the size up one step.

  • Review load. How large and how critical is the diff a human must actually read? Five hundred generated lines in a payments service are not five hundred lines of CRUD; the former gets read line by line, the latter gets skimmed.
  • Cognitive load. How much system context must a reviewer hold in their head before they can trust the change? A 50-line edit to a payment service can be a three-hour review, because the reviewer has to reconstruct how retries, refunds, and reconciliation interact before approving anything. The cost lives in that context, and the line count barely hints at it.
  • Blast radius. How many repos, services, and teams does the change touch? Every additional system multiplies the review conversations and the ways a deploy can go sideways.
  • Test burden. Does existing automation already cover the change, do new automated tests need to be written, or does it demand manual, exploratory, or environment-dependent testing? Each step up that ladder is a real jump in human attention.
  • Coordination. Does shipping require another team’s review, a contract change between services, or a release window? Calendar time spent waiting on other people is invisible to complexity but very visible in the sprint.
  • Risk and irreversibility. Data migrations, public APIs, anything security-facing. What does it cost if this is wrong in production? A change you cannot easily roll back earns a slower, more careful verification pass, no matter how simple its code is. A feature toggle to enable disable the feature or to switch between alternative flows.
